objectives.text: mobile devices and mobile computing platforms that process, store, or transmit CUI are identified.
encryption is employed to protect CUI on identified mobile devices and mobile computing platforms.

assessment.examine: Access control policy; procedures addressing access control for mobile devices; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; encryption mechanisms and associated configuration documentation; system security plan; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with access control responsibilities for mobile devices; system or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Encryption mechanisms protecting confidentiality of information on mobile devices

guidance.summary: Every laptop, tablet, or phone that can hold CUI must encrypt its storage (whole-disk or a managed encrypted container) so that a lost or stolen device does not expose CUI. Identify those devices first, then enforce and prove the encryption; for CMMC, use FIPS-validated methods such as BitLocker with FIPS mode or the vendor's validated mobile encryption.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop lists its five company laptops (engineering and sales) and three company phones as the mobile platforms that hold CUI. BitLocker with TPM and a PIN is enforced on the laptops through GPO/Intune with XTS-AES 256 and recovery keys escrowed to AD/Entra; the phones are enrolled in Intune with encryption required and a 6-digit passcode, and the Intune report shows all eight compliant. Personal devices are blocked from CUI entirely.
typical_evidence: Inventory of mobile devices and platforms that process or store CUI
GPO or Intune BitLocker policy screenshot and manage-bde -status or Intune encryption report for every laptop
Recovery key escrow evidence (AD or Entra BitLocker keys)
Intune compliance report showing mobile device encryption required and met
Documentation of FIPS 140 validation for the encryption used (Windows CMVP certificate, iOS/Android data protection)
common_gaps: Laptops have BitLocker available but it was never turned on, or it is on without a PIN so the drive unlocks at boot
USB drives and external disks holding CUI are unencrypted
No inventory, so a lost laptop cannot be assessed
remediation_steps: List every mobile device and platform that could hold CUI (laptops, tablets, phones, portable drives) with owner and location.

Enforce BitLocker on all laptops via GPO (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > BitLocker Drive Encryption) or Intune endpoint security: TPM + PIN, XTS-AES 256 for OS and fixed drives, recovery keys escrowed to AD/Entra, and 'System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms' enabled.
Require encryption and a passcode on phones and tablets through the Intune compliance policy and block non-compliant devices from Microsoft 365.
Encrypt any portable drives with BitLocker To Go or FIPS-validated hardware-encrypted drives, and block others by GPO.
Report on encryption status monthly (Intune report or a manage-bde script) and fix any device that shows unencrypted.

controls.name: External Connections
controls.statement: Verify and control/limit connections to and use of external systems.
controls.discussion: External systems are systems or components of systems for which organizations typically have no direct supervision and authority over the application of security requirements and controls or the determination of the effectiveness of implemented controls on those systems. External systems include personally owned systems, components, or devices and privately-owned computing and communications devices resident in commercial or public facilities. This requirement also addresses the use of external systems for the processing, storage, or transmission of CUI, including accessing cloud services (e.g., infrastructure as a service, platform as a service, or software as a service) from organizational systems. Organizations establish terms and conditions for the use of external systems in accordance with organizational security policies and procedures. Terms and conditions address as a minimum, the types of applications that can be accessed on organizational systems from external systems. Ifterms and conditions with the owners of external systems cannot be established, organizations may impose restrictions on organizational personnel using those external systems. This requirement recognizes that there are circumstances where individuals using external systems (e.g., contractors, coalition partners) need to access organizational systems. In those situations, organizations need confidence that the external systems contain the necessary controls so as not to compromise, damage, or otherwise harm organizational systems. Verification that the required controls have been effectively implemented can be achieved by third-party, independent assessments, attestations, or other means, depending on the assurance or confidence level required by organizations. Note that while “external” typically refers to outside of the organization’s direct supervision and authority, that is not always the case. Regarding the protection of CUI across an organization, the organization may have systems that process CUI and others that do not. And among the systems that process CUI there are likely access restrictions for CUI that apply between systems. Therefore, from the perspective of a given system, other systems within the organization may be considered “external" to that system.

objectives.text: connections to external systems are identified.
the use of external systems is identified.
connections to external systems are verified.
the use of external systems is verified.
connections to external systems are controlled/limited.
the use of external systems is controlled/limited.

assessment.examine: Access control policy; procedures addressing the use of external systems; terms and conditions for external systems; system security plan; list of applications accessible from external systems; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system connection or processing agreements; account management documents; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with responsibilities for defining terms and conditions for use of external systems to access organizational systems; system or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Mechanisms implementing terms and conditions on use of external systems

guidance.summary: Know every outside system the shop connects to or uses for CUI: cloud services (Microsoft 365 GCC High, customer portals, the ERP vendor's cloud), the MSP's tools, customer and supplier systems, and any personal or contractor devices. Verify that each meets your security expectations (contract terms, FedRAMP or DoD authorization, MSP attestation) and limit what can connect and how; anything unverified is not allowed to handle CUI.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop maintains a list of external systems: GCC High (FedRAMP High and DFARS 7012 support documented by Microsoft), the prime's supplier portal, DoD SAFE, the MSP's RMM and backup platform (covered by the MSP's shared responsibility matrix and attestation), and the machine builder's support connection. Personal devices are prohibited from connecting to the network or Microsoft 365, enforced through Conditional Access and 802.1X. The list is reviewed annually and each entry records how it was verified.
typical_evidence: External system inventory with purpose, CUI involvement, owner, and verification method
Contracts, FedRAMP/DoD authorization evidence, MSP attestation, or shared responsibility matrix for each external system
Policy prohibiting or limiting personal and contractor devices and unapproved cloud services
Firewall/web-filter rules and Conditional Access policies enforcing the limits
Annual review record of the external system list
common_gaps: CUI stored in commercial (non-GCC High) Microsoft 365, Dropbox, or Gmail without anyone realizing these are external systems
The MSP has full access but the shop has never asked what controls the MSP operates
Employees check email from home PCs with no restrictions
The shop cannot produce a list of external systems
remediation_steps: Build the external system inventory: cloud services, customer and supplier portals, MSP platforms, vendor remote access, personal or home devices, contractor systems; mark which carry CUI.

Verify each: for cloud services holding CUI, confirm FedRAMP Moderate-equivalent or DoD authorization and DFARS 7012 flow-down; for the MSP, obtain a written description of their controls or a shared responsibility matrix; for customers and suppliers, rely on the contract terms.
Write the policy: CUI only in the listed systems; personal devices may not connect to the network or Microsoft 365 for CUI; unapproved cloud storage is blocked.
Enforce it with firewall/web-filter blocks on unapproved services, Conditional Access requiring managed devices, and 802.1X or MAC control on the LAN and Wi-Fi.
Review the inventory and verification evidence annually and before adding any new service.

controls.name: Portable Storage Use
controls.statement: Limit use of portable storage devices on external systems.
controls.discussion: Limits on the use of organization-controlled portable storage devices in external systems include complete prohibition of the use of such devices or restrictions on how the devices may be used and under what conditions the devices may be used. Note that while “external” typically refers to outside of the organization’s direct supervision and authority, that is not always the case. Regarding the protection of CUI across an organization, the organization may have systems that process CUI and others that do not. Among the systems that process CUI there are likely access restrictions for CUI that apply between systems. Therefore, from the perspective of a given system, other systems within the organization may be considered “external" to that system.

objectives.text: the use of portable storage devices containing CUI on external systems is identified and documented.
limits on the use of portable storage devices containing CUI on external systems are defined.
the use of portable storage devices containing CUI on external systems is limited as defined.

assessment.examine: Access control policy; procedures addressing the use of external systems; system security plan; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system connection or processing agreements; account management documents; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with responsibilities for restricting or prohibiting use of organization-controlled storage devices on external systems; system or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Mechanisms implementing restrictions on use of portable storage devices

guidance.summary: Decide whether shop-owned USB drives and other portable storage that hold CUI may ever be plugged into systems the shop does not control (a customer's PC, a home computer, a machine builder's laptop). Document the answer and the limits, and enforce them, usually by prohibiting it entirely and blocking USB storage on managed PCs except for approved encrypted drives.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's policy prohibits using company USB drives containing CUI on any external system; the one documented exception is delivering CUI to a customer on a company-issued FIPS-validated hardware-encrypted drive that is checked out and back in on the media log. GPO blocks all removable storage on workstations except the two approved encrypted drive models on the engineering transfer PC, and CNC program transfers use the network DNC share instead of thumb drives.
typical_evidence: Media/portable storage policy stating the prohibition or the limited allowed uses on external systems
Media log showing issued encrypted drives and any use on external systems
GPO or Intune removable storage policy (deny read/write, or allow-list by device ID)
Inventory of approved encrypted USB drives
Training acknowledgement covering portable media rules
common_gaps: Operators carry G-code and drawings between the office and CNCs on personal thumb drives and take them home
No policy statement at all, so the objective 'identified and documented' is unmet even if nobody actually does it
USB blocked on office PCs but not on CNC controllers or the shipping PC
remediation_steps: Document the shop's position: identify whether portable storage with CUI is ever used on external systems (list the cases, for example customer deliveries or machine-builder service) and define the limits: only company-owned, encrypted, logged drives, and never on personal or unknown computers.
Deploy GPO/Intune 'Removable Storage Access' to deny all removable disks on workstations and CNC controllers, with an allow-list for approved encrypted drive hardware IDs on designated PCs.
Issue a small number of FIPS-validated encrypted USB drives, label them, and keep a check-out log.
Provide a network path (DNC share or SharePoint) for CNC program transfer so thumb drives are unnecessary on the floor.
Include the rule in annual training and spot-check USB device logs (Event ID 6416 or EDR device-control reports) quarterly.

controls.name: Control Public Information
controls.statement: Control CUI posted or processed on publicly accessible systems.
controls.discussion: In accordance with laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, or standards, the public is not authorized access to nonpublic information (e.g., information protected under the Privacy Act, CUI, and proprietary information). This requirement addresses systems that are controlled by the organization and accessible to the public, typically without identification or authentication. Individuals authorized to post CUI onto publicly accessible systems are designated. The content of information is reviewed prior to posting onto publicly accessible systems to ensure that nonpublic information is not included.

objectives.text: individuals authorized to post or process information on publicly accessible systems are identified.
procedures to ensure CUI is not posted or processed on publicly accessible systems are identified.
a review process is in place prior to posting of any content to publicly accessible systems.
content on publicly accessible systems is reviewed to ensure that it does not include CUI.
mechanisms are in place to remove and address improper posting of CUI.

assessment.examine: Access control policy; procedures addressing publicly accessible content; system security plan; list of users authorized to post publicly accessible content on organizational systems; training materials and/or records; records of publicly accessible information reviews; records of response to nonpublic information on public websites; system audit logs and records; security awareness training records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with responsibilities for managing publicly accessible information posted on organizational systems; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Mechanisms implementing management of publicly accessible content

guidance.summary: Only a few named people may post to the shop's website, social media, or other public-facing systems, and there must be a written check before anything goes up to make sure it contains no CUI (for example a photo of a part with a customer drawing visible in the background). If CUI is ever posted by mistake, there must be a procedure to take it down and report it.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's website and LinkedIn page can be updated only by the office manager and the owner. Before posting shop photos or capability statements, the poster completes a one-line checklist confirming no customer part numbers, drawings, or marked documents are visible, and the owner approves. The website content is reviewed quarterly, and the incident response plan includes steps to remove a post, contact the hosting vendor, and notify the customer and DoD if CUI was exposed.
typical_evidence: Policy naming authorized posters and the pre-posting review procedure
Completed review checklists or approval emails for recent posts
Quarterly review record of website and social content
Website CMS and social media admin user list
Incident response procedure section for removing improperly posted CUI
common_gaps: Anyone with the marketing login posts photos from the shop floor with parts and drawings visible
No review step exists because 'we never post CUI', which does not satisfy the objectives
No plan for takedown if something slips through
remediation_steps: Name the one or two authorized posters in policy and restrict website CMS and social media admin logins to them, with MFA.
Write a short pre-posting checklist: no marked CUI, no customer drawings, part numbers, or specs, no photos with drawings or travelers visible; require owner approval for shop-floor photos.
Keep the completed checklists or approval emails as the review record and review existing public content quarterly.
Add a takedown procedure to the incident response plan: remove the content immediately, request cache/CDN purge, assess whether CUI was exposed, and report through the DFARS 7012 process if required.
Cover the rule in annual awareness training.

controls.name: Role-Based Risk Awareness
controls.statement: Ensure that managers, systems administrators, and users of organizational systems are made aware of the security risks associated with their activities and of the applicable policies, standards, and procedures related to the security of those systems.
controls.discussion: Organizations determine the content and frequency of security awareness training and security awareness techniques based on the specific organizational requirements and the systems to which personnel have authorized access. The content includes a basic understanding of the need for information security and user actions to maintain security and to respond to suspected security incidents. The content also addresses awareness of the need for operations security. Security awareness techniques include: formal training; offering supplies inscribed with security reminders; generating email advisories or notices from organizational officials; displaying logon screen messages; displaying security awareness posters; and conducting information security awareness events.[SP 800-50] provides guidance on security awareness and training programs.

objectives.text: security risks associated with organizational activities involving CUI are identified.
policies, standards, and procedures related to the security of the system are identified.
managers, systems administrators, and users of the system are made aware of the security risks associated with their activities.
managers, systems administrators, and users of the system are made aware of the applicable policies, standards, and procedures related to the security of the system.

assessment.examine: Security awareness and training policy; procedures addressing security awareness training implementation; relevant codes of federal regulations; security awareness training curriculum; security awareness training materials; system security plan; training records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with responsibilities for security awareness training; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel composing the general system user community; personnel with responsibilities for role-based awareness training
assessment.test: Mechanisms managing security awareness training; mechanisms managing role-based security training

guidance.summary: Everyone who touches the systems, from the owner and managers to shop-floor users and the IT admin, must be made aware of the security risks of what they do with CUI (phishing, mishandling drawings, USB use, remote access) and of the shop's own security policies and procedures. That means identifying the risks and the relevant policies, delivering awareness training to all of them, and keeping records.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop delivers a 45-minute security awareness session at hire and annually, built from a short risk list (phishing, CUI marking and handling, USB and printing, remote work, visitors on the floor) and a walk-through of the shop's acceptable use, CUI handling, and incident reporting procedures. The owner and managers attend the same session plus a 10-minute add-on on their approval responsibilities; the IT person and the MSP's technicians complete it too. Sign-in sheets and quiz results are kept, and quarterly phishing simulations reinforce it.
typical_evidence: Training content (slides or module) showing the risks and policies covered
Written list of identified security risks for CUI activities and the policies and procedures referenced
Training completion records for all users, managers, and administrators, with dates
New-hire onboarding checklist with the training step
Phishing simulation results or awareness reminders (posters, emails)
common_gaps: Training was given once years ago and new hires never got it
The owner, managers, and the MSP skipped it because they are 'not users'
Generic vendor video with no mention of the shop's own CUI procedures or reporting process
remediation_steps: Write a one-page list of the shop's security risks involving CUI and the policies and procedures that address them (acceptable use, CUI handling, media, remote access, incident reporting).
Build or buy an awareness course and add a shop-specific section covering those risks and procedures; include a short quiz.
Deliver it to every user, manager, and administrator (including MSP staff who access your systems) within 30 days of hire and annually; track completion in a spreadsheet or LMS.
Reinforce quarterly with a phishing simulation or a short reminder, and post the incident reporting steps near the shop-floor PCs.
Review and update the content annually and after any incident.

controls.name: Role-Based Training
controls.statement: Ensure that personnel are trained to carry out their assigned information security-related duties and responsibilities.
controls.discussion: Organizations determine the content and frequency of security training based on the assigned duties, roles, and responsibilities of individuals and the security requirements of organizations and the systems to which personnel have authorized access. In addition, organizations provide system developers, enterprise architects, security architects, acquisition/procurement officials, software developers, system developers, systems integrators, system/network administrators, personnel conducting configuration management and auditing activities, personnel performing independent verification and validation, security assessors, and other personnel having access to system-level software, security-related technical training specifically tailored for their assigned duties. Comprehensive role-based training addresses management, operational, and technical roles and responsibilities covering physical, personnel, and technical controls. Such training can include policies, procedures, tools, and artifacts for the security roles defined. Organizations also provide the training necessary for individuals to carry out their responsibilities related to operations and supply chain security within the context of organizational information security programs.[SP 800-181] provides guidance on role-based information security training in the workplace. [SP 800-161] provides guidance on supply chain risk management.

objectives.text: information security-related duties, roles, and responsibilities are defined.
information security-related duties, roles, and responsibilities are assigned to designated personnel.
personnel are adequately trained to carry out their assigned information security-related duties, roles, and responsibilities.

assessment.examine: Security awareness and training policy; procedures addressing security training implementation; codes of federal regulations; security training curriculum; security training materials; system security plan; training records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with responsibilities for role-based security training; personnel with assigned system security roles and responsibilities; personnel with responsibilities for security awareness training; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel representing the general system user community
assessment.test: Mechanisms managing role-based security training; mechanisms managing security awareness training

guidance.summary: Define the security duties in the shop (system administration, log review, backup, incident response, CUI handling authority, physical security) and assign each to named people or the MSP. Then make sure those people have training specific to their duties, beyond the general awareness course, and keep proof of it.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's roles matrix names the IT person as system and security administrator, the MSP as log reviewer and backup operator, the owner as incident response lead and access approver, and the quality manager as CUI custodian. The IT person completed a Windows/Microsoft 365 security administration course and a CMMC practitioner class, the MSP provides certificates for its technicians, and the owner and quality manager completed a 2-hour incident response and CUI handling session. Records are kept with the awareness training records.
typical_evidence: Roles and responsibilities matrix for security duties with named personnel
Job descriptions or appointment letters referencing the security duties
Training certificates, course completions, or MSP staff qualifications tied to each role
Incident response tabletop exercise record for the IR team
Training plan listing required training per role and its frequency
common_gaps: Duties are informal; nobody is officially the log reviewer or the incident lead
The IT person is self-taught with no record of any role-based training
MSP qualifications are assumed but never documented
remediation_steps: Write the security roles matrix: administrator, log/audit reviewer, backup and restore, incident response lead and team, CUI custodian, physical security, training coordinator; assign each to a named person or the MSP and note backups.

Define the training each role needs (for example admin: Windows/Microsoft 365 security configuration and logging; IR lead: incident handling and DFARS 7012 reporting; CUI custodian: marking and handling) and the frequency.
Obtain the training: vendor courses, CMMC/NIST 800-171 practitioner classes, MSP certificates for their staff, and an annual incident response tabletop for the IR team.
Record completions with dates and keep certificates alongside the awareness records; refresh annually or when roles change.

controls.name: Insider Threat Awareness
controls.statement: Provide security awareness training on recognizing and reporting potential indicators of insider threat.
controls.discussion: Potential indicators and possible precursors of insider threat include behaviors such as: inordinate, long-term job dissatisfaction; attempts to gain access to information that is not required for job performance; unexplained access to financial resources; bullying or sexual harassment of fellow employees; workplace violence; and other serious violations of the policies, procedures, directives, rules, or practices of organizations. Security awareness training includes how to communicate employee and management concerns regarding potential indicators of insider threat through appropriate organizational channels in accordance with established organizational policies and procedures. Organizations may consider tailoring insider threat awareness topics to the role (e.g., training for managers may be focused on specific changes in behavior of team members, while training for employees may be focused on more general observations).

objectives.text: potential indicators associated with insider threats are identified.
security awareness training on recognizing and reporting potential indicators of insider threat is provided to managers and employees.

assessment.examine: Security awareness and training policy; procedures addressing security awareness training implementation; security awareness training curriculum; security awareness training materials; insider threat policy and procedures; system security plan; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel that participate in security awareness training; personnel with responsibilities for basic security awareness training; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Mechanisms managing insider threat training

guidance.summary: List the warning signs of a possible insider threat (someone trying to access data they do not need, unusual copying or downloading, working odd hours without reason, expressed grievances, unexplained wealth, repeated policy violations) and train managers and employees to recognize them and how to report concerns. This is usually a module inside the annual awareness training.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's awareness course includes a 10-minute insider threat module listing the indicators (unauthorized attempts to access drawings or the ERP, bulk USB copying, disgruntlement, contacts asking unusual questions about parts, sudden financial change) and explains that concerns go to the owner or the IT person confidentially. Managers get an extra slide on behavior changes to watch for on their teams. Completion is tracked with the annual training.
typical_evidence: Written list of insider threat indicators used in training
Training module content covering recognition and the reporting channel
Completion records for employees and managers
Reporting procedure (who to tell, how, confidentiality and non-retaliation)
common_gaps: Awareness training covers phishing only; insider threat is never mentioned
No defined reporting channel, so employees would not know who to tell
Managers receive the same content as employees with nothing about supervising behavior
remediation_steps: Adopt an indicator list (use CISA/DCSA insider threat indicators as a base) tailored to the shop: access attempts outside job need, mass copying or printing of drawings, after-hours anomalies, job dissatisfaction, unexplained foreign contacts or financial changes.
Add a module to the annual awareness training that covers the indicators and the reporting steps, with a short manager-specific section.
Define the reporting channel in policy (owner or IT, anonymously if desired) and state that reports are handled confidentially and without retaliation.
Track completion for all employees and managers and refresh the indicator list annually.

controls.name: System Auditing
controls.statement: Create and retain system audit logs and records to the extent needed to enable the monitoring, analysis, investigation, and reporting of unlawful or unauthorized system activity.
controls.discussion: An event is any observable occurrence in a system, which includes unlawful or unauthorized system activity. Organizations identify event types for which a logging functionality is needed as those events which are significant and relevant to the security of systems and the environments in which those systems operate to meet specific and ongoing auditing needs. Event types can include password changes, failed logons or failed accesses related to systems, administrative privilege usage, or third-party credential usage. In determining event types that require logging, organizations consider the monitoring and auditing appropriate for each of the CUI security requirements. Monitoring and auditing requirements can be balanced with other system needs. For example, organizations may determine that systems must have the capability to log every file access both successful and unsuccessful, but not activate that capability except for specific circumstances due to the potential burden on system performance. Audit records can be generated at various levels of abstraction, including at the packet level as information traverses the network. Selecting the appropriate level of abstraction is a critical aspect of an audit logging capability and can facilitate the identification of root causes to problems. Organizations consider in the definition of event types, the logging necessary to cover related events such as the steps in distributed, transaction-based processes (e.g., processes that are distributed across multiple organizations) and actions that occur in service-oriented or cloud-based architectures. Audit record content that may be necessary to satisfy this requirement includes time stamps, source and destination addresses, user or process identifiers, event descriptions, success or fail indications, filenames involved, and access control or flow control rules invoked. Event outcomes can include indicators of event success or failure and event-specific results (e.g., the security state of the system after the event occurred). Detailed information that organizations may consider in audit records includes full text recording of privileged commands or the individual identities of group account users. Organizations consider limiting the additional audit log information to only that information explicitly needed for specific audit requirements. This facilitates the use of audit trails and audit logs by not including information that could potentially be misleading or could make it more difficult to locate information of interest. Audit logs are reviewed and analyzed as often as needed to provide important information to organizations to facilitate risk-based decision making.[SP 800-92] provides guidance on security log management.

objectives.text: audit logs needed (i.e., event types to be logged) to enable the monitoring, analysis, investigation, and reporting of unlawful or unauthorized system activity are specified.
the content of audit records needed to support monitoring, analysis, investigation, and reporting of unlawful or unauthorized system activity is defined.
audit records are created (generated).
audit records, once created, contain the defined content.
retention requirements for audit records are defined.
audit records are retained as defined.

assessment.examine: Audit and accountability policy; procedures addressing auditable events; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; procedures addressing control of audit records; procedures addressing audit record generation; system audit logs and records; system auditable events; system incident reports; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with audit and accountability responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel with audit review, analysis and reporting responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Mechanisms implementing system audit logging

guidance.summary: Decide which events must be logged across your systems (logons and failures, account and privilege changes, policy changes, file access on CUI shares, firewall and VPN connections, Microsoft 365 activity), what each record must contain (timestamp, user, source, event type, outcome), and how long logs are kept. Then configure the systems to generate those logs with that content and retain them centrally for the defined period.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's logging standard lists the event types for Windows (Advanced Audit Policy: logon/logoff, account management, policy change, privilege use, object access on the CUI share), the firewall (VPN and denied traffic), and GCC High (unified audit log). Each record must include time, user, device or IP, event, and success or failure. Windows Event Forwarding sends all PC and server logs to the MSP's collector, the firewall sends syslog there, and everything is kept for 1 year (Microsoft 365 audit retention is also set to 1 year). A monthly check confirms all 27 endpoints are still reporting.
typical_evidence: Audit logging standard listing event types, required record content, and retention period per system
GPO Advanced Audit Policy export (auditpol /get /category:*) and SACL/object access settings on CUI folders
Log collector or SIEM configuration showing sources and the retention setting
Sample log records from a workstation, server, firewall, and Microsoft 365 showing the required fields
Microsoft 365 audit log retention policy screenshot
Monthly log source health report
common_gaps: Default Windows audit policy with a 20 MB Security log that overwrites itself in two days and no central collection
Firewall and VPN logs not kept at all; Microsoft 365 auditing never enabled
No written statement of what is logged or how long it is kept
CNC controllers and the standalone shipping PC excluded from logging
remediation_steps: Write the logging standard: event types per system, required content (timestamp, user or process, source device or IP, event description, outcome, object name where relevant), and retention (for example 90 days online, 1 year total).

Deploy Advanced Audit Policy by GPO (Account Logon, Account Management, Logon/Logoff, Policy Change, Privilege Use, System, and Object Access for file share and removable storage) and enable 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings'; add SACLs on CUI folders for write and delete.

Raise the Security log maximum size to 1 GB or more and set up central collection: Windows Event Forwarding to a collector or the MSP's SIEM agent, plus firewall/VPN syslog and the Microsoft 365 unified audit log or Sentinel connector.
Configure retention on the collector or SIEM to the defined period and confirm Microsoft 365 audit retention is at least 1 year.
Verify monthly that every asset (including CNC controllers and the file server) is sending logs and that samples contain the required fields; keep the check as evidence.

controls.name: User Accountability
controls.statement: Ensure that the actions of individual system users can be uniquely traced to those users, so they can be held accountable for their actions.
controls.discussion: This requirement ensures that the contents of the audit record include the information needed to link the audit event to the actions of an individual to the extent feasible. Organizations consider logging for traceability including results from monitoring of account usage, remote access, wireless connectivity, mobile device connection, communications at system boundaries, configuration settings, physical access, nonlocal maintenance, use of maintenance tools, temperature and humidity, equipment delivery and removal, system component inventory, use of mobile code, and use of Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP).

objectives.text: the content of the audit records needed to support the ability to uniquely trace users to their actions is defined.
audit records, once created, contain the defined content.

assessment.examine: Audit and accountability policy; procedures addressing audit records and event types; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; procedures addressing audit record generation; procedures addressing audit review, analysis, and reporting; reports of audit findings; system audit logs and records; system events; system incident reports; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with audit and accountability responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Mechanisms implementing system audit logging

guidance.summary: Audit records must let you tie an action to one specific person: every log entry for a security-relevant action needs the individual user account, not a shared login. Define which fields make that possible (user ID, device, timestamp, action) and make sure shared or generic accounts are eliminated or tightly controlled so the logs point to a real person.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop replaced the shared 'shopfloor' and 'cnc1' logins with individual accounts for each operator, and the two CNC controllers now log operators in with their own AD credentials. The logging standard requires the user name, device name, source IP, and timestamp in every logon, file access, and admin event, and a sample from the SIEM shows a drawing deletion traced to a named engineer at a specific PC and time.
typical_evidence: Logging standard section listing the fields required for traceability (user ID, device or IP, timestamp, action, outcome)
Account inventory showing no shared interactive accounts, or a documented compensating control for any that remain
Sample log records showing individual user IDs for logon, file access, and privileged actions
Screenshot of CNC/HMI or ERP login showing individual accounts
Sign-in sheet or checkout record for any unavoidable shared account
common_gaps: Shared logins on CNC controllers, the shipping PC, or the ERP, so logs show 'operator' for everyone
Service accounts used interactively by humans
Logs record events but omit the user or source, for example a firewall log with IPs but no VPN user mapping
remediation_steps: Define the traceability content in the logging standard: individual user ID, workstation or device and source IP, timestamp synchronized to the authoritative source, event or action, target object, and outcome.

Eliminate shared accounts: create individual AD accounts for shop-floor staff, enable per-operator login on CNC controllers or HMIs where the builder supports it, and per-user logins in the ERP and quoting software.

Where a shared account cannot be removed (some CNC HMIs), keep a physical or electronic sign-in log per shift and restrict the account so the log plus badge records still identify the person; document it in the SSP.
Ensure service accounts cannot log on interactively ('Deny log on locally') and that VPN logs include the user name.
Pull a sample of records quarterly and confirm each can be traced to one person; keep the sample.

controls.name: Event Review
controls.statement: Review and update logged events.
controls.discussion: The intent of this requirement is to periodically re-evaluate which logged events will continue to be included in the list of events to be logged. The event types that are logged by organizations may change over time. Reviewing and updating the set of logged event types periodically is necessary to ensure that the current set remains necessary and sufficient.

objectives.text: a process for determining when to review logged events is defined.
event types being logged are reviewed in accordance with the defined review process.
event types being logged are updated based on the review.

assessment.examine: Audit and accountability policy; procedures addressing audit records and event types; system security plan; list of organization-defined event types to be logged; reviewed and updated records of logged event types; system audit logs and records; system incident reports; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with audit and accountability responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting review and update of logged event types

guidance.summary: Periodically revisit the list of what you log (not the logs themselves) to decide whether it is still the right set: add events for new systems or threats, drop noise. Define when that review happens (for example annually and after any incident or major system change), do it, and record any changes made as a result.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's logging standard states that the logged event list is reviewed every 12 months by the IT person with the MSP, and also after an incident or when a new system is added. The most recent review record shows they added removable-storage events (Event ID 6416) and Entra Conditional Access failures after moving to GCC High, and removed a noisy firewall category. The updated GPO and SIEM rules are referenced in the record.
typical_evidence: Logging standard section defining the review trigger and frequency
Dated review record (meeting note or ticket) listing events considered, added, and removed
Version history of the logged-events list or the audit policy GPO
Change ticket showing the GPO or SIEM update made after the review
common_gaps: Audit policy was set once by the MSP and never revisited
Reviews happen informally with nothing written down
Confusing this with reviewing the logs; the objective is about reviewing the event list
remediation_steps: Add a clause to the logging standard: 'Logged event types are reviewed annually, after any security incident, and when a system is added or removed; the IT administrator and MSP perform the review and record it.'
Put the annual review on the calendar and use a simple template: current event list, changes in systems or threats, events to add or remove, resulting GPO/SIEM changes.
Implement any changes through the normal change process (update GPO/auditpol, SIEM sources) and reference the ticket in the review record.
Keep the review records for at least 3 years as evidence that the process runs.

controls.name: Audit Failure Alerting
controls.statement: Alert in the event of an audit logging process failure.
controls.discussion: Audit logging process failures include software and hardware errors, failures in the audit record capturing mechanisms, and audit record storage capacity being reached or exceeded. This requirement applies to each audit record data storage repository (i.e., distinct system component where audit records are stored), the total audit record storage capacity of organizations (i.e., all audit record data storage repositories combined), or both.

objectives.text: personnel or roles to be alerted in the event of an audit logging process failure are identified.
types of audit logging process failures for which alert will be generated are defined.
identified personnel or roles are alerted in the event of an audit logging process failure.

assessment.examine: Audit and accountability policy; procedures addressing response to audit logging processing failures; system design documentation; system security plan; system configuration settings and associated documentation; list of personnel to be notified in case of an audit logging processing failure; system incident reports; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with audit and accountability responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Mechanisms implementing system response to audit logging processing failures

guidance.summary: If logging stops working (a PC stops forwarding events, the log collector's disk fills, the firewall syslog breaks, the agent is disabled), someone must be told automatically. Define which failures generate an alert and who receives it, and configure the tools so the alert actually reaches those people.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's logging standard names the IT person and the MSP service desk as alert recipients and lists the failure types: an endpoint not sending logs for 24 hours, collector or SIEM storage above 80 percent, the SIEM agent or Windows Event Log service stopped, and the firewall syslog stream down. The MSP's SIEM sends email and ticket alerts for these, and a test in March (stopping the agent on a PC) produced the alert within the hour and is kept as evidence.
typical_evidence: Logging standard section listing failure types and the alert recipients
SIEM or log collector alert rule configuration screenshots (log source silent, disk threshold, service down)
Sample alert email or ticket and its resolution
Test record showing a simulated failure produced an alert
MSP SOW or runbook describing their alert handling
common_gaps: Logs are collected but nothing monitors whether they keep arriving; endpoints drop off silently
Windows Security log set to 'overwrite as needed' with no alert on log-full or storage issues
Alerts go to a mailbox nobody reads
remediation_steps: Define in the logging standard: failure types (source silent for more than 24 hours, agent or service stopped, storage above 80 percent or write errors, forwarding errors) and recipients (IT admin plus MSP service desk, with the owner as escalation).
Configure the SIEM or collector: a 'log source not reporting' rule per endpoint, a disk or storage threshold alert, and heartbeat monitoring of the SIEM agent through the RMM.
On Windows, set the Security log to a large size and alert on Event ID 1104 (log full), 1100 (event logging service shut down), and 4719 (audit policy changed).
Send alerts to a monitored channel (ticketing queue plus email) and confirm delivery to each named person.
Test twice a year by stopping the agent on one PC and keep the resulting alert as evidence.

controls.name: Audit Correlation
controls.statement: Correlate audit record review, analysis, and reporting processes for investigation and response to indications of unlawful, unauthorized, suspicious, or unusual activity.
controls.discussion: Correlating audit record review, analysis, and reporting processes helps to ensure that they do not operate independently, but rather collectively. Regarding the assessment of a given organizational system, the requirement is agnostic as to whether this correlation is applied at the system level or at the organization level across all systems.

objectives.text: audit record review, analysis, and reporting processes for investigation and response to indications of unlawful, unauthorized, suspicious, or unusual activity are defined.
defined audit record review, analysis, and reporting processes are correlated.

assessment.examine: Audit and accountability policy; procedures addressing audit record review, analysis, and reporting; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; procedures addressing investigation of and response to suspicious activities; system audit logs and records across different repositories; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with audit record review, analysis, and reporting responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting analysis and correlation of audit records; mechanisms integrating audit review, analysis and reporting

guidance.summary: Have a defined process for reviewing and analyzing logs and reporting suspicious findings, and make sure the review looks across sources together (workstation, server, firewall, VPN, Microsoft 365) rather than each in isolation, so that a VPN login from abroad can be matched with the file access that followed. A central log tool with cross-source searches and a documented weekly review usually satisfies this at a small shop.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The MSP's SIEM ingests Windows, firewall, VPN, and GCC High logs into one place, and the shop's procedure says the MSP reviews correlated alerts daily and the IT person reviews a weekly summary report. The report joins events by user and device across sources (for example failed VPN logins followed by a successful login and CUI share access). Findings are ticketed and, if suspicious, handed to the incident response process; the weekly sign-off sheet is kept.
typical_evidence: Audit review, analysis, and reporting procedure describing frequency, who performs it, and what is looked for
SIEM or log tool showing all sources in one searchable system with correlation rules or dashboards
Weekly or monthly review reports and sign-offs
Tickets showing an anomaly investigated across sources and the outcome
Reference from the review procedure to the incident response plan
common_gaps: Logs sit in separate places (each PC, the firewall, Microsoft 365) and are only looked at after a problem
Review is 'the MSP watches it' with no documented process or evidence
No connection between a review finding and the incident response plan
remediation_steps: Write the review, analysis, and reporting procedure: the MSP or IT reviews correlated alerts daily and produces a weekly summary; the IT person and owner review monthly; suspicious findings go to the incident response process.

Centralize all log sources (see 3.3.1) in one SIEM or collector and enable correlation rules or saved searches that join by user, device, and IP: failed then successful logons, new admin then policy change, foreign VPN login then file access, USB write after CUI access.
Create a weekly report or dashboard from those searches and a sign-off record.
Reference the incident response plan in the procedure and ticket every escalation so the trail from log to response exists.
Tune the rules quarterly based on what produced noise or was missed.

controls.name: Reduction & Reporting
controls.statement: Provide audit record reduction and report generation to support on-demand analysis and reporting.
controls.discussion: Audit record reduction is a process that manipulates collected audit information and organizes such information in a summary format that is more meaningful to analysts. Audit record reduction and report generation capabilities do not always emanate from the same system or organizational entities conducting auditing activities. Audit record reduction capability can include, for example, modern data mining techniques with advanced data filters to identify anomalous behavior in audit records. The report generation capability provided by the system can help generate customizable reports. Time ordering of audit records can be a significant issue if the granularity of the time stamp in the record is insufficient.

objectives.text: an audit record reduction capability that supports on-demand analysis is provided.
a report generation capability that supports on-demand reporting is provided.

assessment.examine: Audit and accountability policy; procedures addressing audit record reduction and report generation; system design documentation; system security plan; system configuration settings and associated documentation; audit record reduction, review, analysis, and reporting tools; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with audit record reduction and report generation responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Audit record reduction and report generation capability

guidance.summary: You need a tool that can filter, search, and summarize the raw logs on demand (all logons by this user last week; all failed logons; all files deleted on the CUI share) and produce reports from them, without altering the original records. A SIEM, a log collector with a search interface, or scripted PowerShell queries against a collector plus Microsoft 365 audit search can meet this.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The MSP's SIEM lets the IT person filter all collected logs by user, device, event ID, and time and export the result as a PDF or CSV report; GCC High's audit log search does the same for cloud activity. During a customer questionnaire the IT person produced, in ten minutes, a report of everyone who accessed a specific drawing folder in the past 90 days. The original logs remain untouched in the collector.
typical_evidence: SIEM or log tool screenshots of the search/filter interface and saved queries
Sample generated reports (failed logons last 30 days, privileged activity, CUI share access)
Microsoft 365 audit log search screenshot or exported report
Procedure describing how to run on-demand reports and who can
common_gaps: Logs exist only on each PC; answering 'who accessed this folder' means visiting 25 machines
The MSP has a tool but the shop cannot request or produce reports on demand
Reduction is done by deleting or editing logs rather than filtering copies
remediation_steps: Ensure all logs are centralized (see 3.3.1) in a tool with search, filter, and export: the MSP's SIEM, Microsoft Sentinel, a Windows Event Collector with PowerShell queries, or an open-source log server.
Build four to six saved searches and reports: failed logons, account and group changes, privileged actions, CUI share access and deletions, VPN/remote sessions, removable media use.
Confirm reports can be generated on demand by the IT person (not only the MSP) and document the steps.
Use Microsoft 365 audit log search or Purview for cloud activity reports and keep an example export.
Run and file at least one of each report during the weekly or monthly review to show the capability works.

controls.name: Authoritative Time Source
controls.statement: Provide a system capability that compares and synchronizes internal system clocks with an authoritative source to generate time stamps for audit records.
controls.discussion: Internal system clocks are used to generate time stamps, which include date and time. Time is expressed in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), a modern continuation of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), or local time with an offset from UTC. The granularity of time measurements refers to the degree of synchronization between system clocks and reference clocks, for example, clocks synchronizing within hundreds of milliseconds or within tens of milliseconds. Organizations may define different time granularities for different system components. Time service can also be critical to other security capabilities such as access control and identification and authentication, depending on the nature of the mechanisms used to support those capabilities. This requirement provides uniformity of time stamps for systems with multiple system clocks and systems connected over a network. See [IETF 5905].

objectives.text: internal system clocks are used to generate time stamps for audit records.
an authoritative source with which to compare and synchronize internal system clocks is specified.
internal system clocks used to generate time stamps for audit records are compared to and synchronized with the specified authoritative time source.

assessment.examine: Audit and accountability policy; procedures addressing time stamp generation; system design documentation; system security plan; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Mechanisms implementing time stamp generation; mechanisms implementing internal information system clock synchronization

guidance.summary: All systems that write logs must stamp them from their own clock, and those clocks must be kept in sync with a named authoritative time source (such as NIST or the domain controller synced to it) so events from different systems can be lined up. Name the source, configure everything to sync to it, and check that they stay in sync.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's standard names time.nist.gov (with pool.ntp.org as fallback) as the authoritative source. The PDC emulator domain controller syncs to it via w32tm, all domain-joined PCs and the CNC controllers sync from the domain hierarchy, and the firewall and switches point at the same NTP servers. Logs are stamped in UTC with the local offset shown in the SIEM. The IT person runs w32tm /monitor quarterly and keeps the output showing all hosts within 1 second.
typical_evidence: Standard naming the authoritative time source and the sync hierarchy
w32tm /query /status and /configuration output from the PDC emulator
Firewall, switch, and non-domain device NTP settings screenshots
w32tm /monitor output or a SIEM clock-drift report showing hosts within tolerance
Sample log records from different sources with consistent timestamps
common_gaps: PDC emulator left on defaults with the hypervisor host pushing a different time, causing drift
Firewall or CNC controllers on their own clocks, off by minutes
Nobody has ever checked for drift
remediation_steps: Specify the authoritative source in the logging standard (for example NIST time.nist.gov or the ISP's stratum-1 NTP) and the hierarchy: PDC emulator to domain members; firewall, switches, APs, and non-domain devices to the same NTP servers.

Configure the PDC emulator: w32tm /config /manualpeerlist:"time.nist.gov,0x8 pool.ntp.org,0x8" /syncfromflags:manual /reliable:yes /update; disable Hyper-V or VMware time sync on the DC virtual machine.
Confirm domain members use NT5DS (domain hierarchy) via the GPO Windows Time Service settings; set NTP on the firewall, switches, wireless controller, CNC controllers, and any standalone PC.
Have the SIEM normalize to UTC and alert on sources with drift over 5 minutes.
Check quarterly with w32tm /monitor and a spot check of firewall and CNC clocks; record the results.

controls.name: Audit Protection
controls.statement: Protect audit information and audit logging tools from unauthorized access, modification, and deletion.
controls.discussion: Audit information includes all information (e.g., audit records, audit log settings, and audit reports) needed to successfully audit system activity. Audit logging tools are those programs and devices used to conduct audit and logging activities. This requirement focuses on the technical protection of audit information and limits the ability to access and execute audit logging tools to authorized individuals. Physical protection of audit information is addressed by media protection and physical and environmental protection requirements.

objectives.text: audit information is protected from unauthorized access.
audit information is protected from unauthorized modification.
audit information is protected from unauthorized deletion.
audit logging tools are protected from unauthorized access.
audit logging tools are protected from unauthorized modification.
audit logging tools are protected from unauthorized deletion.

assessment.examine: Audit and accountability policy; access control policy and procedures; procedures addressing protection of audit information; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation, system audit logs and records; audit logging tools; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with audit and accountability responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Mechanisms implementing audit information protection

guidance.summary: Logs, log settings and reports, and the tools that collect and manage them must be protected so that only authorized people can read, change, or delete them. Normal users must not be able to clear the Security log or reach the log server; the central copy must be tightly permissioned and backed up; and the SIEM or collector console must require its own admin authentication.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Local Security logs on the 25 PCs are readable only by administrators and are forwarded within minutes to the MSP's collector, so clearing a local log does not remove the evidence. The collector stores logs on a server only the MSP's SIEM admins can access, with 1-year retention on immutable storage and daily backups. Event ID 1102 (log cleared) triggers an alert. The SIEM console requires MFA and only three named accounts have access, and audit policy GPOs can be edited only by the audit-admin group.
typical_evidence: Permission listing on the log server or collector storage and SIEM roles showing limited access
GPO user right 'Manage auditing and security log' restricted to Administrators or log admins
SIEM or collector settings showing immutability or retention lock and backup configuration
Alert rule and sample for Event ID 1102/1104 (log cleared or full) and 4719 (audit policy changed)
Log forwarding configuration showing a near-real-time copy off the endpoint
Change records for audit configuration changes
common_gaps: Logs stored only on the endpoints where a local admin (or malware) can clear them
Log server share is open to Domain Users, or the SIEM console has a shared password
No backups of logs; a ransomware event would erase the evidence
remediation_steps: Forward logs off every endpoint within minutes (WEF or SIEM agent) so the authoritative copy is central.

Restrict access on the collector: OS-level permissions to a small log-admin group, SIEM role-based access with MFA, no shared accounts; separate the SIEM admin role from general domain admin where possible (see 3.3.9).

Protect integrity: enable the SIEM's tamper-evident or immutable storage or retention lock, back up the log store daily to an isolated location, and alert on 1102 (log cleared), 1104, 4719 (audit policy changed), and SIEM configuration changes.
Set the GPO user right 'Manage auditing and security log' to Administrators only and keep 'Access this computer from the network' on the log server restricted.
Review log-admin access and the alert rules quarterly.

controls.name: Audit Management
controls.statement: Limit management of audit logging functionality to a subset of privileged users.
controls.discussion: Individuals with privileged access to a system and who are also the subject of an audit by that system, may affect the reliability of audit information by inhibiting audit logging activities or modifying audit records. This requirement specifies that privileged access be further defined between audit-related privileges and other privileges, thus limiting the users with audit-related privileges.

objectives.text: a subset of privileged users granted access to manage audit logging functionality is defined.
management of audit logging functionality is limited to the defined subset of privileged users.

assessment.examine: Audit and accountability policy; access control policy and procedures; procedures addressing protection of audit information; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; access authorizations; system-generated list of privileged users with access to management of audit logging functionality; access control list; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with audit and accountability responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Mechanisms managing access to audit logging functionality

guidance.summary: Not every admin should be able to change what is logged, turn logging off, or manage the log collector. Name the small subset of privileged users who may manage audit logging (typically the MSP's SIEM admins plus, at most, the shop's IT person as backup) and configure the systems so only they can.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's policy defines the audit-management subset as the two named MSP SIEM administrators; the shop's IT person is a read-only SIEM user and cannot change collection rules or retention. Audit policy settings live in a separate GPO whose edit permission is delegated to an 'Audit-Admins' AD group containing only those two MSP accounts, and the firewall's logging configuration is limited to the same people through a dedicated admin profile.
typical_evidence: Policy or SSP statement naming the audit-management subset
AD group membership export for the audit-admin group
GPO delegation screenshot showing who can edit the audit policy GPO
SIEM or collector role assignments showing admin vs. read-only users
Firewall or switch admin profiles limiting logging configuration
common_gaps: Every Domain Admin can change audit policy and delete collected logs; no subset is defined
The one IT person is both the subject of the logs and the only person who can manage them, with no MSP or owner separation
SIEM users all share the built-in admin account
remediation_steps: Define the subset in policy: for example two named MSP SIEM administrators as audit managers with the IT person read-only; document it in the SSP with the separation of duties matrix (3.1.4).

Create an Audit-Admins AD group with only those accounts; move audit settings into a dedicated GPO and delegate edit rights only to that group; remove other admins' 'Manage auditing and security log' right.
In the SIEM or collector, create named accounts with role-based access: admin role for the subset, read/report role for everyone else; disable the shared admin login.
Apply the same on the firewall and other log sources with per-user admin profiles.
Review the subset membership quarterly and after staffing changes.

controls.name: System Baselining
controls.statement: Establish and maintain baseline configurations and inventories of organizational systems (including hardware, software, firmware, and documentation) throughout the respective system development life cycles.
controls.discussion: Baseline configurations are documented, formally reviewed, and agreed-upon specifications for systems or configuration items within those systems. Baseline configurations serve as a basis for future builds, releases, and changes to systems. Baseline configurations include information about system components (e.g., standard software packages installed on workstations, notebook computers, servers, network components, or mobile devices; current version numbers and update and patch information on operating systems and applications; and configuration settings and parameters), network topology, and the logical placement of those components within the system architecture. Baseline configurations of systems also reflect the current enterprise architecture. Maintaining effective baseline configurations requires creating new baselines as organizational systems change over time. Baseline configuration maintenance includes reviewing and updating the baseline configuration when changes are made based on security risks and deviations from the established baseline configurationOrganizations can implement centralized system component inventories that include components from multiple organizational systems. In such situations, organizations ensure that the resulting inventories include system-specific information required for proper component accountability (e.g., system association, system owner). Information deemed necessary for effective accountability of system components includes hardware inventory specifications, software license information, software version numbers, component owners, and for networked components or devices, machine names and network addresses. Inventory specifications include manufacturer, device type, model, serial number, and physical location.[SP 800-128] provides guidance on security-focused configuration management.

objectives.text: a baseline configuration is established.
the baseline configuration includes hardware, software, firmware, and documentation.
the baseline configuration is maintained (reviewed and updated) throughout the system development life cycle.
a system inventory is established.
the system inventory includes hardware, software, firmware, and documentation.
the inventory is maintained (reviewed and updated) throughout the system development life cycle.

assessment.examine: Configuration management policy; procedures addressing the baseline configuration of the system; procedures addressing system inventory; system security plan; configuration management plan; system inventory records; inventory review and update records; enterprise architecture documentation; system design documentation; system architecture and configuration documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; change control records; system component installation records; system component removal records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with configuration management responsibilities; personnel with responsibilities for establishing the system inventory; personnel with responsibilities for updating the system inventory; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for managing baseline configurations; mechanisms supporting configuration control of the baseline configuration; organizational processes for developing and documenting an inventory of system components; organizational processes for updating inventory of system components; mechanisms supporting or implementing the system inventory; mechanisms implementing updating of the system inventory

guidance.summary: You need a written, agreed-upon 'known good' build for each type of system in the CUI environment (OS version, installed software and versions, firmware, and the security settings applied) plus a complete inventory of the hardware, software and firmware that make up that environment, together with the documentation that goes with them (as-built notes, network diagram). Both the baseline and the inventory must be kept current: reviewed on a schedule and updated whenever something changes, not written once for the assessment and forgotten.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The IT admin keeps a 'Standard Workstation Build v3' document: Windows 11 Pro 23H2, Microsoft 365 apps, the CAD/CAM package, the ERP client, the EDR agent, the list of hardening GPOs applied, and local admin removed. A second document covers the two CNC controllers (Windows 10 IoT LTSC, controller software version, no browser, USB blocked) and a third covers the firewall and switches (model, firmware, config backup location). The MSP's RMM tool exports the hardware/software inventory (hostname, serial, model, OS build, installed applications, BIOS version) monthly, and the admin reviews it against the baseline every quarter, recording any drift and the fix in a ticket.
typical_evidence: Baseline configuration document per system type (workstation, server or GCC High tenant, CNC controller, firewall/switch) with version, date and management approval
Hardware/software inventory export from the RMM, Intune or AD showing hostname, serial, make/model, OS build, installed software, BIOS/firmware version, owner and location
Firewall and switch configuration backups with firmware version and export date
Quarterly inventory/baseline review records (ticket, dated checklist or meeting note) showing additions, removals and drift corrected
Change ticket showing the baseline was updated after a change (for example a new CAD/CAM version)
Current network diagram showing where each component sits
common_gaps: The inventory lives in someone's head or an old spreadsheet that does not match what the RMM reports
CNC controllers, printers, the firewall and switches are left out because 'they are not computers'
A baseline was written once for the assessment and never reviewed; new PCs are built from a different image than the document describes
Firmware/BIOS versions and documentation (as-built notes, network diagram) are missing from the inventory
remediation_steps: Define the CUI system boundary and list every asset class inside it: workstations, laptops, file server or GCC High tenant, CNC controllers, firewall, switches, Wi-Fi access points, printers/scanners and MSP-managed tools.

Pull a complete inventory from the RMM/Intune/AD (hostname, serial, make/model, OS build, installed software, BIOS/firmware version, owner, location, IP/MAC), reconcile it with a physical walk-through of the office and shop floor, and fix discrepancies.

Write a baseline configuration document per system type: OS version, approved software list with versions, GPO/Intune baseline names applied, disabled services and features, local accounts, required agents; attach as-built documentation and the network diagram, and have the owner approve it.
Build new PCs only from the baseline (golden image or Autopilot/Intune profile) and record any deviation as an approved exception in the baseline document.
Create a recurring task (at least quarterly and after any significant change) to re-export the inventory, compare it to the baseline, update both documents and keep the dated review record.
Keep configuration backups of the firewall and switches with firmware versions and refresh them whenever firmware or rules change.

controls.name: Security Configuration Enforcement
controls.statement: Establish and enforce security configuration settings for information technology products employed in organizational systems.
controls.discussion: Configuration settings are the set of parameters that can be changed in hardware, software, or firmware components of the system that affect the security posture or functionality of the system. Information technology products for which security-related configuration settings can be defined include mainframe computers, servers, workstations, input and output devices (e.g., scanners, copiers, and printers), network components (e.g., firewalls, routers, gateways, voice and data switches, wireless access points, network appliances, sensors), operating systems, middleware, and applications. Security parameters are those parameters impacting the security state of systems including the parameters required to satisfy other security requirements. Security parameters include: registry settings; account, file, directory permission settings; and settings for functions, ports, protocols, and remote connections. Organizations establish organization-wide configuration settings and subsequently derive specific configuration settings for systems. The established settings become part of the systems configuration baseline. Common secure configurations (also referred to as security configuration checklists, lockdown and hardening guides, security reference guides, security technical implementation guides) provide recognized, standardized, and established benchmarks that stipulate secure configuration settings for specific information technology platforms/products and instructions for configuring those system components to meet operational requirements. Common secure configurations can be developed by a variety of organizations including information technology product developers, manufacturers, vendors, consortia, academia, industry, federal agencies, and other organizations in the public and private sectors.[SP 800-70] and [SP 800-128] provide guidance on security configuration settings.

objectives.text: security configuration settings for information technology products employed in the system are established and included in the baseline configuration.
security configuration settings for information technology products employed in the system are enforced.
