assessment.examine: Configuration management policy; baseline configuration; procedures addressing configuration settings for the system; configuration management plan; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; security configuration checklists; evidence supporting approved deviations from established configuration settings; change control records; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with security configuration management responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for managing configuration settings; mechanisms that implement, monitor, and/or control system configuration settings; mechanisms that identify and/or document deviations from established configuration settings; processes for managing baseline configurations; mechanisms supporting configuration control of baseline configurations

guidance.summary: Beyond documenting the build, you must choose the specific security settings for each product in scope (password policy, screen lock, host firewall, disabled legacy protocols, USB restrictions, audit logging, encryption, and so on), write them into the baseline, and then enforce them with technology so they stay applied on every device. Hardening guides such as the CIS Benchmarks, Microsoft Security Baselines or DISA STIGs are the normal starting point, and you need a way to prove the settings are actually in place.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop adopts a written Windows hardening standard derived from the Microsoft Security Baseline / CIS Level 1: screen lock at 15 minutes, Windows Firewall on for all profiles, SMBv1 and LLMNR disabled, BitLocker required, PowerShell script block logging on, and USB mass storage blocked except two approved drives. The settings are pushed by GPO on the domain (or Intune configuration and security baseline profiles in GCC High). The MSP runs the compliance report monthly showing all 25 PCs, the server and both CNC controllers compliant, and the firewall is checked quarterly against the vendor's hardening checklist (management interface restricted to the admin VLAN, default account removed, logging enabled).
typical_evidence: Security configuration standard/checklist per platform (Windows workstation, server, firewall, M365 GCC High tenant, CNC controller) that names the benchmark used and lists each adopted setting
GPO reports (gpresult /h or Group Policy Management Console HTML export) or Intune configuration/security baseline profile screenshots showing the settings and their assignments
Intune compliance report, RMM policy-drift report, or CIS-CAT/vulnerability scanner configuration audit showing pass/fail per device
Firewall configuration export showing hardening items (admin access restricted, default credentials changed, logging on)
GCC High tenant settings screenshots (security defaults or Conditional Access, legacy authentication blocked)
Exception register for devices that cannot meet a setting (for example a CNC controller) with the compensating control and approval
common_gaps: Settings are 'recommended' in a policy document but never pushed by GPO or Intune, and PCs drift because users have local admin
CNC controllers and the firewall are excluded from any hardening standard
There is no way to prove enforcement: no compliance report, no periodic configuration scan
Default vendor credentials are still present on switches, printers or controller software
remediation_steps: Choose a benchmark per platform (CIS Benchmark Level 1 or Microsoft Security Baseline for Windows 10/11 and Server; the vendor hardening guide for the firewall and switches; Microsoft guidance for the GCC High tenant) and document which settings you adopt, with a justification for any you skip.

Implement the settings with GPO (on-prem domain) or Intune configuration and security baseline profiles (GCC High): screen lock, host firewall, SMBv1/LLMNR/NetBIOS off, BitLocker, audit policy, removable media control, and PowerShell logging.

For the CNC controllers, apply what the machine vendor supports (host firewall, disabled services, no browser, AutoRun off) and record the remainder as an approved exception with compensating controls such as VLAN isolation.

Turn on an enforcement check: Intune compliance policies, RMM policy-drift alerts, or a monthly CIS-CAT or vulnerability-scanner configuration audit; set a remediation deadline (for example 30 days) for non-compliant devices.
Remove local administrator rights from standard users so the settings cannot be undone, then review the compliance report monthly and keep each report as evidence.
Update the baseline document from 3.4.1 whenever the security settings change so the two stay in sync.

controls.name: System Change Management
controls.statement: Track, review, approve or disapprove, and log changes to organizational systems.
controls.discussion: Tracking, reviewing, approving/disapproving, and logging changes is called configuration change control. Configuration change control for organizational systems involves the systematic proposal, justification, implementation, testing, review, and disposition of changes to the systems, including system upgrades and modifications. Configuration change control includes changes to baseline configurations for components and configuration items of systems, changes to configuration settings for information technology products (e.g., operating systems, applications, firewalls, routers, and mobile devices), unscheduled and unauthorized changes, and changes to remediate vulnerabilities. Processes for managing configuration changes to systems include Configuration Control Boards or Change Advisory Boards that review and approve proposed changes to systems. For new development systems or systems undergoing major upgrades, organizations consider including representatives from development organizations on the Configuration Control Boards or Change Advisory Boards. Audit logs of changes include activities before and after changes are made to organizational systems and the activities required to implement such changes.[SP 800-128] provides guidance on configuration change control.

objectives.text: changes to the system are tracked.
changes to the system are reviewed.
changes to the system are approved or disapproved.
changes to the system are logged.

assessment.examine: Configuration management policy; procedures addressing system configuration change control; configuration management plan; system architecture and configuration documentation; system security plan; change control records; system audit logs and records; change control audit and review reports; agenda/minutes from configuration change control oversight meetings; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with configuration change control responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; members of change control board or similar
assessment.test: Organizational processes for configuration change control; mechanisms that implement configuration change control

guidance.summary: Every change to in-scope systems (new or upgraded software, firmware updates, firewall rules, GPO or Intune changes, new servers or devices) has to be requested and tracked, reviewed by someone, explicitly approved or rejected, and logged with what was done and when. A simple ticket-based process is enough; the point is that changes do not happen ad hoc and there is a record an assessor can follow.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop uses the MSP's ticketing system as its change log. When the CAM vendor releases a new version, the admin opens a 'Change' ticket describing the change, the PCs affected, the security impact and the rollback plan; the owner (or the admin, as the named approver for routine changes) approves inside the ticket; the MSP deploys it; the ticket is closed with the completion date. Firewall rule changes and CNC controller software updates follow the same path, and the firewall's own configuration change log is exported monthly to cross-check.
typical_evidence: Change management procedure defining what counts as a change, change types (standard, normal, emergency), who approves each type and the required ticket fields
Sample change tickets showing request, review notes, approval or rejection with approver name and date, implementation date and outcome
Change log or ticket export for the last 12 months
Firewall configuration audit log and AD GPO version history that reconcile with the tickets
Approved list of standard/pre-approved changes (for example monthly OS patching) with its approval
common_gaps: The MSP or admin makes changes with no record; the only history is memory ('we updated that last spring')
Approval is verbal, so there is no approve/disapprove record
Patches, firewall rule edits and CNC controller software updates are treated as 'not a change'
A ticketing system exists but changes are logged after the fact with no review step
remediation_steps: Write a one-page change procedure: definitions (standard/pre-approved, normal, emergency), the approver for each type, and required fields (description, systems affected, security impact per 3.4.4, rollback, schedule, tester).
Configure a 'Change' ticket type in the ticketing or RMM tool with those fields and a mandatory approval step; a ticket cannot be closed without an approver name and date.

Agree in writing with the MSP that every change to in-scope systems (patch batches, firewall, GPO/Intune, server, CNC controller software) goes through this process, and give the MSP access to submit tickets.
Pre-approve routine changes (monthly OS and third-party patches, AV/EDR definition updates) through a documented standard-change list so the process stays workable.
Review the change log monthly, cross-check it against the firewall audit log and GPO/Intune change history, and record that review.

controls.name: Security Impact Analysis
controls.statement: Analyze the security impact of changes prior to implementation.
controls.discussion: Organizational personnel with information security responsibilities (e.g., system administrators, system security officers, system security managers, and systems security engineers) conduct security impact analyses. Individuals conducting security impact analyses possess the necessary skills and technical expertise to analyze the changes to systems and the associated security ramifications. Security impact analysis may include reviewing security plans to understand security requirements and reviewing system design documentation to understand the implementation of controls and how specific changes might affect the controls. Security impact analyses may also include risk assessments to better understand the impact of the changes and to determine if additional controls are required.[SP 800-128] provides guidance on configuration change control and security impact analysis.

objectives.text: the security impact of changes to the system is analyzed prior to implementation.

assessment.examine: Configuration management policy; procedures addressing security impact analysis for system changes; configuration management plan; security impact analysis documentation; system security plan; analysis tools and associated outputs; change control records; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with responsibility for conducting security impact analysis; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for security impact analysis

guidance.summary: Before a change is made, someone with enough technical knowledge has to think through and write down how it affects security: does it open ports or services, weaken a hardening setting, add a new path for CUI, create new accounts or privileges, or break an existing control? The analysis must happen before approval and implementation; a few specific sentences in the change ticket are sufficient.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's change ticket template has a mandatory 'Security impact analysis' field. When the shop wants to add a remote-support tool for the CNC vendor, the admin writes that it introduces inbound remote access, so it must require MFA and session logging (3.7.5), be limited to the CNC VLAN, and be disabled between sessions; the owner approves on that basis. For the monthly patch batch the field reads 'vendor security patches, no configuration changes, tested on two pilot PCs for 3 days before general deployment'.
typical_evidence: Change procedure stating that a security impact analysis is required before approval
Change tickets with a completed security impact section, including at least one where the analysis led to added controls or a rejection
Pilot/test results for significant changes (for example patches tested on a pilot group before broad deployment)
Updated SSP, baseline or network diagram when a change altered the boundary or a control
common_gaps: Change tickets exist but have no security impact field, or it always says 'N/A'
The analysis is done by the MSP without the shop seeing it, or is written after the change is already live
Nobody with security knowledge is involved; the owner approves with no technical review
remediation_steps: Add a required 'Security impact analysis' field to the change ticket with prompts: new ports/protocols/services? new accounts or privileges? effect on encryption, logging, MFA or the hardening baseline? new CUI flow or boundary change? rollback plan?
Name who performs the analysis (IT admin and/or the MSP engineer) and require the approver to read it before approving.
For significant changes, test on a pilot device or during a maintenance window and record the results in the ticket before broad rollout.
When the analysis shows a control or the boundary is affected, update the SSP, the baseline (3.4.1) and the network diagram as part of closing the ticket.
Spot-check a sample of closed tickets each quarter to confirm the analysis is specific and not boilerplate.

controls.name: Access Restrictions for Change
controls.statement: Define, document, approve, and enforce physical and logical access restrictions associated with changes to organizational systems.
controls.discussion: Any changes to the hardware, software, or firmware components of systems can potentially have significant effects on the overall security of the systems. Therefore, organizations permit only qualified and authorized individuals to access systems for purposes of initiating changes, including upgrades and modifications. Access restrictions for change also include software libraries. Access restrictions include physical and logical access control requirements, workflow automation, media libraries, abstract layers (e.g., changes implemented into external interfaces rather than directly into systems), and change windows (e.g., changes occur only during certain specified times). In addition to security concerns, commonly-accepted due diligence for configuration management includes access restrictions as an essential part in ensuring the ability to effectively manage the configuration.[SP 800-128] provides guidance on configuration change control.

objectives.text: physical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are defined.
physical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are documented.
physical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are approved.
physical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are enforced.
logical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are defined.
logical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are documented.
logical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are approved.
logical access restrictions associated with changes to the system are enforced.

assessment.examine: Configuration management policy; procedures addressing access restrictions for changes to the system; system security plan; configuration management plan; system design documentation; system architecture and configuration documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; logical access approvals; physical access approvals; access credentials; change control records; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with logical access control responsibilities; personnel with physical access control responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for managing access restrictions associated with changes to the system; mechanisms supporting, implementing, and enforcing access restrictions associated with changes to the system

guidance.summary: Only specific, authorized people may make changes to in-scope systems, and that must be true both physically (who can get to the server, firewall and CNC controller cabinets) and logically (who holds admin rights on PCs, the domain or tenant, the firewall and the controllers). You must define those restrictions, document them, have management approve them, and enforce them with locks, access lists and permission settings.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's configuration management policy states that only the IT admin and two named MSP engineers may hold Domain Admin, Entra/Intune administrator and firewall administrator roles; all other employees are standard users; CNC operators have no administrative rights on the controllers. The server and firewall sit in a locked closet whose keys are held by the admin and the owner, and the controller PC cabinets are keyed. The admin exports privileged group membership monthly, and the MSP's named engineer list is reviewed whenever MSP staff change.
typical_evidence: Policy or procedure section defining who may make physical and logical changes to each system class, signed or approved by management
Privileged group membership exports (Domain Admins, local Administrators, Entra/Intune admin roles, firewall and switch admin accounts) with review dates and initials
Key or badge holder list for the server closet and controller cabinets; photos showing the locked rack or closet
MSP contract or roster naming the authorized engineers and their access
Logs showing administrative logins to the firewall, server or tenant tied to change tickets
common_gaps: Everyone, or all shop leads, has local admin so anyone can install or change things
The MSP uses a shared generic admin account with no named individuals
The server or firewall sits in an unlocked office or on a shelf on the shop floor
Restrictions exist in practice but were never written down or approved
remediation_steps: Write into the configuration management (or access control) policy the roles allowed to change each system class (workstations, server/tenant, network gear, CNC controllers), including physical locations and who holds keys, and have the owner approve it.

Enforce logically: remove local admin from users, give the admin and each MSP engineer a separate named admin account, limit Domain Admins/Entra Global Administrator to those accounts, restrict firewall and switch management to a management VLAN or IP allow-list, and require MFA for all admin roles.
Enforce physically: lock the server/firewall closet and controller cabinets, keep a key/badge holder list, and log vendor visits.
Review privileged group membership and key holders at least quarterly and on any staff or MSP change; keep the export with reviewer initials.
Enable logging of administrative actions (firewall admin log, Windows Security log for group changes, Entra audit log) so enforcement can be demonstrated.

controls.name: Least Functionality
controls.statement: Employ the principle of least functionality by configuring organizational systems to provide only essential capabilities.
controls.discussion: Systems can provide a wide variety of functions and services. Some of the functions and services routinely provided by default, may not be necessary to support essential organizational missions, functions, or operations. It is sometimes convenient to provide multiple services from single system components. However, doing so increases risk over limiting the services provided by any one component. Where feasible, organizations limit component functionality to a single function per component. Organizations review functions and services provided by systems or components of systems, to determine which functions and services are candidates for elimination. Organizations disable unused or unnecessary physical and logical ports and protocols to prevent unauthorized connection of devices, transfer of information, and tunneling. Organizations can utilize network scanning tools, intrusion detection and prevention systems, and end-point protections such as firewalls and host-based intrusion detection systems to identify and prevent the use of prohibited functions, ports, protocols, and services.

objectives.text: essential system capabilities are defined based on the principle of least functionality.
the system is configured to provide only the defined essential capabilities.

assessment.examine: Configuration management policy; configuration management plan; procedures addressing least functionality in the system; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; security configuration checklists; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with security configuration management responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes prohibiting or restricting functions, ports, protocols, or services; mechanisms implementing restrictions or prohibition of functions, ports, protocols, or services

guidance.summary: Decide what each type of system actually needs to do (its essential capabilities) and configure it to do only that: remove or disable unneeded software, Windows features, server roles, services and network functions. This is a documented decision per system type followed by configuration that matches it, and it applies to the CNC controllers and the firewall as much as to the office PCs.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's baseline defines a workstation's essential capabilities as office productivity, CAD/CAM, the ERP client and browsing to approved business sites; the file server only runs file services, Active Directory and backup; the CNC controllers run only the machine control software and receive part programs from a restricted share. Accordingly, workstations have no media, gaming or remote-desktop-host features, IIS, Telnet and SMBv1 are not installed, the server has only the required roles, and the controllers have Internet access blocked at the firewall and unused Windows features removed.
typical_evidence: Baseline documents listing essential capabilities and functions per system type and what has been removed or disabled
Export of installed Windows optional features and server roles (Get-WindowsOptionalFeature, Get-WindowsFeature or Server Manager screenshot)
Services list export showing unnecessary services disabled
Firewall rule set restricting the CNC VLAN and server to required destinations only
Vulnerability or configuration scan output showing no unnecessary services listening
common_gaps: No written definition of what is essential; systems are left on vendor defaults
CNC controllers with full Internet access and a browser because operators like to look things up
The file server doubles as a workstation, print server and Wi-Fi controller
Unneeded Windows optional features (SMBv1, Telnet client, Remote Assistance, media features) left enabled
remediation_steps: For each system type, write a short list of essential capabilities (business functions, required software, required services and protocols) in the baseline document; anything not listed is nonessential by definition.

On workstations, remove unneeded applications, disable optional features (SMBv1, Telnet, TFTP, Remote Assistance, Windows Media features, XPS viewer) via GPO/Intune or DISM, and set unneeded services to Disabled.
On the server and tenant, keep only required roles and services; on the firewall, disable unused services (UPnP, unused VPN types, WAN-side administration, unused SSIDs).
On the CNC controllers, remove browsers and media software where the machine vendor allows, block Internet egress at the firewall, and restrict inbound access to the part-program share only.
Verify quarterly with a feature/service export or vulnerability scan, compare against the essential list, and fix drift through a change ticket.

controls.name: Nonessential Functionality
controls.statement: Restrict, disable, or prevent the use of nonessential programs, functions, ports, protocols, and services.
controls.discussion: Restricting the use of nonessential software (programs) includes restricting the roles allowed to approve program execution; prohibiting auto-execute; program blacklisting and whitelisting; or restricting the number of program instances executed at the same time. The organization makes a security-based determination which functions, ports, protocols, and/or services are restricted. Bluetooth, File Transfer Protocol (FTP), and peer-to-peer networking are examples of protocols organizations consider preventing the use of, restricting, or disabling.

objectives.text: essential programs are defined.
the use of nonessential programs is defined.
the use of nonessential programs is restricted, disabled, or prevented as defined.
essential functions are defined.
the use of nonessential functions is defined.
the use of nonessential functions is restricted, disabled, or prevented as defined.
essential ports are defined.
the use of nonessential ports is defined.
the use of nonessential ports is restricted, disabled, or prevented as defined.
essential protocols are defined.
the use of nonessential protocols is defined.
the use of nonessential protocols is restricted, disabled, or prevented as defined.
essential services are defined.
the use of nonessential services is defined.
the use of nonessential services is restricted, disabled, or prevented as defined.

assessment.examine: Configuration management policy; procedures addressing least functionality in the system; configuration management plan; system security plan; system design documentation; security configuration checklists; system configuration settings and associated documentation; specifications for preventing software program execution; documented reviews of programs, functions, ports, protocols, and/or services; change control records; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with responsibilities for reviewing programs, functions, ports, protocols, and services on the system; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Organizational processes for reviewing and disabling nonessential programs, functions, ports, protocols, or services; mechanisms implementing review and handling of nonessential programs, functions, ports, protocols, or services; organizational processes preventing program execution on the system; organizational processes for software program usage and restrictions; mechanisms supporting or implementing software program usage and restrictions; mechanisms preventing program execution on the system

guidance.summary: This builds on 3.4.6 by requiring you to spell out, for each of programs, functions, ports, protocols and services, which ones are essential and which are not, and then to restrict, disable or block the nonessential ones on the endpoints and at the network. Assessors expect a written list (a ports/protocols/services table plus an approved software list) and proof, such as firewall rules, GPO settings and scan results, that the restrictions are really in place.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop keeps a one-page PPS table: inbound to the file server, SMB 445 from the workstation and CNC VLANs and RDP 3389 from the admin's PC only; outbound, HTTPS 443, DNS to the firewall and NTP; everything else denied. FTP, Telnet, SMBv1, LLMNR, NetBIOS and Bluetooth file transfer are listed as prohibited and disabled by GPO. The approved software list names the CAD/CAM, ERP, Microsoft 365 and EDR packages, and AppLocker blocks anything else. The firewall rule set and a quarterly Nmap scan of each VLAN confirm only the listed ports respond, and the scan report is filed with the PPS table.
typical_evidence: Ports/protocols/services (PPS) table listing essential and prohibited items per system type or VLAN with business justification
Approved software list and the list of prohibited software categories
Firewall rule export matching the PPS table, and the Windows Firewall GPO or Intune profile export
GPO/Intune settings disabling SMBv1, LLMNR, NetBIOS over TCP/IP, AutoRun/AutoPlay, Bluetooth and unused services
Network scan results (Nmap or vulnerability scanner) showing only expected ports open, with the reconciliation notes
AppLocker/WDAC or EDR application-control policy export
common_gaps: Firewall still carries 'any/any' inbound or outbound rules from an old vendor setup
No written list, so the shop cannot say which ports and services are essential
Legacy protocols (FTP to CNC controllers, SMBv1 for an old controller) still in use with no documented, mitigated exception
AutoRun and USB unrestricted on shop-floor PCs
remediation_steps: Build the PPS table: for each VLAN and system type, list the required programs, functions, ports, protocols and services with a business justification, mark everything else nonessential/prohibited, have it approved and reference it from the SSP.
Enforce at the network: rewrite firewall rules to default-deny between VLANs and outbound, allowing only the listed ports, and put the CNC controllers on their own VLAN separate from office PCs.
Enforce on endpoints with GPO/Intune: disable SMBv1, LLMNR, NetBIOS over TCP/IP, WPAD, AutoRun/AutoPlay, Bluetooth and unused services; enable Windows Firewall with inbound blocked by default.
Restrict programs: publish the approved software list and enforce it with AppLocker/WDAC or EDR application control (3.4.8), and prevent user installs (3.4.9).
Where an old controller genuinely needs a legacy protocol such as FTP, document the exception, confine it to a dedicated VLAN and host pair, and set a retirement date.
Scan each VLAN quarterly and after network changes, reconcile the results against the PPS table, and log any fixes.

controls.name: Application Execution Policy
controls.statement: Apply deny-by-exception (blacklisting) policy to prevent the use of unauthorized software or deny-all, permit-by-exception (whitelisting) policy to allow the execution of authorized software.
controls.discussion: The process used to identify software programs that are not authorized to execute on systems is commonly referred to as blacklisting. The process used to identify software programs that are authorized to execute on systems is commonly referred to as whitelisting. Whitelisting is the stronger of the two policies for restricting software program execution. In addition to whitelisting, organizations consider verifying the integrity of whitelisted software programs using, for example, cryptographic checksums, digital signatures, or hash functions. Verification of whitelisted software can occur either prior to execution or at system startup.[SP 800-167] provides guidance on application whitelisting.

objectives.text: a policy specifying whether whitelisting or blacklisting is to be implemented is specified.
the software allowed to execute under whitelisting or denied use under blacklisting is specified.
whitelisting to allow the execution of authorized software or blacklisting to prevent the use of unauthorized software is implemented as specified.

assessment.examine: Configuration management policy; procedures addressing least functionality in the system; system security plan; configuration management plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; list of software programs not authorized to execute on the system; list of software programs authorized to execute on the system; security configuration checklists; review and update records associated with list of authorized or unauthorized software programs; change control records; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with responsibilities for identifying software authorized or not authorized to execute on the system; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational process for identifying, reviewing, and updating programs authorized or not authorized to execute on the system; process for implementing blacklisting or whitelisting; mechanisms supporting or implementing blacklisting or whitelisting

guidance.summary: You must decide in writing whether you use an allow-list (only approved software may run) or a deny-list (specific software is blocked), list the software covered, and enforce that decision technically on the systems. Allow-listing is the stronger approach and what assessors generally expect on workstations; relying on antivirus signatures alone as a 'deny-list' is a weak answer.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's policy states that workstations, the server and the CNC controllers use an allow-list: only software in the approved software inventory may execute. The admin enforces it with AppLocker (or WDAC) rules pushed by GPO: publisher rules for Microsoft, the CAD/CAM and ERP vendors and the EDR agent, path rules for Program Files, and a default block for anything in user-writable folders such as Downloads and AppData. AppLocker block events (Event ID 8004) are forwarded to the log collector, and the admin reviews them monthly before adding any new rule through the change process.
typical_evidence: Application execution policy stating the allow-list or deny-list approach and its scope
Approved software list (the allow-list) or the blocked-software list, with version and date
AppLocker/WDAC policy export (XML) or EDR application-control policy screenshot, plus the GPO/Intune assignment showing which devices receive it
Screenshot of a blocked execution attempt and the matching event log entry
Monthly review of block events and exception requests processed through change tickets
common_gaps: The policy says 'whitelisting' but only antivirus is deployed, which is deny-listing at best
AppLocker or WDAC left in audit-only mode indefinitely
Allow-list rules written so broadly (for example all of C:\) that anything runs
CNC controllers and the server excluded from the policy
remediation_steps: Write the policy: state allow-listing (recommended) for workstations, server and CNC controllers, name the approved software inventory as the allow-list, and define how new software is added (change ticket with security impact analysis).

Build the allow-list from the software inventory (3.4.1) and generate AppLocker or WDAC rules (publisher rules preferred, path rules for Program Files and Windows) covering executables, DLLs, scripts, installers and packaged apps.
Run in audit mode for 2-4 weeks, review the AppLocker 8003/8004 events, fix false blocks, then switch to enforce and record the enforcement date.
Deploy the policy by GPO or Intune to every in-scope Windows device, including the CNC controllers after testing with the machine vendor.
Forward block events to central logging, review them monthly, and process additions through change management.
If a system class must use a deny-list, document why, list exactly what is blocked, and add compensating controls (no local admin, EDR with behavioral blocking).

controls.name: User-Installed Software
controls.statement: Control and monitor user-installed software.
controls.discussion: Users can install software in organizational systems if provided the necessary privileges. To maintain control over the software installed, organizations identify permitted and prohibited actions regarding software installation through policies. Permitted software installations include updates and security patches to existing software and applications from organization-approved “app stores.” Prohibited software installations may include software with unknown or suspect pedigrees or software that organizations consider potentially malicious. The policies organizations select governing user-installed software may be organization-developed or provided by some external entity. Policy enforcement methods include procedural methods, automated methods, or both.

objectives.text: a policy for controlling the installation of software by users is established.
installation of software by users is controlled based on the established policy.
installation of software by users is monitored.

assessment.examine: Configuration management policy; procedures addressing user installed software; configuration management plan; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; list of rules governing user-installed software; system monitoring records; system audit logs and records; continuous monitoring strategy; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with responsibilities for governing user-installed software; personnel operating, using, or maintaining the system; personnel monitoring compliance with user-installed software policy; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes governing user-installed software on the system; mechanisms enforcing rules or methods for governing the installation of software by users; mechanisms monitoring policy compliance

guidance.summary: Have a written rule on what software users may install (usually none, except from approved sources), technically enforce it so users cannot install arbitrary programs or browser extensions, and monitor what actually gets installed so violations are caught. It works hand in hand with removing local admin rights and with the allow-list in 3.4.8.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The acceptable use policy says employees may not install software or browser extensions; requests go to IT by ticket. All users are standard users with no local admin, the Microsoft Store is restricted, and installers launched from Downloads are blocked by AppLocker. The MSP's RMM emails a weekly 'new software detected' report; the admin compares it with the approved list and files the review. A shop lead's portable PDF tool copied from a USB stick was caught this way, removed, and the incident noted in the ticket.
typical_evidence: Acceptable use or software installation policy with user acknowledgement records
Report showing standard users are not members of the local Administrators group on any PC
GPO/Intune settings restricting installs (AppLocker installer and script rules, Windows Installer restrictions, Store restrictions, browser extension policy)
Weekly or monthly RMM/Intune 'newly installed software' report with the reviewer's notes
Tickets showing software requests, approvals and denials
common_gaps: Users kept as local admins so CAD/CAM add-ons 'just work'
A policy exists but nothing enforces it and nobody reviews what was installed
Portable apps and browser extensions are not treated as installed software
CNC operators installing USB-delivered vendor utilities on the controllers
remediation_steps: Add a software installation clause to the acceptable use policy: users may not install software or browser extensions; requests go through IT; approved sources are listed; have every user acknowledge it.
Remove local administrator rights from all standard users (manage the built-in local admin with LAPS) and route legitimate installs through the MSP or a privilege-elevation tool.
Enforce with GPO/Intune: AppLocker/WDAC rules for installers and scripts, block or restrict the Microsoft Store to a private store, and control browser extensions through browser policy.
Turn on software inventory reporting in the RMM or Intune with a weekly report or alert for newly installed software; review it and record the review.
Handle exceptions through change tickets and update the approved software list each time.

controls.name: Identification
controls.statement: Identify system users, processes acting on behalf of users, and devices.
controls.discussion: Common device identifiers include Media Access Control (MAC), Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, or device-unique token identifiers. Management of individual identifiers is not applicable to shared system accounts. Typically, individual identifiers are the user names associated with the system accounts assigned to those individuals. Organizations may require unique identification of individuals in group accounts or for detailed accountability of individual activity. In addition, this requirement addresses individual identifiers that are not necessarily associated with system accounts. Organizational devices requiring identification may be defined by type, by device, or by a combination of type/device.[SP 800-63-3] provides guidance on digital identities.

objectives.text: system users are identified.
processes acting on behalf of users are identified.
devices accessing the system are identified.

assessment.examine: Identification and authentication policy; procedures addressing user identification and authentication; system security plan, system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; list of system accounts; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system operations responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; personnel with account management responsibilities; system developers
assessment.test: Organizational processes for uniquely identifying and authenticating users; mechanisms supporting or implementing identification and authentication capability

guidance.summary: Every person, automated process (service account) and device that accesses the CUI environment must have its own unique identifier so activity can be traced back to it. In practice that means one named account per person, named service accounts for scheduled jobs and integrations, and a way to identify each device (domain computer account, certificate, or at least serial and MAC in the inventory).
guidance.machine_shop_example: Each of the 40 employees has a unique AD/Entra account such as jsmith rather than 'shopfloor1', and the CNC operators each sign into the controllers with their own account instead of a shared 'operator' login. The nightly backup and the ERP-to-CAM integration run as documented service accounts (svc-backup, svc-erpsync). All 25 PCs, the server and both controllers are domain-joined with computer accounts and appear in the RMM inventory by hostname and serial; the CUI Wi-Fi uses 802.1X with device certificates so unknown devices cannot join and are visible if they try.
typical_evidence: AD/Entra user export showing one account per person and no shared accounts (or a documented, approved exception)
Service account inventory listing each process account, the system it runs on, its purpose and owner
Device inventory (RMM, Intune or AD computer objects) with hostname, serial and MAC address
Account provisioning procedure with a naming standard and a sample onboarding ticket
Screenshot of the CNC controller login showing individual operator accounts
common_gaps: Shared 'shop' or 'operator' accounts on floor PCs and CNC controllers
Service accounts undocumented, or applications running under a person's account
Devices not tracked; personal phones and laptops on the same Wi-Fi as CUI systems with no identification
Generic admin accounts ('admin', 'msp') used by several people
remediation_steps: Export all accounts from AD/Entra and from each local system (controllers, firewall, ERP); flag shared or generic accounts and convert them to per-person accounts; if a controller cannot support individual logins, document the exception with compensating controls (sign-in log, physical access limits).
Create a service account inventory (name, system, purpose, owner, last review date) and move application processes that run under user accounts to dedicated service accounts.

Ensure every device is identified: domain- or Entra-join all PCs and controllers, keep the RMM/asset inventory current with serial and MAC, and enable 802.1X or at minimum device registration on the CUI Wi-Fi.
Write the provisioning procedure (HR notice, ticket, unique username standard, account creation) and apply it consistently for employees, contractors and MSP staff.
Review the user, service account and device lists quarterly and disable or remove anything unknown.

controls.name: Authentication
controls.statement: Authenticate (or verify) the identities of users, processes, or devices, as a prerequisite to allowing access to organizational systems.
controls.discussion: Individual authenticators include the following: passwords, key cards, cryptographic devices, and one-time password devices. Initial authenticator content is the actual content of the authenticator, for example, the initial password. In contrast, the requirements about authenticator content include the minimum password length. Developers ship system components with factory default authentication credentials to allow for initial installation and configuration. Default authentication credentials are often well known, easily discoverable, and present a significant security risk. Systems support authenticator management by organization-defined settings and restrictions for various authenticator characteristics including minimum password length, validation time window for time synchronous one-time tokens, and number of allowed rejections during the verification stage of biometric authentication. Authenticator management includes issuing and revoking, when no longer needed, authenticators for temporary access such as that required for remote maintenance. Device authenticators include certificates and passwords.[SP 800-63-3] provides guidance on digital identities.

objectives.text: the identity of each user is authenticated or verified as a prerequisite to system access.
the identity of each process acting on behalf of a user is authenticated or verified as a prerequisite to system access.
the identity of each device accessing or connecting to the system is authenticated or verified as a prerequisite to system access.

assessment.examine: Identification and authentication policy; system security plan; procedures addressing authenticator management; procedures addressing user identification and authentication; system design documentation; list of system authenticator types; system configuration settings and associated documentation; change control records associated with managing system authenticators; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with authenticator management responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing authenticator management capability

guidance.summary: Nothing gets into the systems without proving who or what it is: users with passwords plus MFA, service accounts with unique credentials or keys, and devices with certificates, domain membership or equivalent. It also covers managing those authenticators: changing vendor defaults, setting minimum password rules, issuing credentials securely and revoking them when no longer needed.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Users authenticate to their PCs and to GCC High with a password plus MFA; the built-in local administrator on each PC has a unique LAPS-managed password. Service accounts have unique 25+ character passwords stored in the MSP's vault and rotated annually. Both CNC controllers require a login (Windows auto-logon removed), and the default vendor passwords on the controller software, firewall, switches and printers were changed at installation and recorded in the vault. The CUI Wi-Fi uses WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with device certificates, so only company devices can connect; guests use a separate SSID with no path to the CUI network.
typical_evidence: Authenticator management policy (minimum password length, MFA, default credential changes, secure issuance, revocation on termination)
GPO or Entra password policy screenshots and MFA/Conditional Access configuration
Vault entries or a record showing default credentials were changed on the firewall, switches, printers, ERP and CNC controller software
Wi-Fi 802.1X/RADIUS or NAC configuration showing device authentication, and the guest network separation
Service account list with credential rotation dates
Offboarding ticket showing credentials disabled and revoked
common_gaps: Vendor default passwords still in place on network gear, printers or CNC controller software
CNC controller auto-logs into Windows with no password so the machine starts faster
Guest devices and CUI devices on the same pre-shared-key Wi-Fi
Service account passwords never rotated; former MSP staff still know them
remediation_steps: Write the authenticator management policy: minimum password length (for example 14 characters), MFA wherever supported, default credential change on every new device, credentials stored only in the vault, service account rotation (annually and on staff change), and revocation on termination.

Enforce user authentication in AD/Entra: no blank or auto-logon passwords (remove AutoAdminLogon on the controllers), LAPS for local admin accounts, and account lockout after a defined number of failed attempts.
Change every default credential on the firewall, switches, access points, printers, ERP and CNC software and record them in the vault.
Authenticate devices: domain/Entra join, 802.1X with certificates (or at minimum WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise) for CUI Wi-Fi, a separate guest SSID, and certificate- or device-based VPN for remote access.
Give each service account a unique long credential, document the rotation schedule, and complete one rotation as evidence.
Add credential revocation to the offboarding checklist and verify it with a sample ticket.

controls.name: Multifactor Authentication
controls.statement: Use multifactor authentication for local and network access to privileged accounts and for network access to non-privileged accounts.
controls.discussion: Multifactor authentication requires the use of two or more different factors to authenticate. The factors are defined as something you know (e.g., password, personal identification number [PIN]); something you have (e.g., cryptographic identification device, token); or something you are (e.g., biometric). Multifactor authentication solutions that feature physical authenticators include hardware authenticators providing time-based or challenge-response authenticators and smart cards. In addition to authenticating users at the system level (i.e., at logon), organizations may also employ authentication mechanisms at the application level, when necessary, to provide increased information security. Access to organizational systems is defined as local access or network access. Local access is any access to organizational systems by users (or processes acting on behalf of users) where such access is obtained by direct connections without the use of networks. Network access is access to systems by users (or processes acting on behalf of users) where such access is obtained through network connections (i.e., nonlocal accesses). Remote access is a type of network access that involves communication through external networks. The use of encrypted virtual private networks for connections between organization-controlled and non-organization controlled endpoints may be treated as internal networks with regard to protecting the confidentiality of information.[SP 800-63-3] provides guidance on digital identities.

objectives.text: privileged accounts are identified.
multifactor authentication is implemented for local access to privileged accounts.
multifactor authentication is implemented for network access to privileged accounts.
multifactor authentication is implemented for network access to non-privileged accounts.

assessment.examine: Identification and authentication policy; procedures addressing user identification and authentication; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; list of system accounts; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system operations responsibilities; personnel with account management responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing multifactor authentication capability

partial_credit.condition: MFA implemented for remote and privileged users but not for general (non-privileged local) users

guidance.summary: List which accounts are privileged (admins), then require MFA for those accounts everywhere, including logging on locally at the console, and require MFA for every user when they access systems over the network (file server, GCC High, VPN, RDP). The DoD scoring gives partial credit (3 points off instead of 5) when MFA covers remote and privileged users but not general users, but a CMMC certification assessment needs all four objectives met.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's privileged account list names the admin's Domain Admin account, two MSP engineer accounts and the Entra Global Administrator. All users sign into GCC High with Microsoft Authenticator (number matching), the VPN requires MFA, and the domain-joined PCs use Windows Hello for Business (PIN or fingerprint backed by the TPM) so every network access to the file server is MFA-backed. Admin console logins on the server and PCs use a FIDO2 security key, and the firewall admin interface requires a TOTP code. The two CNC controllers are isolated on their own VLAN, operators log in locally with non-privileged accounts, and the SSP documents that arrangement.
typical_evidence: Privileged account inventory
Entra Conditional Access policy requiring MFA for all users and all admin roles (screenshot) and the MFA registration report
Windows Hello for Business, smart card or FIDO2 configuration and the enrollment report for domain-joined PCs
VPN and firewall administrator MFA configuration screenshots
Sign-in logs showing MFA satisfied for network and privileged access
Documented exceptions (for example CNC controller local login) with compensating controls and approval
common_gaps: MFA on email only; the file server, VPN or RDP still accept a password alone
Admins log on locally at the server console with just a password
'Remember MFA for 90 days' or legacy authentication protocols left enabled, which bypass MFA
A shared operator account on the controllers with no MFA and no documented exception
remediation_steps: Identify and document the privileged accounts: Domain Admins, local Administrators, Entra admin roles, firewall/switch admins, and MSP accounts.
Enforce MFA for network access for all users: Entra Conditional Access requiring MFA for all cloud apps in GCC High, MFA on the VPN and any RDP gateway, and block legacy authentication.

Bring the domain-joined Windows logon under MFA with Windows Hello for Business (hybrid-joined, PIN/biometric backed by TPM) or FIDO2 keys/smart cards, so access to the file server and other network resources is MFA-backed.

Require MFA for privileged local access: FIDO2 or smart card for admin console logins on the server and PCs, TOTP or a hardware token for the firewall and switch admin interfaces, and MFA on the MSP's remote tools.

For CNC controllers that cannot support MFA, keep them on an isolated VLAN with non-privileged local accounts, no CUI stored beyond the current job, and document the arrangement and compensating controls in the SSP.
Review the MFA registration and sign-in reports monthly and keep them as evidence.

controls.name: Replay-Resistant Authentication
controls.statement: Employ replay-resistant authentication mechanisms for network access to privileged and nonprivileged accounts.
controls.discussion: Authentication processes resist replay attacks if it is impractical to successfully authenticate by recording or replaying previous authentication messages. Replay-resistant techniques include protocols that use nonces or challenges such as time synchronous or challenge-response one-time authenticators.[SP 800-63-3] provides guidance on digital identities.

objectives.text: replay-resistant authentication mechanisms are implemented for network account access to privileged and non-privileged accounts.

assessment.examine: Identification and authentication policy; procedures addressing user identification and authentication; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; list of privileged system accounts; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system operations responsibilities; personnel with account management responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing identification and authentication capability or replay resistant authentication mechanisms

guidance.summary: Authentication over the network must use protocols an attacker cannot simply record and replay: Kerberos, TLS-protected logins, challenge-response, time-based one-time codes, FIDO2. Practically, that means no LM/NTLMv1, no cleartext or basic authentication, and MFA methods based on one-time codes or keys, for both privileged and non-privileged accounts.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's domain uses Kerberos for logons; LM and NTLMv1 are refused by GPO (LAN Manager authentication level set to 'Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM'), and NTLM auditing shows only one legacy CNC share still using NTLMv2, which is documented. GCC High logins use Microsoft Authenticator with number matching over TLS, the VPN uses IKEv2 with certificates plus a TOTP code, and legacy authentication (POP/IMAP/SMTP basic) is blocked in the tenant.
typical_evidence: GPO export showing 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' set to NTLMv2 only / refuse LM & NTLM
Entra Conditional Access or Exchange authentication policy showing legacy authentication blocked
MFA method configuration (Authenticator with number matching, TOTP, FIDO2)
VPN configuration showing IKEv2/TLS with MFA
SSP or policy statement listing approved authentication protocols
common_gaps: NTLMv1 or LM still enabled for old CNC controllers or printers
Basic authentication left enabled for scanner-to-email or old mail clients
Internal web applications or device admin pages that log in over plain HTTP
SMS as the only MFA factor, which is weak even though it is technically replay-resistant
remediation_steps: Set the LAN Manager authentication level to 5 (send NTLMv2 only, refuse LM & NTLM) by GPO, enable NTLM auditing, and remediate any device that still needs NTLMv1.
Block legacy authentication in the GCC High tenant (Conditional Access block and Exchange authentication policies).
Make sure every network login is over Kerberos, TLS or IKEv2: HTTPS-only admin pages on the firewall, switches and printers, and no FTP or Telnet logins.
Use MFA methods that are challenge- or time-based (Authenticator, TOTP, FIDO2) rather than reusable secrets, and prefer them over SMS.
Document the approved protocol list in the SSP and re-check it annually with a configuration review.

controls.name: Identifier Reuse
controls.statement: Prevent reuse of identifiers for a defined period.
controls.discussion: Identifiers are provided for users, processes acting on behalf of users, or devices (3.5.1). Preventing reuse of identifiers implies preventing the assignment of previously used individual, group, role, or device identifiers to different individuals, groups, roles, or devices.

objectives.text: a period within which identifiers cannot be reused is defined.
reuse of identifiers is prevented within the defined period.

assessment.examine: Identification and authentication policy; procedures addressing identifier management; procedures addressing account management; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; list of system accounts; list of identifiers generated from physical access control devices; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with identifier management responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing identifier management

guidance.summary: When someone leaves or a device is retired, its username or identifier must not be handed to a different person or device for a defined period (many small shops simply choose 'never'). This keeps logs unambiguous: a log entry for 'jsmith' must always mean the same person.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's account management procedure states that usernames are never reused. Departed employees' accounts are disabled immediately, moved to a 'Disabled Users' OU for 90 days, and then deleted, but the username is recorded in an identifier register (a protected spreadsheet) so it is never re-issued. When a second J. Smith is hired, IT assigns jsmith2. The same rule applies to hostnames and service account names.
typical_evidence: Account management policy or procedure with the defined reuse period
Identifier register or AD export of disabled/retired accounts showing they are retained
Offboarding ticket showing the account was disabled rather than deleted or reassigned
Naming standard and an example of a suffixed username created to avoid a collision
common_gaps: No written period; a departed employee's account is renamed for the replacement
Shared or generic accounts passed from person to person
Accounts deleted immediately and the same username recreated for someone else
remediation_steps: Define the period in the account management policy (for example 'identifiers are never reused' or 'not for at least 2 years').
Change offboarding so the account is disabled, kept in a Disabled Users OU for at least the defined period, and the identifier is logged in a register before any deletion.
Adopt a naming standard with a numeric suffix rule to avoid collisions.
Apply the same rule to device names and service accounts.
During the annual account review, confirm no reserved identifier has been re-issued.

controls.name: Identifier Handling
controls.statement: Disable identifiers after a defined period of inactivity.
controls.discussion: Inactive identifiers pose a risk to organizational information because attackers may exploit an inactive identifier to gain undetected access to organizational devices. The owners of the inactive accounts may not notice if unauthorized access to the account has been obtained.

objectives.text: a period of inactivity after which an identifier is disabled is defined.
identifiers are disabled after the defined period of inactivity.

assessment.examine: Identification and authentication policy; procedures addressing identifier management; procedures addressing account management; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; list of system accounts; list of identifiers generated from physical access control devices; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with identifier management responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing identifier management

guidance.summary: Define how long an account may go unused (commonly 30 to 90 days) and disable it automatically or on a regular review once it passes that point. This catches forgotten contractor accounts, seasonal workers and service accounts nobody remembers.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Policy sets 45 days of inactivity for user accounts and 90 days for service accounts. The MSP runs a monthly scheduled PowerShell/Entra report of last sign-in and disables any user account past 45 days, attaching the list to a ticket. The admin approves exceptions in writing (for example an employee on medical leave) with an end date, and the local accounts on the controllers and firewall are checked by hand each quarter.
typical_evidence: Policy with the inactivity thresholds
Monthly inactive-account report and the ticket showing which accounts were disabled
Script schedule or Entra access review configuration
Exception list with approver and end date
common_gaps: No threshold defined; last-logon dates never checked
Service accounts and local accounts on controllers and the firewall not included
The report is produced but accounts stay enabled because nobody acts on it
remediation_steps: Set inactivity thresholds in policy (for example 45 days for users, 90 days for service accounts), covering domain, cloud and local accounts.
Automate a monthly last-logon report (AD lastLogonTimestamp, Entra sign-in activity) and the disable action; keep the output with each run.
Include local accounts on the server, controllers and firewall in a quarterly manual check.
Record exceptions with approver and end date, and re-enable accounts only through a ticket.

controls.name: Password Complexity
controls.statement: Enforce a minimum password complexity and change of characters when new passwords are created.
controls.discussion: This requirement applies to single-factor authentication of individuals using passwords as individual or group authenticators, and in a similar manner, when passwords are used as part of multifactor authenticators. The number of changed characters refers to the number of changes required with respect to the total number of positions in the current password. To mitigate certain brute force attacks against passwords, organizations may also consider salting passwords.

objectives.text: password complexity requirements are defined.
password change of character requirements are defined.
minimum password complexity requirements as defined are enforced when new passwords are created.
minimum password change of character requirements as defined are enforced when new passwords are created.

assessment.examine: Identification and authentication policy; password policy; procedures addressing authenticator management; system security plan; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system design documentation; password configurations and associated documentation; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with authenticator management responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing password-based authenticator management capability

guidance.summary: Define minimum password rules (length and character mix) and a 'change of characters' rule (a new password must differ substantially from the old one), then enforce both technically whenever passwords are created or changed. Windows enforces length and complexity natively but not change of characters, so shops usually meet that objective with a banned-password or password-protection feature plus a long history, and state the rule in policy.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's policy requires at least 14 characters with three of four character classes, no reuse of the previous 24 passwords, and a change-of-character rule that a new password may not simply add or change a few characters of the old one. The Default Domain Policy enforces length and complexity, Entra Password Protection (cloud plus the on-prem DC agent) rejects passwords containing the company name, 'machine', 'shop' or common substitutions, and the 24-password history blocks near-repeats. Local accounts on the controllers and firewall follow the same rule and are set manually by the admin.
typical_evidence: Password policy document stating the complexity and change-of-character requirements
Default Domain Policy or fine-grained password policy screenshot (minimum length, complexity enabled, history)
Entra Password Protection settings screenshot (custom banned list, on-premises enforcement mode)
Screenshot of a rejected weak or too-similar password change attempt
Record of how local accounts on controllers, the firewall and printers are held to the same rule
common_gaps: Windows default 7-character minimum still in place
Change-of-character requirement never defined
Controller, firewall and printer passwords not covered by any rule
MFA used as an excuse to leave weak passwords
remediation_steps: Write the rule: minimum 14 characters (or longer), complexity per your chosen benchmark, a new password must differ from the previous one by a defined amount, and passwords may not contain the username or banned words.
Enforce in AD with the Default Domain Policy or a fine-grained password policy: minimum length 14, complexity enabled, password history 24, minimum age 1 day.
Deploy Entra Password Protection (cloud and the on-premises agent on domain controllers) with a custom banned password list in enforce mode, which also blocks common substitutions of banned terms.
Apply equivalent settings to local accounts on the server, controllers, firewall and network devices where supported, and document manual enforcement where not.
Test by attempting a non-compliant password change and keep the screenshot as evidence.

controls.name: Password Reuse
controls.statement: Prohibit password reuse for a specified number of generations.
controls.discussion: Password lifetime restrictions do not apply to temporary passwords.

objectives.text: the number of generations during which a password cannot be reused is specified.
reuse of passwords is prohibited during the specified number of generations.

assessment.examine: Identification and authentication policy; password policy; procedures addressing authenticator management; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; password configurations and associated documentation; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with authenticator management responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing password-based authenticator management capability

guidance.summary: Specify how many previous passwords a user cannot reuse (Windows supports up to 24) and enforce it on every system that has its own passwords. Temporary passwords are exempt from lifetime rules.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Policy states 24 generations. The Default Domain Policy sets 'Enforce password history' to 24 with a 1-day minimum age, GCC High applies its tenant password history, and the ERP application (which has its own logins) is configured for 24 as well. The firewall admin and controller local accounts are covered procedurally: each password change is recorded in the vault, which shows the previous values are not reused.
typical_evidence: Password policy stating the number of generations
GPO or fine-grained password policy screenshot with Enforce password history = 24 and minimum password age set
GCC High tenant and ERP application password policy settings
Screenshot of a rejected reused password
common_gaps: History left at the default of 0 or a small number
Users cycle through minor variants (addressed together with 3.5.7 change-of-character)
Local accounts on devices with no history enforcement and no procedural record
remediation_steps: Set the number in policy (24 recommended).
Configure Enforce password history = 24 and a minimum password age of 1 day in AD to stop rapid cycling back to an old password.
Confirm the GCC High tenant and any application with its own passwords (ERP, controller software) enforce history or are covered procedurally with vault records.
Test a reuse attempt and keep the screenshot.

controls.name: Temporary Passwords
controls.statement: Allow temporary password use for system logons with an immediate change to a permanent password.
controls.discussion: Changing temporary passwords to permanent passwords immediately after system logon ensures that the necessary strength of the authentication mechanism is implemented at the earliest opportunity, reducing the susceptibility to authenticator compromises.

objectives.text: an immediate change to a permanent password is required when a temporary password is used for system logon.

assessment.examine: Identification and authentication policy; password policy; procedures addressing authenticator management; system security plan; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system design documentation; password configurations and associated documentation; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with authenticator management responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing password-based authenticator management capability

guidance.summary: When IT gives a new hire, or a user with a reset, a temporary password, the system must force them to set their own permanent password at first logon. This applies to AD, GCC High, the VPN, the ERP and any local account you hand out, including temporary vendor accounts.
guidance.machine_shop_example: New user accounts are created with 'User must change password at next logon' checked in AD, and GCC High onboarding uses a Temporary Access Pass that expires after first use and forces MFA registration and a permanent password. The MSP help desk procedure requires the same flag on every password reset. Temporary local admin passwords issued to a vendor are one-time because LAPS rotates the password automatically after the visit.
typical_evidence: Account provisioning and reset procedure requiring a unique temporary password and the change-at-next-logon flag
Screenshot of AD user properties with 'User must change password at next logon' set; Entra force-change or Temporary Access Pass policy
Sample onboarding and reset tickets showing the step
Screenshot of the first-logon prompt forcing a change
common_gaps: The help desk hands out a standard 'Welcome123!' that users keep
The flag is set on new accounts but not on password resets
Shared temporary passwords for controllers or vendors that are never changed afterwards
remediation_steps: Update the provisioning and reset procedures: every temporary password is unique, delivered out of band, and flagged for change at next logon.
Configure 'User must change password at next logon' in AD and force password change in Entra on creation and reset; use Temporary Access Pass for MFA-first onboarding in GCC High.
Train the MSP help desk on the procedure and audit a sample of reset tickets each quarter.
Use LAPS so any temporary local administrator password rotates automatically after use.

controls.name: Cryptographically-Protected Passwords
controls.statement: Store and transmit only cryptographically-protected passwords.
controls.discussion: Cryptographically-protected passwords use salted one-way cryptographic hashes of passwords. See [NIST CRYPTO].

objectives.text: passwords are cryptographically protected in storage.
passwords are cryptographically protected in transit.

assessment.examine: Identification and authentication policy; password policy; procedures addressing authenticator management; system security plan; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system design documentation; password configurations and associated documentation; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with authenticator management responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing password-based authenticator management capability

guidance.summary: Passwords must be stored only as salted one-way hashes and sent over the network only inside encrypted channels. In practice: no passwords in plain-text files, spreadsheets, scripts or sticky notes; no logins over HTTP, FTP or Telnet; reversible encryption disabled in AD; and a proper password manager for IT and MSP credentials.
guidance.machine_shop_example: AD stores password hashes with reversible encryption disabled and LM hash storage off, Entra stores hashes, and the shop uses a password manager with MFA for the admin and MSP shared credentials instead of the old spreadsheet, which was deleted after migration. All logins run over Kerberos, TLS (HTTPS to GCC High, the ERP web portal with a valid certificate) or the IKEv2 VPN; the firewall, switch and printer admin pages are HTTPS-only with HTTP disabled. The backup job and the CNC program-transfer script use a group managed service account and SFTP rather than embedded passwords.
typical_evidence: GPO export showing 'Store passwords using reversible encryption' disabled and 'Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change' enabled
Password manager or vault in use (screenshot, access list) and policy prohibiting plain-text password storage
Configuration showing HTTPS-only management on the firewall, switches and printers with FTP/Telnet/HTTP disabled
Vulnerability scan or configuration review showing no cleartext authentication protocols in use
Review record of scripts and scheduled tasks confirming no embedded credentials
common_gaps: An IT password spreadsheet or Word document on the file server
Passwords embedded in backup or CNC transfer scripts
Printers, scanners or controllers using HTTP or FTP logins
Reversible encryption enabled for an old application
remediation_steps: Set by GPO: reversible encryption disabled and LM hash storage disabled; verify no accounts have the 'store password using reversible encryption' flag.
Move all IT and MSP credentials into a password manager protected by MFA; delete the spreadsheet or document after migration and record that it was destroyed.
Replace cleartext logins: HTTPS with valid certificates for the firewall, switches, printers and ERP; disable HTTP, FTP and Telnet; use SFTP for any controller file transfer that requires a login.
Find and remove embedded credentials in scripts and scheduled tasks; use group managed service accounts or vault retrieval instead.
