Add 'no plain-text passwords' to policy and check quarterly with a search of the file server and mailboxes for password files.

controls.name: Obscure Feedback
controls.statement: Obscure feedback of authentication information.
controls.discussion: The feedback from systems does not provide any information that would allow unauthorized individuals to compromise authentication mechanisms. For some types of systems or system components, for example, desktop or notebook computers with relatively large monitors, the threat (often referred to as shoulder surfing) may be significant. For other types of systems or components, for example, mobile devices with small displays, this threat may be less significant, and is balanced against the increased likelihood of typographic input errors due to the small keyboards. Therefore, the means for obscuring the authenticator feedback is selected accordingly. Obscuring authenticator feedback includes displaying asterisks when users type passwords into input devices or displaying feedback for a very limited time before fully obscuring it.

objectives.text: authentication information is obscured during the authentication process.

assessment.examine: Identification and authentication policy; procedures addressing authenticator feedback; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators; system developers
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing the obscuring of feedback of authentication information during authentication

guidance.summary: When someone types a password, the screen must not display it (dots or asterisks instead), on every login interface in scope: Windows, the CNC controller software, the ERP, web admin pages, the VPN client and the firewall. A brief 'show last character' on small screens is acceptable; a login that echoes the whole password is not.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Windows, GCC High, the VPN client and the ERP login all mask passwords by default. The admin checked the CNC controller software and the ERP web portal, confirmed masking, and filed a screenshot of each in the evidence folder. The policy notes that users must not use 'show password' where others can see the screen, and the two shop-floor monitors were turned away from the walkway.
typical_evidence: Screenshots of each login screen in scope (Windows, controller software, ERP, VPN, firewall/switch admin pages) showing masked input
Policy statement covering obscured authentication feedback and shoulder surfing
Checklist item for verifying masking when a new application or device is introduced
common_gaps: A custom or legacy shop-floor application that echoes the password
Assumed but never verified for the controllers and device admin pages
Passwords displayed in plain text during shared remote-support sessions
remediation_steps: Inventory every login interface in scope (OS, controller software, ERP, web admin pages, VPN, password manager).
Verify each one masks input, capture a screenshot, and fix or replace any that do not (vendor setting or upgrade).
Add the requirement to the authentication policy and to the checklist for onboarding new applications and devices.
Instruct the MSP not to display passwords in shared or recorded sessions.

controls.name: Incident Handling
controls.statement: Establish an operational incident-handling capability for organizational systems that includes preparation, detection, analysis, containment, recovery, and user response activities.
controls.discussion: Organizations recognize that incident handling capability is dependent on the capabilities of organizational systems and the mission/business processes being supported by those systems. Organizations consider incident handling as part of the definition, design, and development of mission/business processes and systems. Incident-related information can be obtained from a variety of sources including audit monitoring, network monitoring, physical access monitoring, user and administrator reports, and reported supply chain events. Effective incident handling capability includes coordination among many organizational entities including mission/business owners, system owners, authorizing officials, human resources offices, physical and personnel security offices, legal departments, operations personnel, procurement offices, and the risk executive. As part of user response activities, incident response training is provided by organizations and is linked directly to the assigned roles and responsibilities of organizational personnel to ensure that the appropriate content and level of detail is included in such training. For example, regular users may only need to know who to call or how to recognize an incident on the system; system administrators may require additional training on how to handle or remediate incidents; and incident responders may receive more specific training on forensics, reporting, system recovery, and restoration. Incident response training includes user training in the identification/reporting of suspicious activities from external and internal sources. User response activities also includes incident response assistance which may consist of help desk support, assistance groups, and access to forensics services or consumer redress services, when required.[SP 800-61] provides guidance on incident handling. [SP 800-86] and [SP 800-101] provide guidance on integrating forensic techniques into incident response. [SP 800-161] provides guidance on supply chain risk management.

objectives.text: an operational incident-handling capability is established.
the operational incident-handling capability includes preparation.
the operational incident-handling capability includes detection.
the operational incident-handling capability includes analysis.
the operational incident-handling capability includes containment.
the operational incident-handling capability includes recovery.
the operational incident-handling capability includes user response activities.

assessment.examine: Incident response policy; contingency planning policy; procedures addressing incident handling; procedures addressing incident response assistance; incident response plan; contingency plan; system security plan; procedures addressing incident response training; incident response training curriculum; incident response training materials; incident response training records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with incident handling responsibilities; personnel with contingency planning responsibilities; personnel with incident response training and operational responsibilities; personnel with incident response assistance and support responsibilities; personnel with access to incident response support and assistance capability; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Incident-handling capability for the organization; organizational processes for incident response assistance; mechanisms supporting or implementing incident response assistance

guidance.summary: You need a working incident response capability, not just a document: people with assigned roles, a written plan that covers preparation, detection, analysis, containment, recovery and what users are expected to do, and the tools (logging, EDR, backups, contact lists) to carry it out. The MSP can do much of the technical work, but the shop owns the plan, the decisions and the reporting.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop has a 10-page incident response plan naming the IT admin as incident lead, the owner as decision maker and the MSP as technical responder with a 24x7 number. Preparation: EDR on every endpoint, centralized logs, tested offline backups, and a printed contact list including the DIBNet reporting steps. Detection comes from EDR, firewall and Microsoft 365 alerts plus employee reports; analysis and containment playbooks cover ransomware, phishing/account compromise, a lost laptop and malware on a CNC controller (isolate the host in EDR, disable the account, block at the firewall); recovery follows the backup restore procedure that was tested last quarter. Users are trained annually to report suspicious email or odd controller behavior to IT within an hour and to leave the machine as it is.
typical_evidence: Incident response plan with roles, phases, playbooks and a contact list, approved and dated
Incident log or tickets from the past year, including false alarms and how they were handled
EDR, firewall and Microsoft 365 alert configuration and sample alerts
Training records showing users were taught how to recognize and report incidents
MSP agreement covering incident response support and response times
Backup restore test record
common_gaps: A generic template plan with no names, phone numbers or shop-specific systems
No detection tooling, so incidents are only found when something breaks
Users do not know who to call, and the only copy of the plan is on the file server that ransomware would encrypt
Recovery never tested; backups online and reachable with the same credentials as the file server
remediation_steps: Write the plan for this environment: roles (incident lead, owner, MSP, contracts/legal and insurance contacts), severity levels, concrete steps for each of the six phases, and playbooks for ransomware, phishing/account compromise, lost or stolen device, and malware on a controller.

Preparation: deploy EDR on all PCs, the server and the controllers (or document the vendor-approved alternative), centralize logs, keep offline or immutable backups, and keep printed and cloud copies of the plan and contact list.
Detection and analysis: define who receives EDR, firewall and Microsoft 365 alerts, the expected triage time, and what to record (time, systems, indicators, CUI involved).
Containment and recovery: document isolation steps (EDR network isolation, disable account, revoke sessions, firewall block) and the restore procedure; test a restore at least annually.
User response: include incident recognition and reporting in annual training and new-hire onboarding, and post the reporting contact on the shop floor.
Exercise the plan (3.6.3) and update it after every incident or exercise.

controls.name: Incident Reporting
controls.statement: Track, document, and report incidents to designated officials and/or authorities both internal and external to the organization.
controls.discussion: Tracking and documenting system security incidents includes maintaining records about each incident, the status of the incident, and other pertinent information necessary for forensics, evaluating incident details, trends, and handling. Incident information can be obtained from a variety of sources including incident reports, incident response teams, audit monitoring, network monitoring, physical access monitoring, and user/administrator reports. Reporting incidents addresses specific incident reporting requirements within an organization and the formal incident reporting requirements for the organization. Suspected security incidents may also be reported and include the receipt of suspicious email communications that can potentially contain malicious code. The types of security incidents reported, the content and timeliness of the reports, and the designated reporting authorities reflect applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, regulations, and policies.[SP 800-61] provides guidance on incident handling.

objectives.text: incidents are tracked.
incidents are documented.
authorities to whom incidents are to be reported are identified.
organizational officials to whom incidents are to be reported are identified.
identified authorities are notified of incidents.
identified organizational officials are notified of incidents.

assessment.examine: Incident response policy; procedures addressing incident monitoring; incident response records and documentation; procedures addressing incident reporting; incident reporting records and documentation; incident response plan; system security plan; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with incident monitoring responsibilities; personnel with incident reporting responsibilities; personnel who have or should have reported incidents; personnel (authorities) to whom incident information is to be reported; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Incident monitoring capability for the organization; mechanisms supporting or implementing tracking and documenting of system security incidents; organizational processes for incident reporting; mechanisms supporting or implementing incident reporting

guidance.summary: Keep a record of every incident (what happened, status, actions, closure) and know exactly who inside the company and which outside authorities must be told, and how fast. For a DoD contractor that means reporting cyber incidents affecting covered defense information to DoD through DIBNet within 72 hours of discovery under DFARS 252.204-7012, plus notifying the prime contractor and cyber insurer as the contracts require.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Incidents are logged in the ticketing system under an 'Incident' category that captures date discovered, reporter, systems, whether CUI was involved, actions, external reports and closure. The plan's reporting section names the owner and IT admin as internal officials to be told immediately, and lists external contacts: DoD DIBNet (dibnet.dod.mil, 72-hour deadline, requires a DoD-approved Medium Assurance certificate), the prime contractor's security point of contact, the cyber insurer's hotline, and the FBI. The shop obtained the certificate in advance and keeps a pre-filled incident collection form template so the 72-hour clock is achievable.
typical_evidence: Incident log or ticket export with status, actions and closure dates
Reporting procedure with the internal escalation list and external contacts, deadlines (72-hour DIBNet, prime contractor, insurer) and the information each report needs
Proof of DIBNet readiness: DoD-approved Medium Assurance certificate and account
Records of notifications made for any actual incident, or exercise records showing the notification steps were rehearsed
Contract clauses (DFARS 252.204-7012 and prime flow-downs) referenced in the procedure
common_gaps: No incident log because 'we have not had any'; phishing attempts and lost phones never recorded
Nobody knows about the 72-hour DIBNet requirement or holds the certificate needed to submit a report
Prime contractor reporting obligations in the flow-down not identified
Incidents handled by the MSP and never reported to the owner
remediation_steps: Create an incident register (ticket category or log) with required fields: date/time discovered, reporter, description, systems, CUI impact, actions, status, closure and external reports made.

List the internal officials (owner, IT admin, contracts manager) and the external authorities (DoD DIBNet within 72 hours per DFARS 252.204-7012, prime contractor POC per contract, cyber insurer, FBI/IC3 as appropriate) with contact details and deadlines in the plan.
Obtain a DoD-approved Medium Assurance certificate now so DIBNet reporting is possible on day one, and store the incident collection form template with the plan.
Require the MSP by contract or SLA to notify the shop of any suspected incident within a set time (for example 1 hour).
Rehearse the reporting path in the annual tabletop and record which notifications would have been made and when.

controls.name: Incident Response Testing
controls.statement: Test the organizational incident response capability.
controls.discussion: Organizations test incident response capabilities to determine the effectiveness of the capabilities and to identify potential weaknesses or deficiencies. Incident response testing includes the use of checklists, walk-through or tabletop exercises, simulations (both parallel and full interrupt), and comprehensive exercises. Incident response testing can also include a determination of the effects on organizational operations (e.g., reduction in mission capabilities), organizational assets, and individuals due to incident response.[SP 800-84] provides guidance on testing programs for information technology capabilities.

objectives.text: the incident response capability is tested.

assessment.examine: Incident response policy; contingency planning policy; procedures addressing incident response testing; procedures addressing contingency plan testing; incident response testing material; incident response test results; incident response test plan; incident response plan; contingency plan; system security plan; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with incident response testing responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel with responsibilities for testing plans related to incident response
assessment.test: Mechanisms and processes for incident response

guidance.summary: Test the incident response plan regularly. For a small shop an annual tabletop exercise walking through a realistic scenario is sufficient, as long as you record who took part, what you found and what you fixed afterwards.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Each year the owner, IT admin and the MSP engineer spend 90 minutes on a tabletop: 'ransomware note on the CAM workstation at 6 a.m., CNC controllers unreachable'. They walk through detection, isolation, DIBNet reporting, restore from backup and customer notification using the actual plan, and document three findings (contact list out of date, restore time unknown, no printed copy of the plan). Each finding becomes a ticket and the plan is revised to a new version.
typical_evidence: Tabletop exercise record: date, scenario, participants, findings and corrective actions
Updated plan version showing the changes made after the exercise
Tickets closing the findings
Optional technical test results (backup restore drill, EDR isolation test, phishing simulation)
common_gaps: The plan has never been exercised, so the first test is a real incident
An exercise was 'done' verbally with no record
Findings never turned into changes to the plan
remediation_steps: Schedule an annual tabletop (calendar entry with owner, IT admin and MSP) and pick a scenario relevant to the shop.
Run the exercise using the written plan, including the reporting steps, and time the key decisions.
Write a one-page after-action report with findings and owners, and open a ticket for each.
Update the plan and re-brief users on any changed reporting instructions.
Add at least one technical element per year (backup restore, EDR isolation drill, phishing simulation).

controls.name: Perform Maintenance
controls.statement: Perform maintenance on organizational systems.
controls.discussion: This requirement addresses the information security aspects of the system maintenance program and applies to all types of maintenance to any system component (including hardware, firmware, applications) conducted by any local or nonlocal entity. System maintenance also includes those components not directly associated with information processing and data or information retention such as scanners, copiers, and printers.

objectives.text: system maintenance is performed.

assessment.examine: System maintenance policy; procedures addressing controlled system maintenance; maintenance records; manufacturer or vendor maintenance specifications; equipment sanitization records; media sanitization records; system security plan; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system maintenance responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel responsible for media sanitization; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for scheduling, performing, documenting, reviewing, approving, and monitoring maintenance and repairs for systems; organizational processes for sanitizing system components; mechanisms supporting or implementing controlled maintenance; mechanisms implementing sanitization of system components

guidance.summary: Keep the systems maintained on a defined schedule (OS and application patching, firmware updates, hardware repairs, controller software updates, backup verification) and keep records of what was done, when and by whom. It covers printers, scanners, network gear and the CNC controllers, not just the PCs.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's maintenance schedule says: OS and third-party patches monthly through the MSP RMM (critical patches within 14 days), firewall and switch firmware quarterly, CNC controller software per vendor bulletin in an agreed production window, server hardware and UPS battery check annually, and a backup restore test quarterly. Each activity is a ticket or an RMM patch report, and the admin reviews the maintenance log with the MSP every quarter.
typical_evidence: Maintenance policy and schedule covering every asset class and who is responsible (shop, MSP, vendor)
RMM or Intune patch compliance reports for the last several months
Tickets for firmware updates, hardware repairs and controller software updates
Vendor maintenance records for the CNC controllers
Backup verification and restore test records
common_gaps: Patching happens 'when convenient' with no records beyond the live RMM dashboard
CNC controllers are never updated because production cannot stop, with no documented risk decision
Network equipment firmware years out of date
Maintenance done by vendors with no record kept at the shop
remediation_steps: Write a maintenance schedule listing each asset class, activity, frequency, responsible party and where the record is kept.
Configure RMM or Intune patch rings with deadlines (for example critical patches within 14 days, all others within 30) and keep the monthly reports.
Put firmware updates for the firewall, switches, access points, printers and PC BIOS on a quarterly ticket.
Agree a maintenance window with production for the CNC controllers, log both vendor and internal updates, and document any deferred update with a risk acceptance and compensating control.
Review the maintenance log quarterly and clear overdue items.

controls.name: System Maintenance Control
controls.statement: Provide controls on the tools, techniques, mechanisms, and personnel used to conduct system maintenance.
controls.discussion: This requirement addresses security-related issues with maintenance tools that are not within the organizational system boundaries that process, store, or transmit CUI, but are used specifically for diagnostic and repair actions on those systems. Organizations have flexibility in determining the controls in place for maintenance tools, but can include approving, controlling, and monitoring the use of such tools. Maintenance tools are potential vehicles for transporting malicious code, either intentionally or unintentionally, into a facility and into organizational systems. Maintenance tools can include hardware, software, and firmware items, for example, hardware and software diagnostic test equipment and hardware and software packet sniffers.

objectives.text: tools used to conduct system maintenance are controlled.
techniques used to conduct system maintenance are controlled.
mechanisms used to conduct system maintenance are controlled.
personnel used to conduct system maintenance are controlled.

assessment.examine: System maintenance policy; procedures addressing system maintenance tools and media; maintenance records; system maintenance tools and associated documentation; maintenance tool inspection records; system security plan; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system maintenance responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for approving, controlling, and monitoring maintenance tools; mechanisms supporting or implementing approval, control, and monitoring of maintenance tools; organizational processes for inspecting maintenance tools; mechanisms supporting or implementing inspection of maintenance tools; organizational process for inspecting media for malicious code; mechanisms supporting or implementing inspection of media used for maintenance

guidance.summary: Control how maintenance is done: which tools (laptops, USB drives, diagnostic software, remote-support apps) may be used, which techniques (for example remote sessions must use MFA and be logged), which mechanisms (the approved remote-access path, approved media) and which people (named MSP engineers, vendor technicians with escort). Approve them, keep the lists, and check tools before use.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The maintenance policy lists the approved tools: the MSP's RMM/remote tool, the admin's maintenance laptop, a labelled shop-owned USB drive that is scanned before every use, and the CNC vendor's diagnostic software with its version recorded. Vendor technicians may not plug their own laptops into the CUI network; they use the shop's laptop or a maintenance VLAN with no CUI access. Remote maintenance goes only through the RMM with per-engineer accounts, MFA and session logging. Authorized maintenance personnel are the admin, two named MSP engineers and the machine vendor's named field engineers; anyone else is escorted (3.7.6).
typical_evidence: Maintenance policy and procedure covering tools, techniques, mechanisms and personnel
Approved maintenance tool list with versions, and the authorized maintenance personnel list
Maintenance log or tickets recording the person, tool and system for each activity
RMM or remote-session logs showing MFA and named accounts
Vendor visit log with escort and equipment brought on site
Media and tool scan records (3.7.4)
common_gaps: Vendor technicians plug personal laptops or USB sticks into the controllers
Any MSP staff member can remote in using a shared account
No list of maintenance tools; unknown diagnostic software found on the controllers
Maintenance performed with no record of who did it or what tool was used
remediation_steps: Write the maintenance control procedure: approved tool list, approved remote path (RMM with MFA and session logs), approved media handling, and the authorized personnel list with an escort rule for everyone else.
Provide shop-owned maintenance equipment (laptop, USB drive) and require vendors to use it or a segregated maintenance VLAN with no CUI access.
Require named individual accounts, MFA and session logging for MSP engineers, and review the session logs monthly.
Log every maintenance event as a ticket with person, tool, system and time, including vendor visits and sign-in.
Inspect or scan tools and media before connection (3.7.4) and review the tool list quarterly.

controls.name: Equipment Sanitization
controls.statement: Ensure equipment removed for off-site maintenance is sanitized of any CUI.
controls.discussion: This requirement addresses the information security aspects of system maintenance that are performed off-site and applies to all types of maintenance to any system component (including applications) conducted by a local or nonlocal entity (e.g., in-contract, warranty, in-house, software maintenance agreement).[SP 800-88] provides guidance on media sanitization.

objectives.text: equipment to be removed from organizational spaces for off-site maintenance is sanitized of any CUI.

assessment.examine: System maintenance policy; procedures addressing controlled system maintenance; maintenance records; manufacturer or vendor maintenance specifications; equipment sanitization records; media sanitization records; system security plan; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system maintenance responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel responsible for media sanitization; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for scheduling, performing, documenting, reviewing, approving, and monitoring maintenance and repairs for systems; organizational processes for sanitizing system components; mechanisms supporting or implementing controlled maintenance; mechanisms implementing sanitization of system components

guidance.summary: Before a PC, laptop, server, controller or drive leaves the building for repair, any CUI on it must be removed, normally by pulling and keeping the drive, wiping it per NIST SP 800-88, or crypto-erasing a BitLocker-encrypted drive, and you must record what was done. Printers and copiers with internal storage count too.
guidance.machine_shop_example: A CAD workstation under warranty needs a motherboard replacement. The admin removes its BitLocker-encrypted SSD, locks it in the server closet, records the chassis and drive serials and the action on the equipment-out form, and ships the chassis without the drive. For a laptop that must go with its drive, the admin performs a documented SP 800-88 purge (or a BitLocker crypto-erase followed by a reinstall) and files the wipe report. Controller repairs are done on site whenever possible; if a controller PC must go out, the program storage drive is removed first.
typical_evidence: Sanitization procedure referencing NIST SP 800-88 methods
Equipment removal and sanitization log with dates, serials, method and the person responsible
Wipe tool reports or a record of BitLocker key destruction
RMA or shipping paperwork showing the drive was removed
Repair vendor agreement clauses on data handling
common_gaps: Laptops sent to a repair shop with the drive intact and BitLocker off
No record of what left the building
Controller PCs sent to the machine vendor with part programs (which may be CUI) still on disk
Copier or printer hard drives returned at lease end without wiping
remediation_steps: Write the procedure: identify CUI on the device, choose a method (remove and retain the drive; SP 800-88 clear or purge; crypto-erase for BitLocker-encrypted drives), and record and approve before shipment.
Enable BitLocker on all PCs and laptops so crypto-erase is possible, with recovery keys escrowed in AD or Entra.
Create an equipment-out form or log (device, serial, drive serial, CUI assessment, method, date, signature).
Prefer on-site repair for the controllers and server; if off-site is unavoidable, remove storage first.
Include printers and copiers with storage in the process and require wipe certificates at lease return.

controls.name: Media Inspection
controls.statement: Check media containing diagnostic and test programs for malicious code before the media are used in organizational systems.
controls.discussion: If, upon inspection of media containing maintenance diagnostic and test programs, organizations determine that the media contain malicious code, the incident is handled consistent with incident handling policies and procedures.

objectives.text: media containing diagnostic and test programs are checked for malicious code before being used in organizational systems that process, store, or transmit CUI.

assessment.examine: System maintenance policy; procedures addressing system maintenance tools; system maintenance tools and associated documentation; maintenance records; system security plan; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system maintenance responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational process for inspecting media for malicious code; mechanisms supporting or implementing inspection of media used for maintenance

guidance.summary: Any USB stick, disc or downloaded diagnostic or test tool, whether from the MSP, a CNC vendor or a hardware vendor, must be scanned for malware before it is used on in-scope systems, and the scans must be recorded. If malware is found, it is handled as an incident.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop has a scanning station (a PC with current EDR/AV that is not on the CUI network) where every vendor USB drive is scanned; the result is noted on the vendor visit form. Diagnostic software downloaded by the MSP is scanned on the maintenance laptop and its hash checked against the vendor's published value before it is installed on a controller. USB ports on the controllers and PCs are otherwise blocked, with only the labelled shop drive allowed by device ID.
typical_evidence: Procedure for scanning maintenance media and tools before use, including handling of infected media
Scan logs from the scanning station or EDR showing vendor media scans
Vendor visit forms noting media scanned, date and result
Screenshot of the USB device control policy on the controllers and PCs
Hash or signature verification records for downloaded diagnostic tools
common_gaps: Vendor technicians plug USB drives straight into the controllers
No scan record even though AV is installed ('it would have caught it')
Downloaded diagnostic tools installed with no check
CNC controller with no AV and unrestricted USB ports
remediation_steps: Write the procedure: all maintenance media and tools are scanned on a designated station with up-to-date AV/EDR before connection, results are logged, and infected media is handled per the incident response plan.
Set up the scanning station and a labelled shop-owned USB drive, and require vendors to transfer tools through it.
Block USB mass storage on the controllers and PCs by default and allow only the approved drive by device ID.
For downloads, verify the vendor's hash or digital signature and scan before installing.
Add 'media scanned (Y/N, date, result)' to the vendor visit and maintenance form and review the forms quarterly.

controls.name: Nonlocal Maintenance
controls.statement: Require multifactor authentication to establish nonlocal maintenance sessions via external network connections and terminate such connections when nonlocal maintenance is complete.
controls.discussion: Nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic activities are those activities conducted by individuals communicating through an external network. The authentication techniques employed in the establishment of these nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions reflect the network access requirements in 3.5.3.

objectives.text: multifactor authentication is used to establish nonlocal maintenance sessions via external network connections.
nonlocal maintenance sessions established via external network connections are terminated when nonlocal maintenance is complete.

assessment.examine: System maintenance policy; procedures addressing nonlocal system maintenance; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; maintenance records; diagnostic records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system maintenance responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for managing nonlocal maintenance; mechanisms implementing, supporting, and managing nonlocal maintenance; mechanisms for strong authentication of nonlocal maintenance diagnostic sessions; mechanisms for terminating nonlocal maintenance sessions and network connections

guidance.summary: When the MSP or a vendor performs maintenance remotely over the Internet, the connection must require MFA and must be closed when the work is done. Always-on vendor tunnels and unattended remote-control agents with static passwords do not meet this.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The MSP connects through its RMM with per-engineer accounts and MFA enforced; sessions are logged with start and end times and close automatically when the engineer disconnects. The CNC vendor's remote diagnostics use a VPN account that is disabled by default: the admin enables it by ticket for the scheduled window, the vendor authenticates with MFA, and afterwards the admin disables the account and confirms in the firewall that the session is gone. The admin reviews the RMM session report monthly.
typical_evidence: Remote maintenance procedure (MFA required, enable-on-request, termination and verification)
RMM and VPN configuration screenshots showing MFA enforcement and session timeouts
Session logs with start and end times and the engineer's name
Tickets showing vendor access enabled for a window and disabled afterwards
Firewall rules or VPN account status showing vendor access disabled by default
common_gaps: A vendor remote-access tool installed on a controller with a static password and always on
MSP remote tool with a shared login and no MFA
Sessions never explicitly ended; unattended access left enabled
No logs of who connected and when
remediation_steps: Inventory every remote maintenance path (MSP RMM, vendor remote tools, VPN accounts, exposed RDP) and remove any that are not approved.
Require MFA on each remaining path (RMM MFA, VPN with MFA) and forbid standalone remote tools with static passwords.
Set vendor accounts and tunnels to disabled by default, enable them per ticket for a time-boxed window, disable them afterwards, and configure session idle timeouts.
Turn on session logging (RMM audit log, VPN log), review it monthly and keep the reports.
Document the procedure in the maintenance policy and the MSP contract.

controls.name: Maintenance Personnel
controls.statement: Supervise the maintenance activities of maintenance personnel without required access authorization.
controls.discussion: This requirement applies to individuals who are performing hardware or software maintenance on organizational systems, while 3.10.1 addresses physical access for individuals whose maintenance duties place them within the physical protection perimeter of the systems (e.g., custodial staff, physical plant maintenance personnel). Individuals not previously identified as authorized maintenance personnel, such as information technology manufacturers, vendors, consultants, and systems integrators, may require privileged access to organizational systems, for example, when required to conduct maintenance activities with little or no notice. Organizations may choose to issue temporary credentials to these individuals based on organizational risk assessments. Temporary credentials may be for one-time use or for very limited time periods.

objectives.text: maintenance personnel without required access authorization are supervised during maintenance activities.

assessment.examine: System maintenance policy; procedures addressing maintenance personnel; service provider contracts; service-level agreements; list of authorized personnel; maintenance records; access control records; system security plan; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system maintenance responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for authorizing and managing maintenance personnel; mechanisms supporting or implementing authorization of maintenance personnel

guidance.summary: Anyone doing maintenance who is not an authorized, vetted user of your systems (a machine tool vendor technician, a copier repair person, a one-off contractor) must be escorted and supervised by an authorized person while they work, and what they can see or do should be limited (temporary credentials, CUI off the screens).
guidance.machine_shop_example: The vendor visit procedure says the IT admin or a designated shop lead signs the technician in, stays with them while they work on a controller or in the server closet, makes sure no CUI drawings are on nearby screens, and signs them out; any temporary account created for the visit is disabled at the end. For remote vendor work the admin watches the session through the RMM's shared view and ends it when the work is done.
typical_evidence: Visitor and maintenance personnel procedure with the supervision requirement
Visitor log with escort names and times for maintenance visits
Authorized maintenance personnel list so 'without required access authorization' is clear
Tickets for temporary credentials issued and revoked
Records of supervised remote sessions
common_gaps: Vendor technician left alone on the shop floor with controllers and network access
No visitor log for maintenance visits
Temporary accounts left active after the visit
remediation_steps: Define the authorized maintenance personnel (IT admin, named MSP engineers) in policy; everyone else requires supervision.
Create a vendor visit checklist: sign-in, escort assigned, CUI screens locked, media scanned, temporary credentials issued and revoked, sign-out.
Train the shop leads who may act as escorts on what supervision means and what to stop.
For remote vendor work, use a shared-screen session observed by the admin and ended when the work is complete.
Review the visitor log quarterly for unescorted maintenance visits.

controls.name: Media Protection
controls.statement: Protect (i.e., physically control and securely store) system media containing CUI, both paper and digital.
controls.discussion: System media includes digital and non-digital media. Digital media includes diskettes, magnetic tapes, external and removable hard disk drives, flash drives, compact disks, and digital video disks. Non-digital media includes paper and microfilm. Protecting digital media includes limiting access to design specifications stored on compact disks or flash drives in the media library to the project leader and any individuals on the development team. Physically controlling system media includes conducting inventories, maintaining accountability for stored media, and ensuring procedures are in place to allow individuals to check out and return media to the media library. Secure storage includes a locked drawer, desk, or cabinet, or a controlled media library. Access to CUI on system media can be limited by physically controlling such media, which includes conducting inventories, ensuring procedures are in place to allow individuals to check out and return media to the media library, and maintaining accountability for all stored media.[SP 800-111] provides guidance on storage encryption technologies for end user devices.

objectives.text: paper media containing CUI is physically controlled.
digital media containing CUI is physically controlled.
paper media containing CUI is securely stored.
digital media containing CUI is securely stored.

assessment.examine: System media protection policy; procedures addressing media storage; procedures addressing media access restrictions; access control policy and procedures; physical and environmental protection policy and procedures; system security plan; media storage facilities; access control records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system media protection responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for restricting information media; mechanisms supporting or implementing media access restrictions

guidance.summary: Any physical thing that holds CUI - printed drawings and travelers, USB sticks, external drives, backup drives, optical discs, even hard disks pulled from old PCs - has to be tracked and locked up when not in use. 'Physically controlled' means you know what CUI media exists, where it is and who has it; 'securely stored' means it lives in a locked drawer, cabinet, safe or room that only authorized people can open. The requirement applies to paper and digital media equally.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop keeps CUI drawings and travelers in a locked flat file in the engineering office; shop-floor copies travel on numbered job clipboards that go back into the locked cabinet at the end of each shift, and the office manager confirms all clipboards are back. Digital CUI lives on the file server (or the GCC High SharePoint site); the only removable media allowed are three serial-numbered, hardware-encrypted USB drives listed in a media log with the current holder's name and kept in the IT closet safe when not signed out. Backup drives rotate through a locked fire safe, and retired hard disks sit in a locked bin until the recycler shreds them.
typical_evidence: Media protection policy or procedure defining what counts as CUI media (paper and digital), where it may be stored and who may access it
Media inventory or log listing each CUI USB drive, external disk, backup drive and paper file set with serial number, storage location and custodian
Photos of the locked cabinet, safe or media closet and the list of who holds keys or combinations
Check-out and check-in log for drawing packages, travelers and removable drives
Periodic inventory reconciliation record (for example quarterly) signed by the responsible person
Screenshot of the endpoint setting that blocks unapproved USB storage, supporting physical control of digital media
common_gaps: CUI prints left on the shop floor, in the printer output tray or in unlocked desk drawers overnight
Unlabeled USB drives and old external disks in desk drawers with no inventory, so nobody can say what CUI media exists
Backup drives or a NAS sitting on an open shelf in a shared office
The policy says 'locked storage' but the cabinet key hangs on a hook next to it or the office door is never locked
remediation_steps: Define CUI media in the policy: paper (drawings, travelers, inspection reports, purchase orders that carry CUI) and digital (USB drives, external and backup drives, optical media, removed hard disks, printer and CNC controller storage).

Build a media inventory: serial-number and label every approved removable drive and backup drive, record its custodian and storage location, and list the paper file locations; reconcile the inventory quarterly and record the result.
Provide locked storage: a locked cabinet or flat file for paper CUI and a safe or locked IT closet for drives and backup media; limit keys and combinations to named people and record who has them.
Set handling rules: CUI prints go back to the locked cabinet at end of shift, nothing is left in printers or on benches, and removable drives are signed out and back in on the log.

Enforce control of digital media technically: block unapproved USB storage on all PCs and controllers by Group Policy (Removable Storage Access) or endpoint management, allowing only the inventoried encrypted drives, and keep CUI files on the file server or GCC High rather than scattered on media.
Train employees on the rules at hire and annually, and spot-check storage areas monthly for the first year, then quarterly.

controls.name: Media Access
controls.statement: Limit access to CUI on system media to authorized users.
controls.discussion: Access can be limited by physically controlling system media and secure storage areas. Physically controlling system media includes conducting inventories, ensuring procedures are in place to allow individuals to check out and return system media to the media library, and maintaining accountability for all stored media. Secure storage includes a locked drawer, desk, or cabinet, or a controlled media library.

objectives.text: access to CUI on system media is limited to authorized users.

assessment.examine: System media protection policy; procedures addressing media storage; physical and environmental protection policy and procedures; access control policy and procedures; system security plan; system media; designated controlled areas; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system media protection and storage responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for storing media; mechanisms supporting or implementing secure media storage and media protection

guidance.summary: Only people who are authorized to see CUI may get at CUI media, whether that is a paper drawing set or a USB drive. In practice that means keeping a written list of who is authorized (usually the same people who have CUI system accounts), keeping media where only they can reach it, and having whoever hands out media check the list. It builds on 3.8.1: that one locks media up, this one decides who gets the key.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's CUI access list names the 12 employees cleared for CUI: engineering, CNC programming, quality, the two owners and the IT admin. Only those people have the combination to the engineering flat file and the IT closet, and the removable-drive log only allows sign-out to names on the list. Drawings needed on the floor are issued to the operator running that job by the engineering lead and collected when the job closes; they stay with the traveler, never in the break room. MSP technicians are not on the CUI list and are told they may not remove media from the building.
typical_evidence: List of personnel authorized to access CUI, approved and dated, consistent with the system account authorization list
Media protection procedure showing media is issued only to authorized users and how the check is performed
Key or combination register for locked media storage showing only authorized names
Removable-media sign-out log with names matching the authorized list
Screenshot of file-server or SharePoint permissions restricting CUI folders to the CUI security group
common_gaps: No written list of who is authorized for CUI, so 'authorized' means whoever asks
Everyone in the office has the cabinet key, including front-desk and part-time staff with no CUI need
MSP staff or contract programmers copy CUI to their own laptops or drives without any authorization
Drawings are copied freely on the shop copier and the extras pile up on benches
remediation_steps: Create and approve a CUI-authorized personnel list (name, role, date authorized) and keep it current with hiring, role changes and terminations (tie it to the 3.9.2 process).
Reissue keys or combinations for locked media storage only to people on the list, and change combinations whenever someone leaves.
Update the media procedure so paper and removable media are issued only by a named custodian, only to people on the list, and recorded on a log.
Keep digital CUI in access-controlled locations (a file server share or SharePoint library restricted to the CUI security group) and block ad hoc copies to unapproved USB devices.
Review the list and the sign-out log quarterly, correct discrepancies, and keep the review record.

controls.name: Media Disposal
controls.statement: Sanitize or destroy system media containing CUI before disposal or release for reuse.
controls.discussion: This requirement applies to all system media, digital and non-digital, subject to disposal or reuse. Examples include: digital media found in workstations, network components, scanners, copiers, printers, notebook computers, and mobile devices; and non-digital media such as paper and microfilm. The sanitization process removes information from the media such that the information cannot be retrieved or reconstructed. Sanitization techniques, including clearing, purging, cryptographic erase, and destruction, prevent the disclosure of information to unauthorized individuals when such media is released for reuse or disposal. Organizations determine the appropriate sanitization methods, recognizing that destruction may be necessary when other methods cannot be applied to the media requiring sanitization. Organizations use discretion on the employment of sanitization techniques and procedures for media containing information that is in the public domain or publicly releasable or deemed to have no adverse impact on organizations or individuals if released for reuse or disposal. Sanitization of non-digital media includes destruction, removing CUI from documents, or redacting selected sections or words from a document by obscuring the redacted sections or words in a manner equivalent in effectiveness to removing the words or sections from the document. NARA policy and guidance control sanitization processes for controlled unclassified information.[SP 800-88] provides guidance on media sanitization.

objectives.text: system media containing CUI is sanitized or destroyed before disposal.
system media containing CUI is sanitized before it is released for reuse.

assessment.examine: System media protection policy; procedures addressing media sanitization and disposal; applicable standards and policies addressing media sanitization; system security plan; media sanitization records; system audit logs and records; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with media sanitization responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for media sanitization; mechanisms supporting or implementing media sanitization

guidance.summary: Before you throw away, sell, donate, return (a leased copier, an RMA'd drive) or reassign anything that has held CUI, the CUI has to be made unrecoverable. For paper that means cross-cut shredding or a shredding service; for drives and devices it means wiping with a NIST SP 800-88 method (or cryptographic erase), degaussing, or physical destruction, and keeping a record of it. This includes hard drives inside PCs, laptops, copiers and CNC controllers, not just USB sticks.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Paper CUI goes into locked shred bins emptied by a bonded shredding vendor that issues a certificate of destruction each month. When a PC is retired, IT pulls the drive: if it will be reused in the shop it is wiped with a NIST 800-88 Purge (ATA secure erase or the vendor's sanitize utility) and the tool's report is filed; if it is being disposed of, it goes into the locked e-waste bin and is drilled or shredded by the recycler, who provides a serialized certificate. When the copier lease ended, the shop had the vendor wipe the copier's internal drive on site before pickup and kept the signed form. USB drives are fully wiped before being reused on a different customer's job.
typical_evidence: Media sanitization and disposal procedure referencing NIST SP 800-88 methods (Clear, Purge, Destroy) for each media type
Sanitization log: asset tag, serial number, date, method, tool used, person, and disposition (reused or destroyed)
Certificates of destruction from the shredding or e-waste vendor listing serial numbers
Wipe tool reports or screenshots (secure-erase log, BitLocker cryptographic erase record)
Asset inventory showing retired devices and their disposal status
Copier or printer lease-return paperwork showing drive removal or wipe
common_gaps: Old PCs, laptops and external drives stacked in a storeroom 'to deal with later' with no process, or donated after a quick format
Copiers and CNC controllers returned to the vendor with their internal drives intact
Paper CUI in the regular recycling or trash
Drives wiped but no record kept, so there is nothing for the assessor to examine
remediation_steps: Write the procedure: for each media type (paper, HDD, SSD, USB flash, optical, phone or tablet, copier drive, controller drive) specify the NIST 800-88 method and who performs it; reuse inside the shop requires at least Purge, disposal requires Purge or Destroy.

Acquire the means: a cross-cut shredder (DIN P-4 or better) or a shredding service that issues certificates, and a wipe tool plus a drill or crusher for drives; put a locked 'awaiting sanitization' bin in the IT closet.
Start a sanitization log and require an entry (serial, method, date, person, result) before any asset leaves inventory or is reassigned; file vendor certificates with it.
Turn on BitLocker on all PCs and laptops so a retired drive can be cryptographically erased by destroying the key, and record that as the method when used.
Add a disposal checkpoint to the asset-retirement and lease-return process: no device leaves the building until the log shows it was sanitized.
Sweep the building once for stray old drives, laptops and USB sticks, sanitize them, and log the batch.

controls.name: Media Markings
controls.statement: Mark media with necessary CUI markings and distribution limitations.
controls.discussion: The term security marking refers to the application or use of human-readable security attributes. System media includes digital and non-digital media. Marking of system media reflects applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, and regulations. See [NARA MARK].

objectives.text: media containing CUI is marked with applicable CUI markings.
media containing CUI is marked with distribution limitations.

assessment.examine: System media protection policy; procedures addressing media marking; physical and environmental protection policy and procedures; system security plan; list of system media marking security attributes; designated controlled areas; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system media protection and marking responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for marking information media; mechanisms supporting or implementing media marking

guidance.summary: Media that holds CUI has to be labeled so anyone handling it knows it is CUI and knows any limits on who it can go to. For paper that means the CUI banner (for example 'CUI' or 'CUI//SP-CTI') plus any limited dissemination control such as NOFORN or the export-control distribution statement on the drawing; for digital media it means a physical label on the drive and a marking in the file, folder or document. Follow the CUI Registry, 32 CFR 2002 and the markings the customer or DoD applied.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop puts the CUI banner and designation indicator block on the cover sheet of every drawing package and traveler that contains customer CUI, and keeps the distribution statement (usually Distribution Statement D or F with the export-control warning) printed on the drawings exactly as received. The three approved encrypted USB drives carry a printed 'CUI - Property of the shop - Return to IT' label. On the file server CUI lives under a top-level 'CUI' folder, and the GCC High SharePoint library applies a 'CUI' sensitivity label so files carry the marking in their header.
typical_evidence: Marking procedure with examples of the CUI banner, designation indicator and distribution statements the shop uses
Sample marked drawing package, traveler and cover sheet
Photos of labeled USB drives, backup drives and file boxes
Screenshot of the CUI folder structure or the sensitivity label configuration
Training record showing employees were taught how to recognize and apply markings
common_gaps: Assuming markings only matter for paper and leaving USB drives and backup disks unlabeled
Stripping the distribution statement when drawings are redrawn or converted into shop travelers
Nobody at the shop knows what a limited dissemination control means, so nothing is marked
Marking everything 'CUI', including public catalogs, so the real markings lose their meaning
remediation_steps: Identify which contracts and documents carry CUI and copy the markings and distribution statements exactly as the customer or DoD applied them (CUI Registry categories such as CTI, 32 CFR 2002 format).
Create a one-page marking guide: banner text, designation indicator block (controlled by, category, distribution or LDC, point of contact), and when to add the export-control warning.
Mark paper at creation: a cover sheet template with the banner and distribution statement, and a rule that shop copies of drawings keep the original statement.
Label physical digital media (printed label with 'CUI' and owner) and mark digital containers (folder names, sensitivity labels, document headers and footers).
Train the people who create or copy CUI (engineering, quality, programming, front office) and spot-check a sample of packages quarterly.

controls.name: Media Accountability
controls.statement: Control access to media containing CUI and maintain accountability for media during transport outside of controlled areas.
controls.discussion: Controlled areas are areas or spaces for which organizations provide physical or procedural controls to meet the requirements established for protecting systems and information. Controls to maintain accountability for media during transport include locked containers and cryptography. Cryptographic mechanisms can provide confidentiality and integrity protections depending upon the mechanisms used. Activities associated with transport include the actual transport as well as those activities such as releasing media for transport and ensuring that media enters the appropriate transport processes. For the actual transport, authorized transport and courier personnel may include individuals external to the organization. Maintaining accountability of media during transport includes restricting transport activities to authorized personnel and tracking and obtaining explicit records of transport activities as the media moves through the transportation system to prevent and detect loss, destruction, or tampering.

objectives.text: access to media containing CUI is controlled.
accountability for media containing CUI is maintained during transport outside of controlled areas.

assessment.examine: System media protection policy; procedures addressing media storage; physical and environmental protection policy and procedures; access control policy and procedures; system security plan; system media; designated controlled areas; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system media protection and storage responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for storing media; mechanisms supporting or implementing media storage and media protection

guidance.summary: When CUI media leaves your controlled area - a drawing set going to a subcontractor, a USB drive going with a programmer to another building, backup disks going off site - you must control who can get at it in transit and be able to show where it was and who had it. That means locked containers or tamper-evident packaging, a named employee or tracked carrier responsible for it, and a log of what left, when, with whom and when it arrived.
guidance.machine_shop_example: When the shop sends CUI drawings to its plating subcontractor, they go in a tamper-evident envelope inside a locked document case, hand-carried by the shipping lead or sent by a tracked carrier with signature required; the transport log records the package contents, tracking number, sender, recipient and delivery confirmation. Weekly backup drives travel to the owner's home safe in a locked hard case and each rotation is logged. Wherever possible the shop avoids physical transport entirely by exchanging files through the GCC High SharePoint site.
typical_evidence: Media transport procedure covering approved containers, approved carriers, custody log and encryption requirements
Media transport or custody log entries with tracking numbers and signatures
Photos of the locked transport cases or tamper-evident envelopes in use
Carrier shipment records with delivery confirmation for CUI packages
Backup media rotation log showing custodian and location
common_gaps: Drawings mailed in a plain envelope or handed to a driver with no record
Backup drives ride home in a glove box with no case and no log
Employees carry CUI on personal unencrypted USB sticks between the office, the shop floor and home
Nobody can say what CUI media is currently outside the building
remediation_steps: Minimize transport: send CUI to customers and subcontractors through an approved encrypted channel (GCC High, the customer's portal, FIPS-validated encrypted email) and reserve physical transport for cases that need it.
Define the transport procedure: authorized couriers (named employees or tracked carriers with signature), locked or tamper-evident containers, and mandatory encryption for digital media (see 3.8.6).
Start a custody log with date, description, media ID, sender, carrier, tracking number, recipient and delivery confirmation, and keep it with the media inventory.
Buy locked document and drive cases and tamper-evident envelopes and keep them with the shipping lead.
Review the log monthly against the media inventory to confirm everything that left came back or was received.

controls.name: Portable Storage Encryption
controls.statement: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of CUI stored on digital media during transport unless otherwise protected by alternative physical safeguards.
controls.discussion: This requirement applies to portable storage devices (e.g., USB memory sticks, digital video disks, compact disks, external or removable hard disk drives). See [NIST CRYPTO].[SP 800-111] provides guidance on storage encryption technologies for end user devices.

objectives.text: the confidentiality of CUI stored on digital media is protected during transport using cryptographic mechanisms or alternative physical safeguards.

assessment.examine: System media protection policy; procedures addressing media transport; system design documentation; system security plan; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system media transport records; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system media transport responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Cryptographic mechanisms protecting information on digital media during transportation outside controlled areas

guidance.summary: Digital media that carries CUI outside your controlled area - USB drives, external disks, backup drives - must be encrypted so that losing it does not disclose CUI, and the encryption should come from a FIPS 140-2 or 140-3 validated module. The only alternative is a documented physical safeguard instead, such as a locked container hand-carried by an authorized employee, and you should state exactly when that applies.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop allows only three inventoried hardware-encrypted USB drives (FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated, certificate number recorded) for moving CNC programs to the controllers or data packages to a subcontractor, and blocks every other USB storage device. The external backup drives that rotate off site are BitLocker-encrypted with the FIPS-compliant algorithms policy enabled and their recovery keys escrowed in Active Directory. One older CNC controller cannot read encrypted drives, so its program drive is hand-carried by the programmer inside the building in a locked case and never leaves the site; the SSP records that as the alternative physical safeguard.
typical_evidence: Policy requiring FIPS-validated encryption for CUI on portable media, with the documented exception for physical safeguards
Inventory of approved encrypted drives with model, FIPS certificate number and custodian
Screenshot of the Group Policy settings 'Deny write access to removable drives not protected by BitLocker' and 'System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms'
Screenshot of BitLocker recovery keys escrowed in Active Directory or Entra ID
Screenshot of the USB device-control rule that blocks non-approved storage
common_gaps: Any USB stick from the drawer gets used to carry programs to the controllers
BitLocker is used on laptops but backup drives and external disks are left unencrypted
Encryption is switched on but the product or mode is not FIPS-validated and nobody can produce the certificate
Recovery keys stored on the same drive or nowhere at all
remediation_steps: Buy hardware-encrypted, FIPS 140-2 or 140-3 validated USB drives for the few legitimate transport cases, record their certificate numbers, and add them to the media inventory.

Enforce BitLocker on removable drives by Group Policy: 'Control use of BitLocker on removable drives' and 'Deny write access to removable drives not protected by BitLocker', with 'System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms for encryption, hashing, and signing' enabled; escrow recovery keys to Active Directory or Entra ID.
Encrypt external backup drives with BitLocker or the backup product's FIPS-validated encryption and record where the keys are kept.
Block all other USB mass storage by Group Policy (Removable Storage Access) or endpoint device control, allowing only the approved drives by hardware ID.
Document in the SSP the alternative physical safeguard for any device that cannot use encrypted media: which media, who carries it, the locked container, and that it never leaves the site.
Verify quarterly that the approved drives are still encrypted and inventoried and that no exceptions have crept in.

controls.name: Removable Media
controls.statement: Control the use of removable media on system components.
controls.discussion: In contrast to requirement 3.8.1, which restricts user access to media, this requirement restricts the use of certain types of media on systems, for example, restricting or prohibiting the use of flash drives or external hard disk drives. Organizations can employ technical and nontechnical controls (e.g., policies, procedures, and rules of behavior) to control the use of system media. Organizations may control the use of portable storage devices, for example, by using physical cages on workstations to prohibit access to certain external ports, or disabling or removing the ability to insert, read, or write to such devices. Organizations may also limit the use of portable storage devices to only approved devices including devices provided by the organization, devices provided by other approved organizations, and devices that are not personally owned. Finally, organizations may control the use of portable storage devices based on the type of device, prohibiting the use of writeable, portable devices, and implementing this restriction by disabling or removing the capability to write to such devices.

objectives.text: the use of removable media on system components is controlled.

assessment.examine: System media protection policy; system use policy; procedures addressing media usage restrictions; system security plan; rules of behavior; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system media use responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for media use; mechanisms restricting or prohibiting use of system media on systems or system components

guidance.summary: You decide, in writing and technically, which removable media (USB sticks, external drives, SD cards, optical discs) may be used on which computers and for what purpose, and you block everything else. 'Controlled' can mean restricted to approved devices, restricted to specific PCs, read-only, or prohibited entirely. The point is that a random stick cannot be plugged into a PC or CNC controller and read from or written to.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Group Policy on all 25 PCs denies read and write access to removable storage, and an endpoint device-control rule allows the three approved encrypted drives by hardware ID on the two CAM programming PCs only. The CNC controllers that run a supported Windows build get the same policy; the two older controllers have USB port locks installed and receive programs over the isolated shop VLAN through DNC instead. The policy states removable media is only for transferring CNC programs and customer data packages, and IT reviews the device-control log monthly for blocked attempts.
typical_evidence: Removable media policy stating which media is allowed, on which systems, for what purposes and who approves exceptions
Group Policy Results (gpresult) report or endpoint-management policy showing Removable Storage Access restrictions
Device-control or endpoint-protection report listing allowed device IDs and blocked events
Approved removable media inventory (shared with 3.8.1)
Photos of USB port locks on legacy CNC controllers and a description of the DNC alternative
Monthly review record of blocked-device events
common_gaps: No technical control at all; the only 'control' is a sentence in the employee handbook
USB blocked on office PCs but wide open on the shop-floor controllers, where sticks are used the most
Exceptions granted to individuals without a record and never removed
Vendor technicians plug in their own drives during maintenance with no oversight
remediation_steps: Write the removable media policy: only inventoried, encrypted, shop-owned media; approved use cases; who may approve exceptions; vendor media must be scanned on an isolated PC first (ties to 3.7.4).

Deploy the Group Policy 'Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Removable Storage Access > All Removable Storage classes: Deny all access' to the domain, with a separate GPO or WMI filter for the few PCs that need the approved drives.
Use device control (Windows Defender device control, Intune, or the EDR product) to allow only the specific hardware IDs of the approved encrypted drives and to log blocked events.
Handle CNC controllers: apply the same policy where the OS supports it; for legacy controllers install USB port locks and move program transfer to DNC or network shares.
Review device-control logs monthly and the exception list quarterly, removing exceptions that are no longer needed.
Cover the rules in new-hire and annual training and post a short notice on the shop floor.

controls.name: Shared Media
controls.statement: Prohibit the use of portable storage devices when such devices have no identifiable owner.
controls.discussion: Requiring identifiable owners (e.g., individuals, organizations, or projects) for portable storage devices reduces the overall risk of using such technologies by allowing organizations to assign responsibility and accountability for addressing known vulnerabilities in the devices (e.g., insertion of malicious code).

objectives.text: the use of portable storage devices is prohibited when such devices have no identifiable owner.

assessment.examine: System media protection policy; system use policy; procedures addressing media usage restrictions; system security plan; rules of behavior; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system design documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system media use responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for media use; mechanisms prohibiting use of media on systems or system components

guidance.summary: If nobody can say who owns a USB stick or external drive, it must not be used on your systems. That covers drives found in the parking lot, giveaway drives from trade shows, drives left behind by a vendor, and the unlabeled sticks in the desk drawer. You need both a written rule and a practical way to know which drives are yours: labels, an inventory, and technical allow-listing.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Every shop-owned drive is labeled with an asset number and custodian and listed in the media inventory; the policy says any drive without a label and inventory entry is treated as unowned and must not be plugged into anything - it goes to IT, who wipes and destroys it or returns it to the vendor. The USB device-control allow-list makes the rule enforceable, because an unknown drive is blocked automatically. Employees covered the rule in security training, including the trade-show-USB example, and signed the acknowledgement.
typical_evidence: Policy statement prohibiting use of portable storage without an identifiable owner and describing how to handle found or vendor drives
Media inventory showing owner or custodian for each portable device
Photos of labeled shop-owned drives
Device-control configuration showing only inventoried devices are allowed
Training material or acknowledgement covering unknown-drive handling
common_gaps: A drawer of anonymous USB sticks that everyone dips into
A policy exists but there is no labeling or inventory, so ownership cannot be established
Vendor-supplied drives with machine software are plugged straight into the controller
No technical enforcement, so the rule depends entirely on memory
remediation_steps: Add a clause to the removable media policy: portable storage with no identifiable owner is prohibited; found drives go to IT; vendor drives are scanned on the isolated station and their owner recorded before use.
Label and inventory every shop-owned portable device with asset number and custodian; wipe or destroy any unlabeled drives collected during the sweep.
Configure device control to allow only inventoried device IDs so unknown drives are blocked rather than trusted.
Cover the rule in annual training with concrete examples and keep the signed acknowledgement.
Reconcile the inventory quarterly and re-sweep desks and the shop floor for stray media.

controls.name: Protect Backups
controls.statement: Protect the confidentiality of backup CUI at storage locations.
controls.discussion: Organizations can employ cryptographic mechanisms or alternative physical controls to protect the confidentiality of backup information at designated storage locations. Backed-up information containing CUI may include system-level information and user-level information. System-level information includes system-state information, operating system software, application software, and licenses. User-level information includes information other than system-level information.

objectives.text: the confidentiality of backup CUI is protected at storage locations.

assessment.examine: Procedures addressing system backup; system configuration settings and associated documentation; security plan; backup storage locations; system backup logs or records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with system backup responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for conducting system backups; mechanisms supporting or implementing system backups

guidance.summary: Backups of CUI have to be protected wherever they sit: the local backup appliance, external drives, the off-site copy and the cloud backup tenant. Protection means encryption (FIPS-validated when you rely on it), access limited to a few named people, and physical security of the storage location. A backup is a complete copy of your CUI, so it needs at least the protection the original gets.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The file server backs up nightly to a local NAS with an encrypted backup repository and weekly to a cloud backup service that stores data in US data centers with AES-256 encryption under a key the shop controls; only the IT admin and the MSP's backup account can log in to the backup console, both with MFA. The rotating external drive is BitLocker-encrypted and stored in the fireproof safe in the owner's office.
