Microsoft 365 GCC High data is backed up with a service that itself runs in a FedRAMP High environment. Restores are tested quarterly and the backup-system access list is reviewed at the same time.
typical_evidence: Backup policy or procedure describing what is backed up, where each copy is stored, and the encryption and access rules
Screenshot of backup job configuration showing encryption enabled and where the key is managed
Screenshot of the backup console user list showing a small set of administrators with MFA
Photos or description of the physical storage location of backup media (safe, locked closet, off-site custodian)
Cloud backup provider's FIPS or FedRAMP statement or the contract clause
Quarterly restore test and access review records
common_gaps: Backup NAS on the open network with the default admin password and no encryption
External backup drives unencrypted and stored on a desk or carried home in a bag
Consumer cloud sync (personal Dropbox or Google Drive) used for CUI backups
The MSP has unrestricted access to backup data and nobody knows where the off-site copy physically is
remediation_steps: Inventory every backup copy of CUI (local appliance, external drives, cloud, MSP-held copies) and record location, encryption status and who has access.
Enable encryption at rest for every backup target using the product's FIPS-validated option; store encryption keys and passphrases in the password manager, not on the appliance.
Lock down access: dedicated backup admin accounts with MFA, no shared logins, default accounts removed; restrict the backup repository share so ordinary users cannot browse it.
Secure the physical location: appliance in the locked server closet, external drives in a safe, off-site copies in a locked location with a documented custodian.
Confirm cloud backup services store data in the US and meet contract requirements (FedRAMP Moderate equivalent or better for GCC High data) and file the evidence.
Review backup access and test a restore quarterly, and log both.

controls.name: Screen Individuals
controls.statement: Screen individuals prior to authorizing access to organizational systems containing CUI.
controls.discussion: Personnel security screening (vetting) activities involve the evaluation/assessment of individual’s conduct, integrity, judgment, loyalty, reliability, and stability (i.e., the trustworthiness of the individual) prior to authorizing access to organizational systems containing CUI. The screening activities reflect applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, and specific criteria established for the level of access required for assigned positions.

objectives.text: individuals are screened prior to authorizing access to organizational systems containing CUI.

assessment.examine: Personnel security policy; procedures addressing personnel screening; records of screened personnel; system security plan; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with personnel security responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for personnel screening

guidance.summary: Before someone is given an account or physical access that reaches CUI, you run a defined screening on them and record that it was done. NIST does not dictate the depth; you define the criteria - typically identity verification, employment and reference checks, a criminal background check, and confirmation of US-person status when export-controlled CUI is involved - and apply them consistently to employees, temps, contractors and MSP staff who get CUI access.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's personnel security procedure requires, before CUI access is granted, an I-9 identity check, a third-party criminal background check, two reference checks, and verification of US-person status for anyone touching ITAR-marked jobs. HR records the completion date on the onboarding checklist and IT will not create the account until HR has signed that line. The MSP contract requires the MSP to background-check any technician assigned to the shop and to certify this annually, and the shop keeps the certification letter.
typical_evidence: Personnel screening policy or procedure defining the criteria and when re-screening occurs
Onboarding checklists showing screening completed before account creation, for a sample of recent hires
Background-check vendor invoices or completion notices (the results themselves can stay confidential)
US-person verification record for export-controlled work
MSP or contractor agreement clause requiring screening and the vendor's attestation
Account-creation tickets dated after the screening completion date
common_gaps: Accounts created on day one before any background check comes back
Screening applied to employees only, not to temps, interns, contract programmers or the MSP
No written criteria, so the assessor cannot tell what 'screened' means
The owner 'knows everyone' and nothing is documented
remediation_steps: Write the screening procedure: criteria (identity, background-check scope, references, US-person status where required), who performs it, and the rule that no CUI system or physical access is granted until it is complete.
Add a screening line with date and HR initials to the onboarding checklist and make IT's account-provisioning ticket depend on it.
Contract a background-check provider and run checks on all current CUI users who were never screened; record completion dates.
Extend the requirement to third parties: add a clause to the MSP and contractor agreements and collect annual attestations.
Define re-screening triggers (for example promotion to an administrator role, or every five years) and audit a sample of records annually.

controls.name: Personnel Actions
controls.statement: Ensure that organizational systems containing CUI are protected during and after personnel actions such as terminations and transfers.
controls.discussion: Protecting CUI during and after personnel actions may include returning system-related property and conducting exit interviews. System-related property includes hardware authentication tokens, identification cards, system administration technical manuals, keys, and building passes. Exit interviews ensure that individuals who have been terminated understand the security constraints imposed by being former employees and that proper accountability is achieved for system-related property. Security topics of interest at exit interviews can include reminding terminated individuals of nondisclosure agreements and potential limitations on future employment. Exit interviews may not be possible for some terminated individuals, for example, in cases related to job abandonment, illnesses, and non-availability of supervisors. For termination actions, timely execution is essential for individuals terminated for cause. In certain situations, organizations consider disabling the system accounts of individuals that are being terminated prior to the individuals being notified. This requirement applies to reassignments or transfers of individuals when the personnel action is permanent or of such extended durations as to require protection. Organizations define the CUI protections appropriate for the types of reassignments or transfers, whether permanent or extended. Protections that may be required for transfers or reassignments to other positions within organizations include returning old and issuing new keys, identification cards, and building passes; changing system access authorizations (i.e., privileges); closing system accounts and establishing new accounts; and providing for access to official records to which individuals had access at previous work locations and in previous system accounts.

objectives.text: a policy and/or process for terminating system access and any credentials coincident with personnel actions is established.
system access and credentials are terminated consistent with personnel actions such as termination or transfer.
the system is protected during and after personnel transfer actions.

assessment.examine: Personnel security policy; procedures addressing personnel transfer and termination; records of personnel transfer and termination actions; list of system accounts; records of terminated or revoked authenticators and credentials; records of exit interviews; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with personnel security responsibilities; personnel with account management responsibilities; system or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for personnel transfer and termination; mechanisms supporting or implementing personnel transfer and termination notifications; mechanisms for disabling system access and revoking authenticators

guidance.summary: You need a written offboarding and role-change process, and proof you follow it. When someone leaves, their accounts are disabled, MFA tokens, keys and badges are returned, shared passwords they knew are changed, and their devices and CUI media are recovered - the same day for terminations. When someone changes roles, their access is adjusted to the new role and the old access removed rather than accumulating. The system has to stay protected both while the change is happening and afterward.
guidance.machine_shop_example: HR opens an offboarding ticket the moment a departure is known. IT disables the AD and Entra ID account and revokes MFA and VPN before the exit interview ends for involuntary terminations and by end of day for voluntary ones, changes the shared CNC-controller and Wi-Fi passwords the person knew, collects the laptop, badge, keys and any encrypted USB drives, and converts the mailbox to a shared mailbox for the manager. When the quality inspector moved into sales, IT removed her from the CUI-Engineering and Quality groups and added the Sales group the same day, and the transfer checklist shows both changes. A quarterly access review catches anything missed.
typical_evidence: Personnel action (offboarding and transfer) procedure with timelines and responsibilities for HR, managers, IT and the MSP
Completed offboarding checklists or tickets for recent departures showing account-disable time, MFA and VPN revocation, equipment return and shared-password changes
Transfer tickets showing security-group membership changes
AD or Entra ID export of disabled accounts with dates matching HR termination dates
Key, badge and asset return records
Quarterly access review record
common_gaps: IT finds out about departures weeks later, and accounts of former employees are still enabled
Shared shop-floor logins and Wi-Fi keys never changed after someone leaves
Transfers keep all old permissions, so long-tenured staff can access everything
MSP or vendor accounts never removed when the technician leaves the MSP
remediation_steps: Write the procedure: HR notifies IT of every termination and transfer the same day; IT disables accounts and revokes MFA, VPN, remote access and cloud sessions within 24 hours (immediately for involuntary departures); managers collect devices, badges, keys and media; shared credentials the person knew are rotated.
Build offboarding and transfer checklists (ticket templates) that record timestamps and who did each step, and require the manager's sign-off.
Eliminate or inventory shared accounts (controllers, Wi-Fi, vendor portals) so rotation on departure is a known, short list.
For transfers, define access by role (security groups per department) and require removal of the old role's groups when the new role is added.
Run a quarterly review comparing HR's active roster against enabled accounts in AD or Entra ID, the file server, GCC High, VPN and the MSP's tools, and document the fixes.
Include the MSP: require notification and account removal when their staff assigned to the shop change.

controls.name: Limit Physical Access
controls.statement: Limit physical access to organizational systems, equipment, and the respective operating environments to authorized individuals.
controls.discussion: This requirement applies to employees, individuals with permanent physical access authorization credentials, and visitors. Authorized individuals have credentials that include badges, identification cards, and smart cards. Organizations determine the strength of authorization credentials needed consistent with applicable laws, directives, policies, regulations, standards, procedures, and guidelines. This requirement applies only to areas within facilities that have not been designated as publicly accessible. Limiting physical access to equipment may include placing equipment in locked rooms or other secured areas and allowing access to authorized individuals only; and placing equipment in locations that can be monitored by organizational personnel. Computing devices, external disk drives, networking devices, monitors, printers, copiers, scanners, facsimile machines, and audio devices are examples of equipment.

objectives.text: authorized individuals allowed physical access are identified.
physical access to organizational systems is limited to authorized individuals.
physical access to equipment is limited to authorized individuals.
physical access to operating environments is limited to authorized individuals.

assessment.examine: Physical and environmental protection policy; procedures addressing physical access authorizations; system security plan; authorized personnel access list; authorization credentials; physical access list reviews; physical access termination records and associated documentation; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with physical access authorization responsibilities; personnel with physical access to system facility; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for physical access authorizations; mechanisms supporting or implementing physical access authorizations

guidance.summary: You need a list of who is allowed into the areas where your systems, equipment (server, network gear, PCs, CNC controllers, printers that output CUI) and CUI work areas are, and you need locks, badges or other controls that keep everyone else out. 'Operating environments' means the rooms and areas themselves - the office, the server closet, the shop floor - not just the boxes. Anyone not on the list is a visitor and is handled under 3.10.3.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop is divided into a public lobby, the office, the shop floor and the server and network closet. Exterior doors are locked and employees use badge fobs; the customer and delivery lobby is separated from the office and shop by a locked door with a buzzer. The server closet has its own keyed lock with keys held only by the IT admin and the owner, and the firewall and switches are inside it. The authorized access list, maintained by the office manager, names every employee and the areas each may enter; the two contract programmers are on it for the office only. Monitors that display CUI face away from the lobby window.
typical_evidence: Physical access policy and the authorized personnel list by area, dated and approved
Facility diagram showing controlled areas, doors, and where systems and equipment are located
Badge or fob system user list or key register matching the authorized list
Photos of locks on the server closet, network cabinet and exterior doors
Access-control system configuration showing which groups can open which doors
Record of the last review of the authorized list
common_gaps: The server sits under a desk in the open office, or the network switch is in an unlocked utility closet shared with the landlord
Customers and delivery drivers can walk from the lobby straight onto the shop floor
No written list of authorized individuals, so the assessor cannot verify who should be inside
Master keys held by many people, including cleaners and former employees
remediation_steps: Map the facility: identify where the server, network equipment, PCs, CNC controllers, printers and CUI work areas are, and define the controlled areas around them.
Create the authorized access list by area (employees, contractors, MSP), approve it, and tie additions and removals to onboarding and offboarding.

Physically secure equipment: move the server, firewall and switches into a locked closet or cabinet, lock the office and shop-floor doors from the lobby, and add privacy screens or reorient monitors visible from public areas.
Issue controlled credentials (badges or fobs, or keyed locks with a key register) so only listed people can open each area, and remove access for anyone not on the list.
Review the list and the badge or key records quarterly and whenever personnel change.

controls.name: Monitor Facility
controls.statement: Protect and monitor the physical facility and support infrastructure for organizational systems.
controls.discussion: Monitoring of physical access includes publicly accessible areas within organizational facilities. This can be accomplished, for example, by the employment of guards; the use of sensor devices; or the use of video surveillance equipment such as cameras. Examples of support infrastructure include system distribution, transmission, and power lines. Security controls applied to the support infrastructure prevent accidental damage, disruption, and physical tampering. Such controls may also be necessary to prevent eavesdropping or modification of unencrypted transmissions. Physical access controls to support infrastructure include locked wiring closets; disconnected or locked spare jacks; protection of cabling by conduit or cable trays; and wiretapping sensors.

objectives.text: the physical facility where organizational systems reside is protected.
the support infrastructure for organizational systems is protected.
the physical facility where organizational systems reside is monitored.
the support infrastructure for organizational systems is monitored.

assessment.examine: Physical and environmental protection policy; procedures addressing physical access monitoring; system security plan; physical access logs or records; physical access monitoring records; physical access log reviews; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with physical access monitoring responsibilities; personnel with incident response responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for monitoring physical access; mechanisms supporting or implementing physical access monitoring; mechanisms supporting or implementing the review of physical access logs

guidance.summary: Beyond locking doors, you protect and watch the building and the things your systems depend on: power, network cabling and wiring closets, cooling for the server closet, and the internet demarcation point. 'Protected' means physical safeguards such as locks, cabinets, cable routing away from public areas and UPS or surge protection; 'monitored' means you can detect and review intrusion or tampering - an alarm system, cameras, door sensors, environmental alerts - and someone actually reviews what they produce.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The building has a monitored burglar alarm with door and motion sensors armed after hours, and cameras cover the entrances, the lobby, the shop floor and the server closet door with 90 days of retention. The server closet has a UPS, a temperature sensor that emails IT above 85 F, and a door contact that logs openings to the alarm panel. Network cable runs are in the ceiling, the demarcation box is locked, and the patch panel is inside the locked closet. The office manager reviews alarm events weekly and IT reviews camera footage whenever an alarm or badge anomaly occurs.
typical_evidence: Facility protection description in the SSP or a physical security plan covering doors, closets, cabling, power and environmental controls
Alarm monitoring contract and sample alarm event reports
Camera system screenshots showing coverage and retention settings
Photos of the locked wiring closet, patch panel, demarcation point and UPS
Environmental monitoring alerts or logs for the server closet
Record of periodic review of monitoring output (weekly alarm review, incident follow-up)
common_gaps: No alarm or cameras, or cameras nobody reviews that overwrite after three days
Network cabling and switches in a shared landlord closet that other tenants can enter
The server closet doubles as a storage room and is propped open in summer for cooling
Support infrastructure (power panel, internet demarcation) outside the controlled area with no lock
remediation_steps: Walk the facility and list the support infrastructure: power panels, UPS, cooling for the closet, wiring closets, patch panels, the demarcation point, and any cabling that passes through public or shared areas.

Protect it: lock wiring closets and the demarcation box, put switches in a locked cabinet, route exposed cabling in conduit, add a UPS and a temperature sensor for the server closet, and remove storage and the door prop.

Monitor it: install or extend a monitored alarm with door contacts on exterior doors and the server closet, add cameras covering entrances and the closet, set retention to at least 30 to 90 days, and send environmental alerts to IT.
Assign review duties: alarm events reviewed weekly, camera and door logs reviewed on alarm or badge anomalies, and findings recorded in the ticket system.
Document the protections and monitoring in the SSP and test the alarm and sensors annually.

controls.name: Escort Visitors
controls.statement: Escort visitors and monitor visitor activity.
controls.discussion: Individuals with permanent physical access authorization credentials are not considered visitors. Audit logs can be used to monitor visitor activity.

objectives.text: visitors are escorted.
visitor activity is monitored.

assessment.examine: Physical and environmental protection policy; procedures addressing physical access control; system security plan; physical access control logs or records; inventory records of physical access control devices; system entry and exit points; records of key and lock combination changes; storage locations for physical access control devices; physical access control devices; list of security safeguards controlling access to designated publicly accessible areas within facility; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with physical access control responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for physical access control; mechanisms supporting or implementing physical access control; physical access control devices

guidance.summary: Anyone not on the authorized access list is a visitor: customers, auditors, delivery drivers past the lobby, machine-tool technicians, and MSP staff who are not listed. Visitors must be accompanied by an authorized employee while inside controlled areas, and what they do must be observed so they cannot wander, photograph CUI or connect to equipment.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Visitors sign in at the lobby, receive a red 'VISITOR - ESCORT REQUIRED' badge and are met by their host, who stays with them for the whole visit; delivery drivers stay in the lobby or the shipping dock, where there is no CUI. A machine-tool technician working on a CNC controller for a full day is assigned the shop supervisor as escort, who logs the work in the maintenance record and watches any USB or laptop connection. Employees are trained to challenge anyone without a badge.
typical_evidence: Visitor policy defining who is a visitor, escort responsibilities and monitoring expectations
Visitor sign-in log with host or escort name and badge number
Photos of visitor badges and signage
Maintenance records showing an escort for vendor technicians
Training material telling employees to challenge unescorted visitors
common_gaps: Vendor technicians and delivery drivers roam the shop floor unaccompanied
A visitor log exists but the escort column is blank or the escort goes back to their desk
MSP technicians treated as visitors but never escorted, or treated as employees but never put on the list
No visitor badge, so employees cannot tell who belongs there
remediation_steps: Define visitor and escort rules in the physical security policy, including that vendor and MSP personnel not on the authorized list are visitors.
Set up the lobby: a sign-in log (paper or tablet), numbered visitor badges, a bell or phone to call the host, and signage stating visitors must be escorted.
Assign an escort for every visit before the visitor enters a controlled area and require the escort to stay with them, including during long maintenance visits.
Train all employees to challenge unbadged or unescorted people and to report it.
Have the office manager spot-check the log against badges weekly and record the check.

controls.name: Physical Access Logs
controls.statement: Maintain audit logs of physical access.
controls.discussion: Organizations have flexibility in the types of audit logs employed. Audit logs can be procedural (e.g., a written log of individuals accessing the facility), automated (e.g., capturing ID provided by a PIV card), or some combination thereof. Physical access points can include facility access points, interior access points to systems or system components requiring supplemental access controls, or both. System components (e.g., workstations, notebook computers) may be in areas designated as publicly accessible with organizations safeguarding access to such devices.

objectives.text: audit logs of physical access are maintained.

assessment.examine: Physical and environmental protection policy; procedures addressing physical access control; system security plan; physical access control logs or records; inventory records of physical access control devices; system entry and exit points; records of key and lock combination changes; storage locations for physical access control devices; physical access control devices; list of security safeguards controlling access to designated publicly accessible areas within facility; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with physical access control responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for physical access control; mechanisms supporting or implementing physical access control; physical access control devices

guidance.summary: You keep records of who physically entered the areas where your systems are and when. An electronic badge system does this automatically for employees; if you use keys, you need a documented alternative such as a sign-in sheet for the server closet and after-hours entry. Visitor logs from 3.10.3 are part of this. Logs must be retained long enough to support an investigation (a year is common) and someone should review them.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The badge system logs every fob use at the exterior doors and the office door and keeps two years of history; IT exports the log monthly to a restricted folder on the file server. The server closet is keyed, so a clipboard inside the door records date, time, name and reason for every entry, and the MSP technician signs it during visits. The lobby visitor log is scanned monthly. The owner reviews the after-hours badge report each month and notes anything odd.
typical_evidence: Badge or access-control system log export covering the assessment period
Server closet entry log sheets
Visitor sign-in logs (paper or electronic) with dates, names, host and times in and out
Log retention statement in the policy and evidence of retained logs (for example 12 months)
Record of periodic log review
common_gaps: Keyed locks with no log at all, so there is no record of who entered
Badge system logs exist but retention is 30 days and nobody exports them
Visitor log entries missing time out or host names
Logs kept but never reviewed and not tied to the incident process
remediation_steps: Decide the logging method per area: electronic badge logs for exterior and office doors, a sign-in sheet or door-contact log for the server closet, and the visitor log for the lobby.
Configure the access-control system to retain at least 12 months of events, or export the log monthly to a protected folder if the panel cannot.
Put the closet entry log in place and require every entry to be recorded, including MSP and vendor visits.
Define retention (12 months minimum) and storage (locked cabinet or restricted folder) in the policy.
Review the after-hours and closet logs monthly, note anomalies, and keep the review record.

controls.name: Manage Physical Access
controls.statement: Control and manage physical access devices.
controls.discussion: Physical access devices include keys, locks, combinations, and card readers.

objectives.text: physical access devices are identified.
physical access devices are controlled.
physical access devices are managed.

assessment.examine: Physical and environmental protection policy; procedures addressing physical access control; system security plan; physical access control logs or records; inventory records of physical access control devices; system entry and exit points; records of key and lock combination changes; storage locations for physical access control devices; physical access control devices; list of security safeguards controlling access to designated publicly accessible areas within facility; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with physical access control responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for physical access control; mechanisms supporting or implementing physical access control; physical access control devices

guidance.summary: Physical access devices are keys, badges and fobs, lock combinations and alarm codes. You need an inventory of them (which exist and who holds each), rules for issuing and returning them, and a process to change locks or combinations and deactivate fobs when someone leaves or a device is lost. This is credential management for the building, the same way account management is for the network.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The office manager keeps a key and fob register: every door key is stamped with a number, each fob's ID and holder is listed, the server closet key is limited to two people, and alarm codes are unique per user. Issue and return are signed on the register and are steps on the onboarding and offboarding checklists. When a fob is reported lost it is deactivated in the badge software the same day; when the shop supervisor left, his alarm code was deleted that day and the exterior locks he had keys to were rekeyed within a week.
typical_evidence: Key, badge and code register showing device ID, area, holder, and issue and return dates
Badge system export of active credentials matching the register
Onboarding and offboarding checklist lines for physical access devices
Records of lost-device deactivation, rekeying or combination changes
Periodic reconciliation of the register (for example semiannual)
common_gaps: Nobody knows how many keys exist or who has them; former employees and the landlord hold masters
One shared alarm code for the whole company that has never changed
Fobs of departed employees still active
The server closet combination written on a sticky note
remediation_steps: Inventory every physical access device: keys (by lock), fobs and badges, lock combinations and alarm codes, and identify the holder of each.
Rekey or reprogram anything whose holders cannot be accounted for and reduce master keys to a minimum.
Establish the register and an issue and return procedure with signatures, and add the items to onboarding and offboarding checklists (deactivate the fob and code the day someone leaves).
Use individual alarm codes and fobs rather than shared ones so activity can be attributed to a person.
Reconcile the register against the badge system and the physical keys semiannually and record the result.

controls.name: Alternative Work Sites
controls.statement: Enforce safeguarding measures for CUI at alternate work sites.
controls.discussion: Alternate work sites may include government facilities or the private residences of employees. Organizations may define different security requirements for specific alternate work sites or types of sites depending on the work-related activities conducted at those sites.[SP 800-46] and [SP 800-114] provide guidance on enterprise and user security when teleworking.

objectives.text: safeguarding measures for CUI are defined for alternate work sites.
safeguarding measures for CUI are enforced for alternate work sites.

assessment.examine: Physical and environmental protection policy; procedures addressing alternate work sites for personnel; system security plan; list of safeguards required for alternate work sites; assessments of safeguards at alternate work sites; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel approving use of alternate work sites; personnel using alternate work sites; personnel assessing controls at alternate work sites; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for security at alternate work sites; mechanisms supporting alternate work sites; safeguards employed at alternate work sites; means of communications between personnel at alternate work sites and security personnel

guidance.summary: If anyone works with CUI somewhere other than your facility - at home, at a customer site, in a hotel - you must define what protections apply there (which devices, encryption, VPN, screen privacy, no printing, no family access, physical storage) and actually enforce them. If you do not allow CUI work off site, say so in policy and enforce that instead. Either way the assessor wants the written rule and evidence that it holds.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop allows the two owners and the engineering lead to work from home on shop-issued BitLocker-encrypted laptops that connect over VPN with MFA; CUI may only be accessed through the VPN or GCC High, never downloaded to personal devices, never printed at home, and laptops are locked in a cabinet when not in use. Everyone else is prohibited from CUI work off site, and Conditional Access blocks GCC High sign-in from unmanaged devices. The rules are in the telework agreement each of the three signed, and IT checks device compliance in the endpoint-management console monthly.
typical_evidence: Telework or alternate work site policy listing the required safeguards, or a policy prohibiting CUI work off site
Signed telework agreements for approved remote workers
Screenshots of technical enforcement: VPN with MFA, Conditional Access or device-compliance policies, BitLocker status, disabled local printing and USB on laptops
List of approved remote workers and their assigned devices
Periodic compliance check record
common_gaps: Staff read CUI email on personal phones and home PCs with no policy at all
A policy is written but nothing technical stops CUI from being downloaded to a personal device
Drawings printed at home that then sit on a kitchen table
No list of who is even allowed to work remotely
remediation_steps: Decide and document whether CUI work is allowed off site; if yes, list the approved people, their devices, and the safeguards (encrypted shop-owned laptop, VPN with MFA, no personal devices, no home printing, locked storage, privacy screen, screen lock after 15 minutes).
Have each approved remote worker sign a telework agreement that restates the safeguards.

Enforce technically: Conditional Access or VPN policies that only allow managed, compliant devices; BitLocker; USB and local printers blocked on laptops by Group Policy or Intune; mobile email restricted with app-protection policies.
Cover customer-site work: what may be carried, on which device, and how it is secured in the hotel or vehicle.
Check device compliance monthly and remove remote access for anyone who is no longer approved.

controls.name: Risk Assessments
controls.statement: Periodically assess the risk to organizational operations (including mission, functions, image, or reputation), organizational assets, and individuals, resulting from the operation of organizational systems and the associated processing, storage, or transmission of CUI.
controls.discussion: Clearly defined system boundaries are a prerequisite for effective risk assessments. Such risk assessments consider threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood, and impact to organizational operations, organizational assets, and individuals based on the operation and use of organizational systems. Risk assessments also consider risk from external parties (e.g., service providers, contractors operating systems on behalf of the organization, individuals accessing organizational systems, outsourcing entities). Risk assessments, either formal or informal, can be conducted at the organization level, the mission or business process level, or the system level, and at any phase in the system development life cycle.[SP 800-30] provides guidance on conducting risk assessments.

objectives.text: the frequency to assess risk to organizational operations, organizational assets, and individuals is defined.

risk to organizational operations, organizational assets, and individuals resulting from the operation of an organizational system that processes, stores, or transmits CUI is assessed with the defined frequency.

assessment.examine: Risk assessment policy; security planning policy and procedures; procedures addressing organizational risk assessments; system security plan; risk assessment; risk assessment results; risk assessment reviews; risk assessment updates; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with risk assessment responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for risk assessment; mechanisms supporting or for conducting, documenting, reviewing, disseminating, and updating the risk assessment

guidance.summary: You write down how often you will assess risk - at least annually, plus whenever something big changes such as a new system, a move or an incident - and then you actually do it on that schedule and keep the result. A risk assessment lists the systems that handle CUI, the threats and vulnerabilities that matter to them, how likely and how damaging each is to operations, assets and people, and what you decided to do about it. It does not have to be long, but it has to be real and specific to your shop.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Policy sets an annual risk assessment each January plus a reassessment after major changes. The IT admin and the owner spend an afternoon on a spreadsheet: assets (file server, GCC High tenant, 25 PCs, 2 CNC controllers, firewall, backups), threats (ransomware via email, lost laptop, controller malware from vendor USB, an insider copying drawings, power loss), likelihood and impact scored 1 to 5, current controls, and resulting risk. The top risks - unpatched CNC controllers and no offline backup - become POA&M items with owners and dates. The signed assessment is filed with last year's and referenced in the SSP.
typical_evidence: Risk assessment policy or SSP text defining the frequency and triggers
The most recent risk assessment report or spreadsheet with date, participants, scope, method and results
The prior year's assessment showing the frequency is being met
Risk register with treatment decisions and links to POA&M items
Evidence of an event-driven reassessment (for example after migrating to GCC High)
common_gaps: The only 'risk assessment' is the SPRS self-score, which assesses controls, not risk
A template downloaded years ago with no shop-specific assets or threats and never updated
Frequency undefined, or defined as annual but the last one was three years ago
Risks identified but no decisions or follow-up, so nothing changes
remediation_steps: Set the frequency and triggers in policy: annually and on major changes (new system, cloud migration, facility change, significant incident).
Pick a lightweight method in the style of NIST SP 800-30 (asset, threat, vulnerability, likelihood, impact, risk level) and build a spreadsheet template.
Run the assessment with the owner, IT and the MSP, using the asset inventory, vulnerability scan results and incident history as inputs; document scope and participants.
Record a treatment decision for each significant risk (accept, mitigate, transfer) and feed mitigations into the POA&M (3.12.2) with owners and dates.
Have the owner sign the report, file it, calendar the next one, and keep at least three years of assessments.

controls.name: Vulnerability Scan
controls.statement: Scan for vulnerabilities in organizational systems and applications periodically and when new vulnerabilities affecting those systems and applications are identified.
controls.discussion: Organizations determine the required vulnerability scanning for all system components, ensuring that potential sources of vulnerabilities such as networked printers, scanners, and copiers are not overlooked. The vulnerabilities to be scanned are readily updated as new vulnerabilities are discovered, announced, and scanning methods developed. This process ensures that potential vulnerabilities in the system are identified and addressed as quickly as possible. Vulnerability analyses for custom software applications may require additional approaches such as static analysis, dynamic analysis, binary analysis, or a hybrid of the three approaches. Organizations can employ these analysis approaches in source code reviews and in a variety of tools (e.g., static analysis tools, web-based application scanners, binary analyzers) and in source code reviews. Vulnerability scanning includes: scanning for patch levels; scanning for functions, ports, protocols, and services that should not be accessible to users or devices; and scanning for improperly configured or incorrectly operating information flow control mechanisms. To facilitate interoperability, organizations consider using products that are Security Content Automated Protocol (SCAP)-validated, scanning tools that express vulnerabilities in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) naming convention, and that employ the Open Vulnerability Assessment Language (OVAL) to determine the presence of system vulnerabilities. Sources for vulnerability information include the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) listing and the National Vulnerability Database (NVD). Security assessments, such as red team exercises, provide additional sources of potential vulnerabilities for which to scan. Organizations also consider using scanning tools that express vulnerability impact by the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). In certain situations, the nature of the vulnerability scanning may be more intrusive or the system component that is the subject of the scanning may contain highly sensitive information. Privileged access authorization to selected system components facilitates thorough vulnerability scanning and protects the sensitive nature of such scanning.[SP 800-40] provides guidance on vulnerability management.

objectives.text: the frequency to scan for vulnerabilities in organizational systems and applications is defined.
vulnerability scans are performed on organizational systems with the defined frequency.
vulnerability scans are performed on applications with the defined frequency.
vulnerability scans are performed on organizational systems when new vulnerabilities are identified.
vulnerability scans are performed on applications when new vulnerabilities are identified.

assessment.examine: Risk assessment policy; procedures addressing vulnerability scanning; risk assessment; system security plan; security assessment report; vulnerability scanning tools and associated configuration documentation; vulnerability scanning results; patch and vulnerability management records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with risk assessment, security assessment and vulnerability scanning responsibilities; personnel with vulnerability scan analysis and remediation responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for vulnerability scanning, analysis, remediation, and information sharing; mechanisms supporting or implementing vulnerability scanning, analysis, remediation, and information sharing

guidance.summary: You run a vulnerability scanner against all your systems (PCs, the server, controllers where possible, the firewall and network devices) and the applications on them (operating systems, Office, browsers, CAD/CAM, the CNC software, anything internet-facing) on a schedule you have written down, and you also scan when a significant new vulnerability is announced. Credentialed (authenticated) scans are expected so that missing application patches are found, not just open ports.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The MSP runs a credentialed vulnerability scan of every PC, the server, the firewall and the two Windows CNC controllers every month using a commercial scanner agent, plus an external scan of the firewall's public address; the policy states monthly internal, monthly external, and out-of-cycle scans within 72 hours when CISA or a vendor announces a critical vulnerability affecting Windows, the firewall or the CNC software. The scans check installed applications, not just the OS. Reports go to the IT admin, who logs the results and tracks fixes under 3.11.3. The controller that cannot take an agent is scanned over the network during the maintenance window.
typical_evidence: Vulnerability management policy stating scan frequency for systems and applications and the trigger for out-of-cycle scans
Monthly scan reports (internal credentialed and external) for the past 12 months
Scanner configuration showing the scope covers all assets in the inventory and uses credentialed or agent mode
Evidence of an out-of-cycle scan after a major vulnerability announcement (ticket and report)
Subscription to CISA and vendor advisories (email screenshot)
Asset inventory reconciliation against scan targets
common_gaps: No scanner at all; 'we run Windows Update' is offered as the scan
Scans only cover office PCs; the file server, firewall and CNC controllers are excluded
Unauthenticated scans that miss application vulnerabilities
No process to scan when a major vulnerability is announced; scans only run on the calendar
remediation_steps: Define the frequency in policy: at least monthly credentialed internal scans of all systems and applications, monthly external scans of internet-facing addresses, and out-of-cycle scans within a set window (for example 72 hours) when new critical vulnerabilities affecting your products are announced.

Deploy a vulnerability scanner (agent-based on PCs and the server, network scans for the firewall, switches and controllers) with credentials so application-level checks run, and confirm the scan scope matches the hardware inventory from 3.4.1.
Subscribe to the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities alerts and the firewall, Windows and CNC/CAM vendor advisories, and assign someone to trigger out-of-cycle scans.
Schedule the scans, deliver reports to IT automatically, and store 12 months of reports.
Add a scan-coverage check to the quarterly review: any asset not scanned in the last cycle is investigated.

controls.name: Vulnerability Remediation
controls.statement: Remediate vulnerabilities in accordance with risk assessments.
controls.discussion: Vulnerabilities discovered, for example, via the scanning conducted in response to 3.11.2, are remediated with consideration of the related assessment of risk. The consideration of risk influences the prioritization of remediation efforts and the level of effort to be expended in the remediation for specific vulnerabilities.

objectives.text: vulnerabilities are identified.
vulnerabilities are remediated in accordance with risk assessments.

assessment.examine: Risk assessment policy; procedures addressing vulnerability scanning; risk assessment; system security plan; security assessment report; vulnerability scanning tools and associated configuration documentation; vulnerability scanning results; patch and vulnerability management records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with risk assessment, security assessment and vulnerability scanning responsibilities; personnel with vulnerability scan analysis responsibilities; personnel with vulnerability remediation responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities; system or network administrators
assessment.test: Organizational processes for vulnerability scanning, analysis, remediation, and information sharing; mechanisms supporting or implementing vulnerability scanning, analysis, remediation, and information sharing

guidance.summary: Findings from your scans and advisories have to be fixed on a schedule that follows the risk - critical and actively exploited vulnerabilities fast, low ones on a longer timeline - and tracked until closed. Where something cannot be fixed (an old CNC controller), you document the risk decision and a compensating control. The assessor wants to see both the identification (scan output) and the record of each item being fixed or formally accepted.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The policy sets remediation targets: critical or known-exploited within 14 days, high within 30 days, medium within 90 days, low at the next patch cycle, with exceptions approved by the owner in writing. The MSP pushes Windows and third-party patches weekly, and each monthly scan is compared with the previous one to confirm findings dropped off. The two CNC controllers run an old Windows build the machine vendor will not update; the risk assessment accepted that with compensating controls (isolated VLAN, no internet, USB blocked, application allow-listing) and it is tracked as a POA&M item re-evaluated each year.
typical_evidence: Vulnerability management policy with risk-based remediation timelines
Scan-to-scan comparison or trend report showing findings closed
Patch deployment reports from the endpoint-management or RMM tool
Tickets tracking specific vulnerabilities from finding to closure
Documented risk acceptance or exception records with compensating controls and review dates
POA&M entries for long-term items such as unpatchable controllers
common_gaps: Scans run but nobody acts on the reports; the same criticals appear every month
No defined timelines, so 'we will get to it' is the standard
Third-party applications (browsers, PDF readers, Java, CAD viewers) never patched, only Windows
Legacy controllers ignored rather than isolated and documented as accepted risk
remediation_steps: Set remediation timelines by severity in policy (for example critical or KEV within 14 days, high 30, medium 90, low at next cycle) and an exception process approved by the owner.
Enable automated OS and third-party patching through the endpoint-management or RMM tool for all PCs and the server, and schedule firewall firmware updates quarterly or on advisory.
Review each monthly scan report, open a ticket for every finding above low with an owner and due date, and close it when the next scan confirms the finding is gone.
For items that cannot be fixed, record a risk acceptance with compensating controls (network isolation, allow-listing, USB blocking), the owner's signature and a review date, and add it to the POA&M.
Report remediation status (open findings by severity, overdue count) to the owner monthly.

controls.name: Security Control Assessment
controls.statement: Periodically assess the security controls in organizational systems to determine if the controls are effective in their application.
controls.discussion: Organizations assess security controls in organizational systems and the environments in which those systems operate as part of the system development life cycle. Security controls are the safeguards or countermeasures organizations implement to satisfy security requirements. By assessing the implemented security controls, organizations determine if the security safeguards or countermeasures are in place and operating as intended. Security control assessments ensure that information security is built into organizational systems; identify weaknesses and deficiencies early in the development process; provide essential information needed to make risk-based decisions; and ensure compliance to vulnerability mitigation procedures. Assessments are conducted on the implemented security controls as documented in system security plans. Security assessment reports document assessment results in sufficient detail as deemed necessary by organizations, to determine the accuracy and completeness of the reports and whether the security controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended, and producing the desired outcome with respect to meeting security requirements. Security assessment results are provided to the individuals or roles appropriate for the types of assessments being conducted. Organizations ensure that security assessment results are current, relevant to the determination of security control effectiveness, and obtained with the appropriate level of assessor independence. Organizations can choose to use other types of assessment activities such as vulnerability scanning and system monitoring to maintain the security posture of systems during the system life cycle.[SP 800-53] provides guidance on security and privacy controls for systems and organizations. [SP 800-53A] provides guidance on developing security assessment plans and conducting assessments.

objectives.text: the frequency of security control assessments is defined.
security controls are assessed with the defined frequency to determine if the controls are effective in their application.

assessment.examine: Security assessment and authorization policy; procedures addressing security assessment planning; procedures addressing security assessments; security assessment plan; system security plan; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with security assessment responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting security assessment, security assessment plan development, and security assessment reporting

guidance.summary: On a schedule you have defined (at least annually) you check every one of the 110 requirements to see whether it is actually working the way your SSP says - not just whether a policy exists. The assessment can be done by you, the MSP or an outside firm, but it must be written down, cover each requirement using the 800-171A objectives, and produce findings that go into the POA&M. This is the periodic deep check; 3.12.3 is the continuous watching in between.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Policy requires a full self-assessment against NIST SP 800-171A every 12 months and a targeted assessment after major changes. Each September the IT admin and the MSP walk through all 110 requirements using the 800-171A objectives: examining artifacts, interviewing the office manager and shop supervisor, and testing settings (trying a blocked USB stick, checking MFA on a test account, attempting a restore). Results are recorded per objective (met, not met, not applicable) in the assessment workbook, the SPRS score is recalculated and resubmitted, and every 'not met' goes to the POA&M with an owner and date.
typical_evidence: Assessment policy or SSP section defining frequency and method
Completed assessment workbook or report with date, assessor, per-objective results and evidence references
Prior assessment reports showing the cycle is being followed
SPRS submission record consistent with the assessment
POA&M entries created from assessment findings
Third-party or MSP assessment engagement letter, if used
common_gaps: The SPRS self-score was entered once years ago and never revisited
The assessment is a checklist of 'do we have a policy' with no testing of whether controls work
Findings noted but never turned into POA&M items
Frequency not written down anywhere
remediation_steps: Write the assessment policy: full assessment of all 110 requirements at least annually, targeted reassessment after significant changes, who performs it, and how results are recorded.
Build an assessment workbook with every 800-171A objective (320 objectives) and columns for status, evidence location and notes.
Perform the assessment using examine, interview and test methods, and collect evidence artifacts into an organized evidence folder per control.
Record findings, update the SSP where actual implementation differs from what was written, and create POA&M items for every unmet objective with owner and due date.
Recalculate and resubmit the SPRS score within 30 days of completing the assessment, and calendar the next one.

controls.name: Plan of Action
controls.statement: Develop and implement plans of action designed to correct deficiencies and reduce or eliminate vulnerabilities in organizational systems.
controls.discussion: The plan of action is a key document in the information security program. Organizations develop plans of action that describe how any unimplemented security requirements will be met and how any planned mitigations will be implemented. Organizations can document the system security plan and plan of action as separate or combined documents and in any chosen format. Federal agencies may consider the submitted system security plans and plans of action as critical inputs to an overall risk management decision to process, store, or transmit CUI on a system hosted by a nonfederal organization and whether it is advisable to pursue an agreement or contract with the nonfederal organization. [NIST CUI] provides supplemental material for Special Publication 800-171 including templates for plans of action.

objectives.text: deficiencies and vulnerabilities to be addressed by the plan of action are identified.
a plan of action is developed to correct identified deficiencies and reduce or eliminate identified vulnerabilities.
the plan of action is implemented to correct identified deficiencies and reduce or eliminate identified vulnerabilities.

assessment.examine: Security assessment and authorization policy; procedures addressing plan of action; system security plan; security assessment plan; security assessment report; security assessment evidence; plan of action; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with plan of action development and implementation responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Mechanisms for developing, implementing, and maintaining plan of action

guidance.summary: Every requirement you have not fully met, and every significant weakness found by assessments, scans or incidents, goes onto a plan of action and milestones (POA&M) that says what is wrong, what you will do about it, who owns it, what resources it needs and when it will be done. Then you work the plan and update it as items close. A POA&M that never changes is a sign it is not being implemented.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop keeps a POA&M spreadsheet with one row per open item, for example: '3.13.11 - backup encryption not FIPS-validated; action: move to the backup product's FIPS mode; owner: IT admin; resources: $2,400 license; milestones: quote by Oct 15, deploy by Nov 30; status: in progress.' Items come from the annual assessment, the monthly scans and the incident log. The owner and IT review it monthly, close items with a link to the evidence, and keep closed rows in a history tab. The assessor can see items opened, worked and closed across the past year.
typical_evidence: Current POA&M with weakness, source, planned actions, owner, resources, milestones with dates, and status
POA&M history showing items closed with dates and evidence references
Monthly review meeting notes or tickets showing progress
Assessment report, scan reports or incident records that fed the POA&M
POA&M template consistent with the NIST CUI POA&M format
common_gaps: No POA&M, or one created for the SPRS submission and never touched again
Items with no owner, date or resources, so nothing ever moves
Only assessment findings tracked; scan results and incident lessons never make it in
Items closed with no evidence
remediation_steps: Adopt a POA&M template with columns for control ID, weakness description, source (assessment, scan, incident), planned actions, owner, resources needed, milestones and dates, status, completion date and evidence.
Populate it from the latest self-assessment, the last vulnerability scan and the risk assessment, including every requirement that is not fully implemented.
Assign an owner and realistic dates to each item (a CMMC conditional certification allows 180 days for POA&M closeout, so plan tighter than that).
Review the POA&M monthly with the owner: update status, reallocate resources, and close items only with evidence attached.
Keep closed items in a history tab and reference the POA&M from the SSP.

controls.name: Security Control Monitoring
controls.statement: Monitor security controls on an ongoing basis to ensure the continued effectiveness of the controls.
controls.discussion: Continuous monitoring programs facilitate ongoing awareness of threats, vulnerabilities, and information security to support organizational risk management decisions. The terms continuous and ongoing imply that organizations assess and analyze security controls and information security-related risks at a frequency sufficient to support risk-based decisions. The results of continuous monitoring programs generate appropriate risk response actions by organizations. Providing access to security information on a continuing basis through reports or dashboards gives organizational officials the capability to make effective and timely risk management decisions. Automation supports more frequent updates to hardware, software, firmware inventories, and other system information. Effectiveness is further enhanced when continuous monitoring outputs are formatted to provide information that is specific, measurable, actionable, relevant, and timely. Monitoring requirements, including the need for specific monitoring, may also be referenced in other requirements.[SP 800-137] provides guidance on continuous monitoring.

objectives.text: security controls are monitored on an ongoing basis to ensure the continued effectiveness of those controls.

assessment.examine: Security planning policy; organizational procedures addressing system security plan development and implementation; procedures addressing system security plan reviews and updates; enterprise architecture documentation; system security plan; records of system security plan reviews and updates; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with security planning and system security plan implementation responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for system security plan development, review, update, and approval; mechanisms supporting the system security plan

guidance.summary: Between annual assessments you continuously check that key controls still work: reviewing logs and alerts, confirming patches applied, checking backup success, reviewing account and access lists, verifying MFA and encryption status, watching scan trends. You should have a written monitoring schedule (what is checked, how often, by whom) and records showing the checks happened. This is what keeps controls from quietly decaying between assessments.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's continuous monitoring plan is a one-page table: daily - EDR and backup job alerts reviewed by IT; weekly - patch compliance report and firewall alerts; monthly - vulnerability scan review, review of new and disabled accounts, USB block log, physical access logs; quarterly - full access recertification, BitLocker and MFA status export, restore test, POA&M review; annually - full assessment, policy review, training. Each check is a recurring ticket in the MSP's system that is closed with a note or screenshot, so a year of evidence accumulates on its own.
typical_evidence: Continuous monitoring plan or schedule listing controls, what is checked, frequency and owner
Recurring ticket or checklist history showing checks were performed on schedule
Dashboards or reports used: EDR, patch compliance, backup success, MFA coverage, scan trends
Quarterly access review records
Evidence that a monitoring finding led to a fix (ticket or POA&M item)
common_gaps: Controls set up once and never checked; MFA quietly disabled for a user, backups failing for months
Alerts go to a mailbox nobody reads
No schedule, so monitoring is whatever the MSP happens to notice
Monitoring happens but leaves no record
remediation_steps: Write a monitoring schedule that maps each key control to a check, a frequency and an owner (daily alerts, weekly patch and backup status, monthly scan, account and log reviews, quarterly recertification and restore tests, annual assessment).
Turn on the dashboards and reports the checks depend on (EDR, RMM patch compliance, backup job status, Entra ID or AD MFA and sign-in reports, scanner trends) and route alerts to a monitored queue.
Create recurring tickets or a checklist for each check and require a note or screenshot when it is closed.
Feed any failure into the incident process or the POA&M and record the fix.
Review the monitoring records quarterly with the owner and adjust the schedule after each annual assessment.

controls.name: System Security Plan
controls.statement: Develop, document, and periodically update system security plans that describe system boundaries, system environments of operation, how security requirements are implemented, and the relationships with or connections to other systems.
controls.discussion: System security plans relate security requirements to a set of security controls. System security plans also describe, at a high level, how the security controls meet those security requirements, but do not provide detailed, technical descriptions of the design or implementation of the controls. System security plans contain sufficient information to enable a design and implementation that is unambiguously compliant with the intent of the plans and subsequent determinations of risk if the plan is implemented as intended. Security plans need not be single documents; the plans can be a collection of various documents including documents that already exist. Effective security plans make extensive use of references to policies, procedures, and additional documents (e.g., design and implementation specifications) where more detailed information can be obtained. This reduces the documentation requirements associated with security programs and maintains security-related information in other established management/operational areas related to enterprise architecture, system development life cycle, systems engineering, and acquisition. Federal agencies may consider the submitted system security plans and plans of action as critical inputs to an overall risk management decision to process, store, or transmit CUI on a system hosted by a nonfederal organization and whether it is advisable to pursue an agreement or contract with the nonfederal organization.[SP 800-18] provides guidance on developing security plans. [NIST CUI] provides supplemental material for Special Publication 800-171 including templates for system security plans.

objectives.text: a system security plan is developed.
the system boundary is described and documented in the system security plan.
the system environment of operation is described and documented in the system security plan.
the security requirements identified and approved by the designated authority as non-applicable are identified.
the method of security requirement implementation is described and documented in the system security plan.
the relationship with or connection to other systems is described and documented in the system security plan.
the frequency to update the system security plan is defined.
system security plan is updated with the defined frequency.

assessment.examine: Security planning policy; procedures addressing system security plan development and implementation; procedures addressing system security plan reviews and updates; enterprise architecture documentation; system security plan; records of system security plan reviews and updates; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with security planning and system security plan implementation responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for system security plan development, review, update, and approval; mechanisms supporting the system security plan

guidance.summary: The SSP is the master document describing your CUI environment: what is in scope (the boundary), what the environment looks like (hardware, software, network, cloud services, locations, people), how each of the 110 requirements is implemented or why it is not applicable and who approved that, and what other systems you connect to (GCC High, the MSP's tools, customer portals). You define how often it is updated - at least annually and after major changes - and you keep it current. Without an SSP a DoD assessment cannot be scored at all, which is why the requirement carries no point value.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's SSP is a 60-page document: a scope section with a network diagram showing the CUI VLAN (25 PCs, file server, 2 CNC controllers, firewall), the GCC High tenant, the MSP's remote-management connection and the out-of-scope guest Wi-Fi; an asset list; a table of people and roles; and, for each of the 110 requirements, a paragraph stating how it is implemented and pointing to the policy or setting. The one requirement marked not applicable (3.13.14, because the shop has no VoIP) carries the owner's signed approval. The version table shows annual updates each September and an extra update after the GCC High migration.
typical_evidence: The SSP itself, with version history, approval signature and date
Network or boundary diagram and asset inventory referenced by the SSP
Per-requirement implementation statements covering all 110 requirements
Signed not-applicable determinations by the designated authority (the owner)
Interconnection list or agreements for external systems (GCC High, MSP, customer portals)
Policy or SSP clause defining the update frequency and evidence of updates
common_gaps: No SSP, or a generic template with the vendor's name still in it
Boundary not defined, so the assessor cannot tell whether the shop-floor controllers or the guest Wi-Fi are in scope
Implementation statements that just restate the requirement ('the organization limits access') instead of describing what is actually done
Not-applicable decisions made by IT with no documented approval, and the SSP never updated since it was first written
remediation_steps: Start from the NIST CUI SSP template and set the boundary: list every asset that stores, processes or transmits CUI, the security-protection assets (firewall, EDR, backup), and what is out of scope; draw the network diagram.
Describe the environment of operation: locations, hardware, software, cloud services, users and roles, and the CUI data flow from customer receipt to delivery.

For each of the 110 requirements write a specific implementation statement (what, where, who, which setting or policy) and mark its status (implemented, partially implemented, planned, not applicable).
Document each not-applicable determination with a rationale and the owner's signature as the designated authority.
List external connections (GCC High, MSP remote management, customer portals, email gateway) and how each is protected or covered by agreement.
Set the update frequency in the SSP (annually and after significant change), maintain a version table, and have the owner approve each version.

controls.name: Boundary Protection
controls.statement: Monitor, control, and protect communications (i.e., information transmitted or received by organizational systems) at the external boundaries and key internal boundaries of organizational systems.
controls.discussion: Communications can be monitored, controlled, and protected at boundary components and by restricting or prohibiting interfaces in organizational systems. Boundary components include gateways, routers, firewalls, guards, network-based malicious code analysis and virtualization systems, or encrypted tunnels implemented within a system security architecture (e.g., routers protecting firewalls or application gateways residing on protected subnetworks). Restricting or prohibiting interfaces in organizational systems includes restricting external web communications traffic to designated web servers within managed interfaces and prohibiting external traffic that appears to be spoofing internal addresses. Organizations consider the shared nature of commercial telecommunications services in the implementation of security requirements associated with the use of such services. Commercial telecommunications services are commonly based on network components and consolidated management systems shared by all attached commercial customers and may also include third party-provided access lines and other service elements. Such transmission services may represent sources of increased risk despite contract security provisions.[SP 800-41] provides guidance on firewalls and firewall policy. [SP 800-125B] provides guidance on security for virtualization technologies.

objectives.text: the external system boundary is defined.
key internal system boundaries are defined.
communications are monitored at the external system boundary.
communications are monitored at key internal boundaries.
communications are controlled at the external system boundary.
communications are controlled at key internal boundaries.
communications are protected at the external system boundary.
communications are protected at key internal boundaries.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing boundary protection; system security plan; list of key internal boundaries of the system; system design documentation; boundary protection hardware and software; enterprise security architecture documentation; system audit logs and records; system configuration settings and associated documentation; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; system developer; personnel with boundary protection responsibilities
assessment.test: Mechanisms implementing boundary protection capability

guidance.summary: Watch, control and protect the traffic that crosses the edge of your CUI environment and the important boundaries inside it. In a small shop this is the firewall at the internet edge plus whatever separates the CUI network from the guest Wi-Fi, the shop floor and any vendor connections. You must be able to say where the boundary is, what crosses it and how it is monitored.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop draws a one-page network diagram showing the CUI enclave (engineering PCs, file server, the two CNC controllers) behind a next-generation firewall, with guest Wi-Fi and the front-office camera system on separate VLANs that cannot reach it. The firewall runs deny-by-default inbound, logs all allowed and denied sessions to the MSP's collector, and the MSP reviews the weekly report. Remote users reach the enclave only through the firewall's VPN, and there is no direct RDP from the internet.
typical_evidence: Network diagram showing the external boundary, internal VLAN boundaries and where CUI lives
Firewall configuration export or screenshot of the rule base showing default-deny inbound
Firewall/VPN logs or SIEM dashboard showing monitored boundary traffic
Change-control tickets for firewall rule changes
Host firewall settings enforced by policy on endpoints (Bulwark check os.firewall.enabled)
common_gaps: No current network diagram, so the assessment boundary cannot be demonstrated
Flat network where the guest Wi-Fi, cameras and CNC machines share the CUI subnet
Firewall logs generated but never reviewed by anyone
Port-forwarded RDP left open from a previous support arrangement
remediation_steps: Draw and date a network diagram that marks the CUI enclave, every boundary device and every external connection.
Set the perimeter firewall to deny inbound by default and remove any port forwards you cannot justify in writing.
Separate guest Wi-Fi, IoT/cameras and shop-floor devices onto VLANs with explicit rules to the CUI enclave.
Enable logging on all boundary rules and forward the logs to a collector retained for at least 90 days.
Assign a named person to review boundary logs weekly and record the review.
Enable and enforce the host firewall on every endpoint so internal boundaries are protected too.

controls.name: Security Engineering
controls.statement: Employ architectural designs, software development techniques, and systems engineering principles that promote effective information security within organizational systems.
controls.discussion: Organizations apply systems security engineering principles to new development systems or systems undergoing major upgrades. For legacy systems, organizations apply systems security engineering principles to system upgrades and modifications to the extent feasible, given the current state of hardware, software, and firmware components within those systems. The application of systems security engineering concepts and principles helps to develop trustworthy, secure, and resilient systems and system components and reduce the susceptibility of organizations to disruptions, hazards, and threats. Examples of these concepts and principles include developing layered protections; establishing security policies, architecture, and controls as the foundation for design; incorporating security requirements into the system development life cycle; delineating physical and logical security boundaries; ensuring that developers are trained on how to build secure software; and performing threat modeling to identify use cases, threat agents, attack vectors and patterns, design patterns, and compensating controls needed to mitigate risk. Organizations that apply security engineering concepts and principles can facilitate the development of trustworthy, secure systems, system components, and system services; reduce risk to acceptable levels; and make informed risk-management decisions.[SP 800-160-1] provides guidance on systems security engineering.

objectives.text: architectural designs that promote effective information security are identified.
software development techniques that promote effective information security are identified.
systems engineering principles that promote effective information security are identified.
identified architectural designs that promote effective information security are employed.
