identified software development techniques that promote effective information security are employed.
identified systems engineering principles that promote effective information security are employed.

assessment.examine: Security planning policy; procedures addressing system security plan development and implementation; procedures addressing system security plan reviews and updates; enterprise architecture documentation; system security plan; records of system security plan reviews and updates; system and communications protection policy; procedures addressing security engineering principles used in the specification, design, development, implementation, and modification of the system; security architecture documentation; security requirements and specifications for the system; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with responsibility for determining information system security requirements; personnel with information system design, development, implementation, and modification responsibilities; personnel with security planning and system security plan implementation responsibilities; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for system security plan development, review, update, and approval; mechanisms supporting the system security plan; processes for applying security engineering principles in system specification, design, development, implementation, and modification; automated mechanisms supporting the application of security engineering principles in information system specification, design, development, implementation, and modification

guidance.summary: Apply architectural and engineering principles when you design or change the system, rather than bolting security on afterwards. For a small shop this means having written design principles you actually follow: least privilege, defence in depth, segmentation, secure defaults, and a rule that changes are reviewed for security before they go in.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's four-page system security architecture document states its principles: CUI stays in the enclave, no CUI on personal devices, admin work is done from a separate admin account, every new system is hardened against a CIS benchmark before it is connected, and every change goes through the MSP's change ticket with a security note. When the owner wanted a new quoting app, the MSP documented where its data lives and confirmed it holds no CUI before installing it.
typical_evidence: System security architecture or design-principles document
Change-management procedure requiring a security review step
Hardening standard or benchmark used for new builds (CIS, DISA STIG, vendor baseline)
Sample change tickets showing the security review was performed
Architecture review notes from the last significant system change
common_gaps: Security decisions made ad hoc by whoever installs the system
No written principles, so an assessor has nothing to examine
New machines joined to the network without hardening
Changes made directly on production with no record
remediation_steps: Write a short system security architecture document stating your principles and the CUI boundary.
Adopt a published hardening baseline and record which benchmark and version you use.
Add a mandatory security-impact question to your change ticket template.
Build new endpoints from the hardened image, then verify with an automated check before release.
Review the architecture document annually and after any significant change, and date the review.

controls.name: Role Separation
controls.statement: Separate user functionality from system management functionality.
controls.discussion: System management functionality includes functions necessary to administer databases, network components, workstations, or servers, and typically requires privileged user access. The separation of user functionality from system management functionality is physical or logical. Organizations can implement separation of system management functionality from user functionality by using different computers, different central processing units, different instances of operating systems, or different network addresses; virtualization techniques; or combinations of these or other methods, as appropriate. This type of separation includes web administrative interfaces that use separate authentication methods for users of any other system resources. Separation of system and user functionality may include isolating administrative interfaces on different domains and with additional access controls.

objectives.text: user functionality is identified.
system management functionality is identified.
user functionality is separated from system management functionality.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing application partitioning; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system security plan; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; system developer
assessment.test: Separation of user functionality from system management functionality

guidance.summary: Keep user-facing functionality separate from system management functionality so ordinary users never see or reach administrative interfaces. In practice: administrators use separate admin accounts, management consoles are not published to normal users, and servers do not double as workstations.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The IT person signs in day to day as jsmith and only uses jsmith-adm to open the firewall console, the RMM portal and the file server. The server runs no user applications and nobody browses the web from it. The ERP's admin module is restricted to a role that only two people hold.
typical_evidence: Account list showing separate administrative accounts
Role/permission export from the ERP, RMM or file server showing management roles restricted
Screenshot showing management consoles reachable only from admin workstations or accounts
Policy statement requiring separate admin credentials
common_gaps: One account used for both email and firewall administration
Server used as a general-purpose desktop
Management web interfaces reachable from any workstation on the LAN
remediation_steps: Create a separate administrative account for every person who administers systems.
Remove day-to-day users from administrative roles in the ERP, RMM and cloud tenants.
Restrict management consoles by IP, VLAN or conditional access so only admin systems reach them.
Stop using servers as workstations; install no user productivity software on them.
Verify separation at least annually as part of the access review.

controls.name: Shared Resource Control
controls.statement: Prevent unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources.
controls.discussion: The control of information in shared system resources (e.g., registers, cache memory, main memory, hard disks) is also commonly referred to as object reuse and residual information protection. This requirement prevents information produced by the actions of prior users or roles (or the actions of processes acting on behalf of prior users or roles) from being available to any current users or roles (or current processes acting on behalf of current users or roles) that obtain access to shared system resources after those resources have been released back to the system. This requirement also applies to encrypted representations of information. This requirement does not address information remanence, which refers to residual representation of data that has been nominally deleted; covert channels (including storage or timing channels) where shared resources are manipulated to violate information flow restrictions; or components within systems for which there are only single users or roles.

objectives.text: unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources is prevented.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing application partitioning; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; system developer
assessment.test: Separation of user functionality from system management functionality

guidance.summary: Make sure information does not leak from one user or process to another through shared resources such as memory, temporary files, clipboards or reused disk space. On modern operating systems this is largely inherited from the platform, but you must confirm it is enabled and not defeated by shared profiles or shared scratch folders.
guidance.machine_shop_example: All PCs run a current, supported Windows build with default memory and object protections intact, users have separate profiles, and the shared 'scratch' folder on the file server was removed in favour of per-user folders. The CNC controllers' shared program directory is read-only to operators and cleared between jobs, so one customer's drawing cannot be picked up by the next operator.
typical_evidence: Evidence that systems run supported OS versions with default protections (Bulwark check os.patch.os_supported)
File server permission export showing per-user home folders instead of a shared scratch area
Procedure for clearing temporary job files on shared shop-floor systems
Screenshot of user profile separation on a shared-use workstation
common_gaps: A shared 'transfer' or 'scratch' folder everyone can read and write
Shared local accounts on shop-floor PCs so profiles and temp files are common
End-of-life operating systems where platform protections are no longer patched
remediation_steps: Remove open shared folders and replace them with per-user or per-project folders with explicit permissions.
Give every operator an individual account on shared-use machines.
Keep operating systems on supported, patched releases.
Document a routine for clearing temporary job files from shop-floor systems between jobs.
Disable clipboard and drive redirection in remote sessions unless there is a documented need.

controls.name: Public-Access System Separation
controls.statement: Implement subnetworks for publicly accessible system components that are physically or logically separated from internal networks.
controls.discussion: Subnetworks that are physically or logically separated from internal networks are referred to as demilitarized zones (DMZs). DMZs are typically implemented with boundary control devices and techniques that include routers, gateways, firewalls, virtualization, or cloud-based technologies. [SP 800-41] provides guidance on firewalls and firewall policy. [SP 800-125B] provides guidance on security for virtualization technologies.

objectives.text: publicly accessible system components are identified.
subnetworks for publicly accessible system components are physically or logically separated from internal networks.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing boundary protection; system security plan; list of key internal boundaries of the system; system design documentation; boundary protection hardware and software; system configuration settings and associated documentation; enterprise security architecture documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; system developer; personnel with boundary protection responsibilities
assessment.test: Mechanisms implementing boundary protection capability

guidance.summary: Anything the public can reach must sit on a separate, isolated subnetwork, not inside the network that holds CUI. For most shops that means the website and any customer portal are hosted externally, and guest Wi-Fi is on its own VLAN with no route into the enclave.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The company website and RFQ portal are hosted by a third party outside the shop's network. Guest Wi-Fi for visiting customers is a separate SSID on its own VLAN with client isolation and a firewall rule that permits internet only. The DMZ VLAN that once hosted an FTP drop was retired when file exchange moved to the GCC High tenant.
typical_evidence: Network diagram showing publicly accessible components outside the CUI enclave or in a DMZ
Firewall rules proving no route from the guest/DMZ VLAN to the CUI enclave
Hosting contract or DNS records showing the website is externally hosted
Wireless controller configuration showing guest SSID isolation
common_gaps: Guest Wi-Fi bridged onto the main LAN
A web server or file-drop hosted on the same subnet as engineering PCs
Firewall rules that allow the DMZ to initiate connections into the enclave
remediation_steps: Move any publicly reachable service off the CUI network, ideally to an external host.
Put guest and visitor wireless on a dedicated VLAN with client isolation and internet-only rules.
Write explicit deny rules from public segments to the CUI enclave and log them.
Retire legacy public services such as FTP drops in favour of the cloud tenant.
Re-test the isolation after any firewall or wireless change.

controls.name: Network Communication by Exception
controls.statement: Deny network communications traffic by default and allow network communications traffic by exception (i.e., deny all, permit by exception).
controls.discussion: This requirement applies to inbound and outbound network communications traffic at the system boundary and at identified points within the system. A deny-all, permit-by-exception network communications traffic policy ensures that only those connections which are essential and approved are allowed.

objectives.text: network communications traffic is denied by default.
network communications traffic is allowed by exception.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing boundary protection; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; system developer; personnel with boundary protection responsibilities
assessment.test: Mechanisms implementing traffic management at managed interfaces

guidance.summary: Network traffic must be denied by default and allowed only by explicit exception, at the perimeter and on the hosts. Every allowed flow should be justified and documented.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The firewall's inbound policy is deny-all with a short, documented list of exceptions (VPN and nothing else), and outbound is restricted to the categories the shop needs, with the CNC VLAN allowed to reach only the file server and the vendor update host. Windows Defender Firewall is enforced by Group Policy on every endpoint with inbound default-block, and the rule list is exported quarterly.
typical_evidence: Firewall rule base export showing default-deny with an explicit allow list
Documented justification for each inbound and outbound exception
Group Policy or MDM setting enforcing host firewall default-block inbound (Bulwark check os.firewall.default_inbound_block)
Quarterly rule review record with sign-off
common_gaps: Any-any outbound rules and stale allow rules for systems that no longer exist
Host firewalls turned off during troubleshooting and never turned back on
Exceptions added by phone with no ticket or justification
remediation_steps: Set the perimeter firewall's default inbound and outbound actions to deny, then add only justified rules.
Enforce the host firewall by policy so users cannot disable it, with inbound default-block.
Document the business justification and owner for every exception.
Review the rule base quarterly and remove anything unjustified or unused.
Alert on host-firewall state changes through the RMM.

controls.name: Split Tunneling
controls.statement: Prevent remote devices from simultaneously establishing non-remote connections with organizational systems and communicating via some other connection to resources in external networks (i.e., split tunneling).
controls.discussion: Split tunneling might be desirable by remote users to communicate with local system resources such as printers or file servers. However, split tunneling allows unauthorized external connections, making the system more vulnerable to attack and to exfiltration of organizational information. This requirement is implemented in remote devices (e.g., notebook computers, smart phones, and tablets) through configuration settings to disable split tunneling in those devices, and by preventing configuration settings from being readily configurable by users. This requirement is implemented in the system by the detection of split tunneling (or of configuration settings that allow split tunneling) in the remote device, and by prohibiting the connection if the remote device is using split tunneling.

objectives.text: remote devices are prevented from simultaneously establishing non-remote connections with the system and communicating via some other connection to resources in external networks (i.e., split tunneling).

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing boundary protection; system security plan; system design documentation; system hardware and software; system architecture; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; system developer; personnel with boundary protection responsibilities
assessment.test: Mechanisms implementing boundary protection capability; mechanisms supporting or restricting non-remote connections

guidance.summary: When a remote device is connected to your network, it must not simultaneously route traffic to other networks, unless the remote endpoint is under your control and the configuration is documented. The point is to stop a laptop becoming a bridge between the internet and your CUI network.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The firewall's VPN profile pushes a full-tunnel configuration: while the estimator's laptop is on the VPN all traffic goes through the shop's firewall and is inspected, and the client blocks local LAN access. The setting is locked in the VPN client profile so a user cannot switch it off.
typical_evidence: VPN profile or client configuration showing split tunneling disabled (full tunnel)
Screenshot of the VPN client settings locked against user modification
Remote access policy statement prohibiting split tunneling
Firewall documentation of the remote-access configuration
common_gaps: Default split-tunnel VPN profiles left in place for performance reasons
Users able to edit the VPN client profile
Personal devices connecting to the VPN with no control over local routing
remediation_steps: Configure the VPN to full-tunnel and disable local LAN access in the client profile.
Lock the profile so users cannot change the tunnel mode.
State the requirement in the remote access policy and in user training.
Test from a remote laptop that traffic exits through the shop's firewall.
If a business need requires split tunneling, document the exception, the compensating controls and the approval.

controls.name: Data in Transit
controls.statement: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure of CUI during transmission unless otherwise protected by alternative physical safeguards.
controls.discussion: This requirement applies to internal and external networks and any system components that can transmit information including servers, notebook computers, desktop computers, mobile devices, printers, copiers, scanners, and facsimile machines. Communication paths outside the physical protection of controlled boundaries are susceptible to both interception and modification. Organizations relying on commercial providers offering transmission services as commodity services rather than as fully dedicated services (i.e., services which can be highly specialized to individual customer needs), may find it difficult to obtain the necessary assurances regarding the implementation of the controls for transmission confidentiality. In such situations, organizations determine what types of confidentiality services are available in commercial telecommunication service packages. If it is infeasible or impractical to obtain the necessary safeguards and assurances of the effectiveness of the safeguards through appropriate contracting vehicles, organizations implement compensating safeguards or explicitly accept the additional risk. An example of an alternative physical safeguard is a protected distribution system (PDS) where the distribution medium is protected against electronic or physical intercept, thereby ensuring the confidentiality of the information being transmitted. See [NIST CRYPTO].

objectives.text: cryptographic mechanisms intended to prevent unauthorized disclosure of CUI are identified.
alternative physical safeguards intended to prevent unauthorized disclosure of CUI are identified.
either cryptographic mechanisms or alternative physical safeguards are implemented to prevent unauthorized disclosure of CUI during transmission.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing transmission confidentiality and integrity; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; system developer
assessment.test: Cryptographic mechanisms or mechanisms supporting or implementing transmission confidentiality; organizational processes for defining and implementing alternative physical safeguards

guidance.summary: CUI must be encrypted whenever it moves over a network, unless an alternative physical safeguard protects it. Email, file transfer, remote access, wireless and management sessions all count. Identify which mechanism protects each path.
guidance.machine_shop_example: CUI travels only over TLS 1.2 or better: SharePoint and Outlook in GCC High, SMB 3 with encryption enabled on the file server share, SFTP for the one customer who still needs it, and the IPsec VPN for remote work. Legacy SSL/TLS versions are disabled on servers and endpoints, and the old unencrypted FTP transfer to a vendor was replaced with a GCC High sharing link.
typical_evidence: List of CUI transmission paths and the encryption protecting each one
Server/endpoint TLS configuration showing legacy protocols disabled (Bulwark check os.crypto.legacy_tls_disabled)
SMB signing and encryption settings on the file server
Email encryption configuration or S/MIME certificates
Screenshot of SFTP or portal transfer replacing plain FTP
common_gaps: CUI drawings emailed as plain attachments to personal addresses
Plain FTP or HTTP transfers to customers or vendors
TLS 1.0/1.1 still enabled on the file server or ERP
Wireless using WPA2-Personal with a shared key posted in the shop
remediation_steps: Inventory every path CUI takes across a network and note the encryption in use.
Disable SSL 2.0/3.0 and TLS 1.0/1.1 on servers, endpoints and network devices.
Enable SMB signing and encryption on shares holding CUI.
Replace plain FTP/HTTP transfers with SFTP, HTTPS or a cloud sharing link.
Move CUI email to the GCC High tenant and train staff never to send CUI to personal addresses.
Move wireless to WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X.

controls.name: Connections Termination
controls.statement: Terminate network connections associated with communications sessions at the end of the sessions or after a defined period of inactivity.
controls.discussion: This requirement applies to internal and external networks. Terminating network connections associated with communications sessions include de-allocating associated TCP/IP address or port pairs at the operating system level, or de-allocating networking assignments at the application level if multiple application sessions are using a single, operating system-level network connection. Time periods of user inactivity may be established by organizations and include time periods by type of network access or for specific network accesses.

objectives.text: a period of inactivity to terminate network connections associated with communications sessions is defined.
network connections associated with communications sessions are terminated at the end of the sessions.
network connections associated with communications sessions are terminated after the defined period of inactivity.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing network disconnect; system design documentation; system security plan; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; system developer
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing network disconnect capability

guidance.summary: Network connections must be torn down when a session ends or after a defined period of inactivity, so an abandoned session cannot be reused.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The VPN drops idle sessions after 30 minutes and forces reauthentication every 8 hours. RDP sessions to the file server disconnect after 15 minutes idle and are logged off after an hour. SSH on the Linux backup host uses ClientAliveInterval so dead sessions close automatically.
typical_evidence: VPN configuration showing idle and maximum session timeouts
Group Policy settings for Remote Desktop idle/disconnect limits (Bulwark check os.session.idle_timeout)
SSH server configuration with ClientAlive settings
Session termination settings in the ERP or cloud tenant
common_gaps: VPN sessions that stay up for days
RDP sessions left disconnected but active indefinitely
Cloud sessions with very long refresh-token lifetimes
remediation_steps: Set an idle timeout of 30 minutes or less and a maximum session lifetime on the VPN.
Configure Remote Desktop idle-session and disconnected-session limits by policy.
Set ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax on any SSH service.
Tune cloud session lifetimes and require reauthentication for risky sign-ins.
Verify the settings from a test session and record the result.

controls.name: Key Management
controls.statement: Establish and manage cryptographic keys for cryptography employed in organizational systems.
controls.discussion: Cryptographic key management and establishment can be performed using manual procedures or mechanisms supported by manual procedures. Organizations define key management requirements in accordance with applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, policies, directives, regulations, and standards specifying appropriate options, levels, and parameters.[SP 800-56A] and [SP 800-57-1] provide guidance on cryptographic key management and key establishment.

objectives.text: cryptographic keys are established whenever cryptography is employed.
cryptographic keys are managed whenever cryptography is employed.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing cryptographic key establishment and management; system security plan; system design documentation; cryptographic mechanisms; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel with responsibilities for cryptographic key establishment and management
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing cryptographic key establishment and management

guidance.summary: Cryptographic keys and certificates used in the system must be generated, stored, distributed, rotated and destroyed under a documented process. This includes BitLocker recovery keys, VPN certificates, SSH keys and TLS certificates.
guidance.machine_shop_example: BitLocker recovery keys escrow automatically into Entra ID and only the two admins can read them. VPN certificates are issued from the firewall's internal CA with a two-year life and revoked the day an employee leaves. TLS certificates for the ERP renew automatically with monitoring 30 days out, and the one SSH key pair for the backup job is stored in the password manager with a documented rotation date.
typical_evidence: Key management procedure covering generation, storage, distribution, rotation and destruction
BitLocker/FileVault recovery key escrow configuration and access restriction
Certificate inventory with issue and expiry dates and owners
Revocation record for a departed employee's certificate
Password manager or HSM record showing where private keys live
common_gaps: Recovery keys stored in a spreadsheet on the file server
Certificates that expire unnoticed and are reissued in a panic
Shared SSH keys with no owner and no rotation
No revocation step in the offboarding checklist
remediation_steps: Write a one-page key management procedure covering every key type you use.
Escrow disk-encryption recovery keys to Entra ID, Intune or an equivalent protected store.
Build a certificate inventory with expiry dates and set renewal alerts.
Add certificate and key revocation to the offboarding checklist.
Store private keys and recovery keys in a password manager with restricted access and audit logging.

controls.name: CUI Encryption
controls.statement: Employ FIPS-validated cryptography when used to protect the confidentiality of CUI.
controls.discussion: Cryptography can be employed to support many security solutions including the protection of controlled unclassified information, the provision of digital signatures, and the enforcement of information separation when authorized individuals have the necessary clearances for such information but lack the necessary formal access approvals. Cryptography can also be used to support random number generation and hash generation. Cryptographic standards include FIPSvalidated cryptography and/or NSA-approved cryptography. See [NIST CRYPTO]; [NIST CAVP]; and [NIST CMVP].

objectives.text: FIPS-validated cryptography is employed to protect the confidentiality of CUI.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing cryptographic protection; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; cryptographic module validation certificates; list of FIPS-validated cryptographic modules; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; system developer; personnel with responsibilities for cryptographic protection
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing cryptographic protection

partial_credit.condition: Encryption is employed to protect CUI but is not FIPS-validated

guidance.summary: Where you use cryptography to protect the confidentiality of CUI, it must be FIPS-validated: the module must appear on the NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program list and be operated in its validated (FIPS) mode. Merely 'using AES-256' is not enough; the module and its configuration matter. This requirement carries partial credit in DoD scoring: if encryption is used but is not FIPS-validated, 3 points are deducted instead of 5.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop runs BitLocker with the Windows cryptographic modules in FIPS mode (the Group Policy 'System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms' is enabled and the CMVP certificate numbers for the Windows build are recorded), uses GCC High whose services are FIPS-validated, and its firewall VPN runs in FIPS mode with the vendor's certificate number written into the SSP. The certificate numbers and validated versions are listed in an appendix so an assessor can check them.
typical_evidence: Table of every cryptographic module protecting CUI with its CMVP certificate number and validated version
Group Policy or configuration evidence that FIPS mode is enabled (Bulwark check os.crypto.fips_mode)
Vendor documentation or FedRAMP package confirming FIPS-validated modules
BitLocker/FileVault status output
Firewall/VPN configuration showing FIPS mode enabled
common_gaps: Using encryption that is strong but not FIPS-validated, or validated but not run in FIPS mode
No record of CMVP certificate numbers, so the claim cannot be verified
Consumer cloud storage or zip encryption used for CUI
Assuming 'AES-256' on a NAS or CNC controller is FIPS-validated
remediation_steps: List every place cryptography protects CUI: disks, file transfer, email, VPN, backups, removable media.
For each, find the CMVP certificate number for the exact module and version, and record it.
Enable FIPS mode where the platform supports it and confirm the application still works.
Replace any mechanism you cannot tie to a CMVP certificate with one you can.
Keep the module table current when you upgrade operating systems or appliances.
If a gap remains, record it on the POA&M: partial implementation deducts 3 points instead of 5.

controls.name: Collaborative Device Control
controls.statement: Prohibit remote activation of collaborative computing devices and provide indication of devices in use to users present at the device.
controls.discussion: Collaborative computing devices include networked white boards, cameras, and microphones. Indication of use includes signals to users when collaborative computing devices are activated. Dedicated video conferencing systems, which rely on one of the participants calling or connecting to the other party to activate the video conference, are excluded.

objectives.text: collaborative computing devices are identified.
collaborative computing devices provide indication to users of devices in use.
remote activation of collaborative computing devices is prohibited.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing collaborative computing; access control policy and procedures; system security plan; system design documentation; system audit logs and records; system configuration settings and associated documentation; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; system developer; personnel with responsibilities for managing collaborative computing devices
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing management of remote activation of collaborative computing devices; mechanisms providing an indication of use of collaborative computing devices

guidance.summary: Cameras and microphones on devices in the CUI environment must not activate remotely without the user knowing, and users must be able to tell when they are on. Indication and control matter more than banning the devices.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Laptops keep their camera indicator lights enabled, Teams shows an in-call indicator, and privacy shutters were issued for the two conference-room laptops. Policy forbids leaving a meeting connected in an unattended room, and the shop-floor tablet has its microphone disabled in device settings because nothing needs it.
typical_evidence: Policy statement covering cameras, microphones and collaborative devices
Device settings or MDM profile disabling unused cameras/microphones
Photograph or purchase record of privacy shutters
User training material covering meeting etiquette in areas where CUI is discussed
common_gaps: Conference-room systems that can be joined remotely without local indication
Smart speakers or assistants in areas where CUI is discussed
No policy at all, so there is nothing for an assessor to examine
remediation_steps: Write a short policy on collaborative computing devices in CUI areas.
Disable cameras and microphones that serve no business purpose through MDM or device settings.
Ensure indicators are enabled and issue privacy shutters where useful.
Remove consumer voice assistants from areas where CUI is discussed.
Cover the rules in annual awareness training.

controls.name: Mobile Code
controls.statement: Control and monitor the use of mobile code.
controls.discussion: Mobile code technologies include Java, JavaScript, ActiveX, Postscript, PDF, Flash animations, and VBScript. Decisions regarding the use of mobile code in organizational systems are based on the potential for the code to cause damage to the systems if used maliciously. Usage restrictions and implementation guidance apply to the selection and use of mobile code installed on servers and mobile code downloaded and executed on individual workstations, notebook computers, and devices (e.g., smart phones). Mobile code policy and procedures address controlling or preventing the development, acquisition, or introduction of unacceptable mobile code in systems, including requiring mobile code to be digitally signed by a trusted source. [SP 800-28] provides guidance on mobile code.

objectives.text: use of mobile code is controlled.
use of mobile code is monitored.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing mobile code; mobile code usage restrictions, mobile code implementation policy and procedures; system audit logs and records; system security plan; list of acceptable mobile code and mobile code technologies; list of unacceptable mobile code and mobile technologies; authorization records; system monitoring records; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel with responsibilities for managing mobile code
assessment.test: Organizational process for controlling, authorizing, monitoring, and restricting mobile code; mechanisms supporting or implementing the management of mobile code; mechanisms supporting or implementing the monitoring of mobile code

guidance.summary: Mobile code such as JavaScript, ActiveX, macros, Java applets and scripts must be controlled: decide what is allowed, and enforce it.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Office macros from the internet are blocked by policy and only macros signed by the shop's certificate run; the two legacy Excel quoting workbooks were signed after review. Browsers run with default script protections, Java was uninstalled from every PC, and PowerShell runs in Constrained Language Mode for standard users with script block logging on.
typical_evidence: Policy defining which mobile code is permitted and how it is approved
Group Policy or Intune settings blocking internet-sourced macros
Evidence that unused runtimes (Java, Flash, ActiveX) are removed (Bulwark check os.inventory.software)
Code-signing certificate and the list of signed internal macros
PowerShell logging configuration (Bulwark check os.audit.powershell_logging)
common_gaps: Macros enabled globally because one old spreadsheet needs them
Java or other legacy runtimes left installed and unpatched
No definition of acceptable mobile code, so nothing can be enforced
remediation_steps: Write a short acceptable-mobile-code statement covering macros, scripts and browser code.
Block macros in files from the internet and require signed macros for internal ones.
Uninstall unused runtimes and browser plug-ins.
Enable PowerShell script block logging and constrained language for standard users.
Review the exception list annually.

controls.name: Voice over Internet Protocol
controls.statement: Control and monitor the use of Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) technologies.
controls.discussion: VoIP has different requirements, features, functionality, availability, and service limitations when compared with the Plain Old Telephone Service (POTS) (i.e., the standard telephone service). In contrast, other telephone services are based on high-speed, digital communications lines, such as Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) and Fiber Distributed Data Interface (FDDI). The main distinctions between POTS and non-POTS services are speed and bandwidth. To address the threats associated with VoIP, usage restrictions and implementation guidelines are based on the potential for the VoIP technology to cause damage to the system if it is used maliciously. Threats to VoIP are similar to those inherent with any Internet-based application.[SP 800-58] provides guidance on Voice Over IP Systems.

objectives.text: use of Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) technologies is controlled.
use of Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) technologies is monitored.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing VoIP; VoIP usage restrictions; VoIP implementation guidance; system security plan; system design documentation; system audit logs and records; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system monitoring records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel with responsibilities for managing VoIP
assessment.test: Organizational process for authorizing, monitoring, and controlling VoIP; mechanisms supporting or implementing authorizing, monitoring, and controlling VoIP

guidance.summary: If you use VoIP, decide how it must be configured and used, and monitor it, because phone systems sit on the same network as everything else.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The hosted VoIP service is on its own VLAN, the admin portal uses MFA, default handset passwords were changed, SIP is restricted to the provider's addresses at the firewall, and call detail records are reviewed monthly for unexpected international calls. If VoIP were not in use, the SSP would say so and the requirement would be marked not applicable with that justification.
typical_evidence: VoIP usage policy and configuration standard
VLAN and firewall rules restricting SIP traffic
Evidence that default handset and portal credentials were changed
Monthly call-record review notes
If not applicable: an SSP statement that no VoIP is used
common_gaps: Handsets left on default passwords
SIP open to the internet, leading to toll fraud
VoIP admin portal without MFA
Marking the requirement not applicable while a softphone is in daily use
remediation_steps: Confirm whether VoIP or softphones are in use anywhere, including in the ERP or Teams.
Put voice traffic on its own VLAN and restrict SIP to the provider's addresses.
Change default credentials and enable MFA on the provider portal.
Review call records monthly for anomalies.
If genuinely unused, record the not-applicable justification in the SSP.

controls.name: Communications Authenticity
controls.statement: Protect the authenticity of communications sessions.
controls.discussion: Authenticity protection includes protecting against man-in-the-middle attacks, session hijacking, and the insertion of false information into communications sessions. This requirement addresses communications protection at the session versus packet level (e.g., sessions in service-oriented architectures providing web-based services) and establishes grounds for confidence at both ends of communications sessions in ongoing identities of other parties and in the validity of information transmitted.[SP 800-77], [SP 800-95], and [SP 800-113] provide guidance on secure communications sessions.

objectives.text: the authenticity of communications sessions is protected.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing session authenticity; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing session authenticity

guidance.summary: Protect the authenticity of communication sessions, so a session cannot be hijacked or spoofed. This is delivered by the protocols you choose: TLS with valid certificates, SMB signing, IPsec, DNSSEC where available, and session management that resists replay.
guidance.machine_shop_example: All internal file access uses SMB signing (required on both client and server), web applications use TLS 1.2+ with certificates from a trusted CA, the VPN uses IKEv2 with certificate authentication, and email authentication is enforced with SPF, DKIM and DMARC so spoofed messages are rejected.
typical_evidence: SMB signing configuration on servers and clients (Bulwark check os.crypto.smb_signing)
TLS configuration and certificate details for internal applications
VPN configuration showing certificate-based authentication
SPF, DKIM and DMARC DNS records and the DMARC report summary
Evidence that legacy protocols are disabled
common_gaps: SMB signing left optional so downgrade attacks are possible
Self-signed or expired certificates that train users to click through warnings
No DMARC policy, so the shop's domain can be spoofed
Pre-shared key VPNs shared among all users
remediation_steps: Require SMB signing on servers and workstations by policy.
Replace self-signed certificates with ones from a trusted CA and monitor expiry.
Move VPN authentication to certificates or EAP-TLS rather than shared keys.
Publish SPF, DKIM and DMARC records and move DMARC to quarantine or reject.
Disable legacy authentication protocols in the cloud tenant.

controls.name: Data at Rest
controls.statement: Protect the confidentiality of CUI at rest.
controls.discussion: Information at rest refers to the state of information when it is not in process or in transit and is located on storage devices as specific components of systems. The focus of protection at rest is not on the type of storage device or the frequency of access but rather the state of the information. Organizations can use different mechanisms to achieve confidentiality protections, including the use of cryptographic mechanisms and file share scanning. Organizations may also use other controls including secure off-line storage in lieu of online storage when adequate protection of information at rest cannot otherwise be achieved or continuous monitoring to identify malicious code at rest. See [NIST CRYPTO].

objectives.text: the confidentiality of CUI at rest is protected.

assessment.examine: System and communications protection policy; procedures addressing protection of information at rest; system security plan; system design documentation; list of information at rest requiring confidentiality protections; system configuration settings and associated documentation; cryptographic mechanisms and associated configuration documentation; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; system developer
assessment.test: Mechanisms supporting or implementing confidentiality protections for information at rest

guidance.summary: CUI stored on any device or medium must be protected, normally with encryption. That covers laptops, desktops, servers, backups, removable drives and mobile devices.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Every PC and laptop has BitLocker on with recovery keys escrowed to Entra ID, the file server's CUI volume is encrypted, backups are encrypted both in transit and at rest with keys held by the shop, and the two USB drives used for CNC program transfer are hardware-encrypted and inventoried. The CNC controllers, which cannot support encryption, hold no CUI at rest: programs are deleted at the end of each job under a documented procedure.
typical_evidence: Disk encryption status for every endpoint and server (Bulwark check os.disk.encryption)
Backup encryption configuration and key custody record
Inventory of encrypted removable media
Documented compensating procedure for devices that cannot be encrypted
Cloud tenant encryption-at-rest documentation
common_gaps: Servers left unencrypted because they are 'physically secure'
Backup drives taken home unencrypted
CUI copied to unencrypted USB sticks for the shop floor
Legacy equipment holding drawings with no compensating control
remediation_steps: Enable full-disk encryption on every endpoint and server and escrow the recovery keys.
Turn on encryption for backups and confirm you hold the keys.
Issue hardware-encrypted USB drives and inventory them; block all others.
For equipment that cannot encrypt, document the compensating controls and a deletion routine.
Verify encryption status continuously and treat any unencrypted device as a finding.

controls.name: Flaw Remediation
controls.statement: Identify, report, and correct system flaws in a timely manner.
controls.discussion: Organizations identify systems that are affected by announced software and firmware flaws including potential vulnerabilities resulting from those flaws and report this information to designated personnel with information security responsibilities. Security-relevant updates include patches, service packs, hot fixes, and anti-virus signatures. Organizations address flaws discovered during security assessments, continuous monitoring, incident response activities, and system error handling. Organizations can take advantage of available resources such as the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) database or Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) database in remediating flaws discovered in organizational systems. Organization-defined time periods for updating security-relevant software and firmware may vary based on a variety of factors including the criticality of the update (i.e., severity of the vulnerability related to the discovered flaw). Some types of flaw remediation may require more testing than other types of remediation.[SP 800-40] provides guidance on patch management technologies.

objectives.text: the time within which to identify system flaws is specified.
system flaws are identified within the specified time frame.
the time within which to report system flaws is specified.
system flaws are reported within the specified time frame.
the time within which to correct system flaws is specified.
system flaws are corrected within the specified time frame.

assessment.examine: System and information integrity policy; procedures addressing flaw remediation; procedures addressing configuration management; system security plan; list of flaws and vulnerabilities potentially affecting the system; list of recent security flaw remediation actions performed on the system (e.g., list of installed patches, service packs, hot fixes, and other software updates to correct system flaws); test results from the installation of software and firmware updates to correct system flaws; installation/change control records for security-relevant software and firmware updates; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel installing, configuring, and maintaining the system; personnel with responsibility for flaw remediation; personnel with configuration management responsibility
assessment.test: Organizational processes for identifying, reporting, and correcting system flaws; organizational process for installing software and firmware updates; mechanisms supporting or implementing reporting, and correcting system flaws; mechanisms supporting or implementing testing software and firmware updates

guidance.summary: Find, report and fix system flaws within timeframes you have defined in writing. The assessor checks three things: that you set the timeframes, that flaws are actually identified and reported inside them, and that they are corrected inside them. Patching is the main evidence.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's patch policy says critical and security updates are installed within 14 days of release and everything else within 30, with the MSP's RMM pushing Windows and third-party updates every Wednesday night. The monthly RMM report shows compliance per device, exceptions (the two CNC controllers on a vendor-approved firmware schedule) are documented, and anything that misses the window becomes a ticket.
typical_evidence: Written flaw remediation / patch management policy with defined timeframes
Monthly patch compliance report per device from the RMM or WSUS
Vulnerability scan reports showing findings and their closure dates
Ticket history for exceptions and late patches
Automated check evidence of last update and pending updates (Bulwark checks os.patch.last_update, os.patch.pending_updates)
common_gaps: No written timeframe, so 'timely' cannot be assessed
Servers or CNC controllers excluded from patching with no documented exception
Patches deployed but never verified, so failures go unnoticed
End-of-life operating systems that can no longer be patched
remediation_steps: Write the timeframes down: for example critical within 14 days, others within 30, with named approval for exceptions.
Enable automatic or RMM-managed patching for operating systems and third-party applications.
Produce a monthly compliance report and open tickets for every device that missed the window.
Document vendor-constrained systems (CNC controllers, test equipment) with their own schedule and compensating controls.
Replace or isolate systems whose vendor no longer issues security updates.
Track remaining gaps on the POA&M with dates.

controls.name: Malicious Code Protection
controls.statement: Provide protection from malicious code at designated locations within organizational systems.
controls.discussion: Designated locations include system entry and exit points which may include firewalls, remoteaccess servers, workstations, electronic mail servers, web servers, proxy servers, notebook computers, and mobile devices. Malicious code includes viruses, worms, Trojan horses, and spyware. Malicious code can be encoded in various formats (e.g., UUENCODE, Unicode), contained within compressed or hidden files, or hidden in files using techniques such as steganography. Malicious code can be inserted into systems in a variety of ways including web accesses, electronic mail, electronic mail attachments, and portable storage devices. Malicious code insertions occur through the exploitation of system vulnerabilities. Malicious code protection mechanisms include anti-virus signature definitions and reputationbased technologies. A variety of technologies and methods exist to limit or eliminate the effects of malicious code. Pervasive configuration management and comprehensive software integrity controls may be effective in preventing execution of unauthorized code. In addition to commercial off-the-shelf software, malicious code may also be present in custom-built software. This could include logic bombs, back doors, and other types of cyber-attacks that could affect organizational missions/business functions. Traditional malicious code protection mechanisms cannot always detect such code. In these situations, organizations rely instead on other safeguards including secure coding practices, configuration management and control, trusted procurement processes, and monitoring practices to help ensure that software does not perform functions other than the functions intended.[SP 800-83] provides guidance on malware incident prevention.

objectives.text: designated locations for malicious code protection are identified.
protection from malicious code at designated locations is provided.

assessment.examine: System and information integrity policy; configuration management policy and procedures; procedures addressing malicious code protection; records of malicious code protection updates; malicious code protection mechanisms; system security plan; system configuration settings and associated documentation; record of actions initiated by malicious code protection mechanisms in response to malicious code detection; scan results from malicious code protection mechanisms; system design documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel installing, configuring, and maintaining the system; personnel with responsibility for malicious code protection; personnel with configuration management responsibility
assessment.test: Organizational processes for employing, updating, and configuring malicious code protection mechanisms; organizational process for addressing false positives and resulting potential impact; mechanisms supporting or implementing employing, updating, and configuring malicious code protection mechanisms; mechanisms supporting or implementing malicious code scanning and subsequent actions

guidance.summary: Anti-malware protection must be running at the places you have designated: endpoints, servers, email and any gateway. Decide where protection belongs, then prove it is there and enabled.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint runs on all 25 PCs and the file server with real-time protection and tamper protection on, managed centrally so users cannot disable it. Email is filtered in the GCC High tenant. The two CNC controllers cannot run an agent, so they sit on a restricted VLAN with no internet access and USB media scanned on a standalone kiosk first, and this is documented as a compensating control.
typical_evidence: List of designated locations for malicious code protection
Central anti-malware console showing every endpoint protected and real-time protection on (Bulwark check os.malware.protection_enabled)
Email filtering configuration
Documented compensating controls for devices that cannot run an agent
Alert history showing detections and responses
common_gaps: Anti-malware installed but real-time protection disabled for performance on CAD machines
No central console, so nobody notices when an agent stops reporting
Shop-floor and legacy systems silently unprotected and undocumented
Free consumer antivirus with no management
remediation_steps: Designate in writing where malicious code protection is required.
Deploy a centrally managed anti-malware product to every endpoint and server and enable tamper protection.
Turn on email and web filtering at the gateway or in the cloud tenant.
For devices that cannot run an agent, document the compensating controls: network isolation, media scanning, allow-listing.
Alert on agents that stop reporting and treat them as incidents.
Review detections monthly.

controls.name: Security Alerts & Advisories
controls.statement: Monitor system security alerts and advisories and take action in response.
controls.discussion: There are many publicly available sources of system security alerts and advisories. For example, the Department of Homeland Security’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) generates security alerts and advisories to maintain situational awareness across the federal government and in nonfederal organizations. Software vendors, subscription services, and industry information sharing and analysis centers (ISACs) may also provide security alerts and advisories. Examples of response actions include notifying relevant external organizations, for example, external mission/business partners, supply chain partners, external service providers, and peer or supporting organizations[SP 800-161] provides guidance on supply chain risk management.

objectives.text: response actions to system security alerts and advisories are identified.
system security alerts and advisories are monitored.
actions in response to system security alerts and advisories are taken.

assessment.examine: System and information integrity policy; procedures addressing security alerts, advisories, and directives; system security plan; records of security alerts and advisories; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: Personnel with security alert and advisory responsibilities; personnel implementing, operating, maintaining, and using the system; personnel, organizational elements, and external organizations to whom alerts, advisories, and directives are to be disseminated; system or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities
assessment.test: Organizational processes for defining, receiving, generating, disseminating, and complying with security alerts, advisories, and directives; mechanisms supporting or implementing definition, receipt, generation, and dissemination of security alerts, advisories, and directives; mechanisms supporting or implementing security directives

guidance.summary: Monitor security alerts and advisories from credible sources and act on them. Someone must be subscribed, someone must read them, and there must be a record of what you did when one applied to you.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The IT person subscribes to CISA alerts, the Microsoft security update guide and the firewall vendor's advisories, and the MSP forwards anything relevant. Each advisory that applies is logged in a simple register with the date received, affected systems, action taken and date closed. When the firewall vendor published a critical advisory, the register shows the firmware was applied within three days.
typical_evidence: Subscription evidence (CISA, vendor bulletins, ISAC membership)
Advisory register showing received, assessed, action taken and closed dates
Sample advisory with the resulting change ticket
Procedure naming who monitors advisories and how they are dispositioned
Internal notification to staff when user action was required
common_gaps: Alerts delivered to a mailbox nobody reads
No record connecting an advisory to the action taken
Relying entirely on the MSP with nothing in writing about who is responsible
Advisories tracked informally in email threads
remediation_steps: Subscribe to CISA advisories and the vendor bulletins for every product in the boundary.
Name the person responsible for monitoring and a backup.
Keep a simple advisory register with dates and dispositions.
Tie applicable advisories to change tickets so remediation is evidenced.
Define how internal alerts reach staff when user action is needed.
Review the register quarterly.

controls.name: Update Malicious Code Protection
controls.statement: Update malicious code protection mechanisms when new releases are available.
controls.discussion: Malicious code protection mechanisms include anti-virus signature definitions and reputationbased technologies. A variety of technologies and methods exist to limit or eliminate the effects of malicious code. Pervasive configuration management and comprehensive software integrity controls may be effective in preventing execution of unauthorized code. In addition to commercial off-the-shelf software, malicious code may also be present in custom-built software. This could include logic bombs, back doors, and other types of cyber-attacks that could affect organizational missions/business functions. Traditional malicious code protection mechanisms cannot always detect such code. In these situations, organizations rely instead on other safeguards including secure coding practices, configuration management and control, trusted procurement processes, and monitoring practices to help ensure that software does not perform functions other than the functions intended.

objectives.text: malicious code protection mechanisms are updated when new releases are available.

assessment.examine: System and information integrity policy; configuration management policy and procedures; procedures addressing malicious code protection; malicious code protection mechanisms; records of malicious code protection updates; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; scan results from malicious code protection mechanisms; record of actions initiated by malicious code protection mechanisms in response to malicious code detection; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel installing, configuring, and maintaining the system; personnel with responsibility for malicious code protection; personnel with configuration management responsibility
assessment.test: Organizational processes for employing, updating, and configuring malicious code protection mechanisms; organizational process for addressing false positives and resulting potential impact; mechanisms supporting or implementing malicious code protection mechanisms (including updates and configurations); mechanisms supporting or implementing malicious code scanning and subsequent actions

guidance.summary: Anti-malware definitions and engines must be updated whenever new releases are available. This is mostly about proving updates actually land on every device, including ones that are rarely online.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Defender definitions update automatically several times a day; the console flags any device whose signatures are more than three days old, and the weekly report shows all devices current. A CAD laptop that had been off for two weeks showed up in the report, was updated on its return, and the ticket is retained.
typical_evidence: Anti-malware console report showing signature age per device (Bulwark check os.malware.signatures_current)
Configuration showing automatic definition updates enabled
Exception report and remediation tickets for stale devices
Engine version report after a major product update
common_gaps: Laptops that are rarely connected drifting months out of date
Update source blocked by firewall rules for isolated segments
No alerting on stale signatures
remediation_steps: Enable automatic definition and engine updates on every endpoint.
Alert when signatures exceed a defined age, for example three days.
Allow the update source through the firewall for isolated segments or provide an internal distribution point.
Check the console weekly and remediate stale devices.
Record the review so there is evidence it happens.

controls.name: System & File Scanning
controls.statement: Perform periodic scans of organizational systems and real-time scans of files from external sources as files are downloaded, opened, or executed.
controls.discussion: Periodic scans of organizational systems and real-time scans of files from external sources can detect malicious code. Malicious code can be encoded in various formats (e.g., UUENCODE, Unicode), contained within compressed or hidden files, or hidden in files using techniques such as steganography. Malicious code can be inserted into systems in a variety of ways including web accesses, electronic mail, electronic mail attachments, and portable storage devices. Malicious code insertions occur through the exploitation of system vulnerabilities.

objectives.text: the frequency for malicious code scans is defined.
malicious code scans are performed with the defined frequency.
real-time malicious code scans of files from external sources as files are downloaded, opened, or executed are performed.

assessment.examine: System and information integrity policy; configuration management policy and procedures; procedures addressing malicious code protection; malicious code protection mechanisms; records of malicious code protection updates; system security plan; system design documentation; system configuration settings and associated documentation; scan results from malicious code protection mechanisms; record of actions initiated by malicious code protection mechanisms in response to malicious code detection; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel installing, configuring, and maintaining the system; personnel with responsibility for malicious code protection; personnel with configuration management responsibility
assessment.test: Organizational processes for employing, updating, and configuring malicious code protection mechanisms; organizational process for addressing false positives and resulting potential impact; mechanisms supporting or implementing malicious code protection mechanisms (including updates and configurations); mechanisms supporting or implementing malicious code scanning and subsequent actions

guidance.summary: Run periodic scans of your systems and real-time scans of files from external sources as they are downloaded, opened or executed. Define the frequency, then show the scans happen.
guidance.machine_shop_example: A weekly full scan runs Saturday night on every PC and the server, with real-time scanning on for downloads, email attachments and removable media. The console shows the last scan time per device; devices that miss two consecutive scans generate a ticket. USB drives brought in by customers are scanned on a standalone kiosk before use.
typical_evidence: Scan schedule configuration and the defined frequency in policy
Console report of last scan time per device (Bulwark check os.malware.last_scan)
Real-time protection settings covering downloads and removable media
Procedure for scanning incoming removable media
Scan results showing detections and their disposition
common_gaps: Scheduled scans disabled because they slow CAM workstations
Real-time scanning exclusions added broadly, for example the whole jobs folder
No defined frequency in writing
Customer USB drives plugged straight into shop-floor PCs
remediation_steps: Write the scan frequency into policy, for example weekly full plus continuous real-time.
Schedule scans outside production hours and verify they complete.
Review and minimise scan exclusions; document any that remain and why.
Set up a scanning routine or kiosk for incoming removable media.
Alert on devices that miss consecutive scans.

controls.name: Monitor Communications for Attacks
controls.statement: Monitor organizational systems, including inbound and outbound communications traffic, to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks.
controls.discussion: System monitoring includes external and internal monitoring. External monitoring includes the observation of events occurring at the system boundary (i.e., part of perimeter defense and boundary protection). Internal monitoring includes the observation of events occurring within the system. Organizations can monitor systems, for example, by observing audit record activities in real time or by observing other system aspects such as access patterns, characteristics of access, and other actions. The monitoring objectives may guide determination of the events. System monitoring capability is achieved through a variety of tools and techniques (e.g., intrusion detection systems, intrusion prevention systems, malicious code protection software, scanning tools, audit record monitoring software, network monitoring software). Strategic locations for monitoring devices include selected perimeter locations and near server farms supporting critical applications, with such devices being employed at managed system interfaces. The granularity of monitoring information collected is based on organizational monitoring objectives and the capability of systems to support such objectives. System monitoring is an integral part of continuous monitoring and incident response programs. Output from system monitoring serves as input to continuous monitoring and incident response programs. A network connection is any connection with a device that communicates through a network (e.g., local area network, Internet). A remote connection is any connection with a device communicating through an external network (e.g., the Internet). Local, network, and remote connections can be either wired or wireless. Unusual or unauthorized activities or conditions related to inbound/outbound communications traffic include internal traffic that indicates the presence of malicious code in systems or propagating among system components, the unauthorized exporting of information, or signaling to external systems. Evidence of malicious code is used to identify potentially compromised systems or system components. System monitoring requirements, including the need for specific types of system monitoring, may be referenced in other requirements.[SP 800-94] provides guidance on intrusion detection and prevention systems.

objectives.text: the system is monitored to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks.
inbound communications traffic is monitored to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks.
outbound communications traffic is monitored to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks.

assessment.examine: System and information integrity policy; procedures addressing system monitoring tools and techniques; continuous monitoring strategy; system and information integrity policy; procedures addressing system monitoring tools and techniques; facility diagram or layout; system security plan; system monitoring tools and techniques documentation; system design documentation; locations within system where monitoring devices are deployed; system protocols; system configuration settings and associated documentation; system audit logs and records; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel installing, configuring, and maintaining the system; personnel with responsibility monitoring the system; personnel with responsibility for the intrusion detection system
assessment.test: Organizational processes for system monitoring; mechanisms supporting or implementing intrusion detection capability and system monitoring; mechanisms supporting or implementing system monitoring capability; organizational processes for intrusion detection and system monitoring; mechanisms supporting or implementing the monitoring of inbound and outbound communications traffic

guidance.summary: Monitor the system, including inbound and outbound traffic, to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks. Somebody or something must be watching, and there must be evidence of that watching.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The firewall's IPS is enabled in blocking mode on the internet edge, its logs and the endpoint detection alerts flow to the MSP's monitoring service, and the MSP reviews and triages alerts 24/7 with monthly reports to the owner. Outbound traffic is inspected for known command-and-control destinations, and the monthly report lists what was detected and what was done.
typical_evidence: IPS/IDS configuration on the boundary device
SIEM or managed detection service configuration and coverage list
Monthly monitoring report with alerts and dispositions
Contract or statement of work showing the MSSP's monitoring responsibilities
Endpoint detection and response console showing alert history
common_gaps: Logs collected but no alerting or review
Only inbound traffic watched, with outbound ignored
MSP assumed to be monitoring with nothing in the contract saying so
Alerts going to an unmonitored shared mailbox
remediation_steps: Enable IPS on the boundary firewall and put it in blocking mode after tuning.
Forward firewall, endpoint and server logs to a SIEM or managed detection service.
Define which alerts require action and who responds, including out of hours.
Get monitoring responsibilities written into the MSP or MSSP contract and reflected in the responsibility matrix.
Review the monthly report with the owner and keep it as evidence.
Monitor outbound traffic for command-and-control and data-exfiltration indicators.

controls.name: Identify Unauthorized Use
controls.statement: Identify unauthorized use of organizational systems.
controls.discussion: System monitoring includes external and internal monitoring. System monitoring can detect unauthorized use of organizational systems. System monitoring is an integral part of continuous monitoring and incident response programs. Monitoring is achieved through a variety of tools and techniques (e.g., intrusion detection systems, intrusion prevention systems, malicious code protection software, scanning tools, audit record monitoring software, network monitoring software). Output from system monitoring serves as input to continuous monitoring and incident response programs. Unusual/unauthorized activities or conditions related to inbound and outbound communications traffic include internal traffic that indicates the presence of malicious code in systems or propagating among system components, the unauthorized exporting of information, or signaling to external systems. Evidence of malicious code is used to identify potentially compromised systems or system components. System monitoring requirements, including the need for specific types of system monitoring, may be referenced in other requirements.[SP 800-94] provides guidance on intrusion detection and prevention systems.

objectives.text: authorized use of the system is defined.
unauthorized use of the system is identified.

assessment.examine: Continuous monitoring strategy; system and information integrity policy; procedures addressing system monitoring tools and techniques; facility diagram/layout; system security plan; system design documentation; system monitoring tools and techniques documentation; locations within system where monitoring devices are deployed; system configuration settings and associated documentation; other relevant documents or records
assessment.interview: System or network administrators; personnel with information security responsibilities; personnel installing, configuring, and maintaining the system; personnel with responsibility for monitoring the system
assessment.test: Organizational processes for system monitoring; mechanisms supporting or implementing system monitoring capability

guidance.summary: Define what authorized use of your system looks like, then be able to spot use that falls outside it: unusual logons, unexpected software, data moving where it should not, accounts doing things they never do.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The acceptable use policy defines authorized use, and the monitoring stack backs it up: alerts fire on logons outside working hours from the shop's accounts, on new admin group membership, on USB mass-storage use, and on large downloads from SharePoint. The IT person reviews the weekly exception report; when an estimator downloaded 400 drawings at 11 pm, the alert triggered a conversation and a documented outcome the same week.
typical_evidence: Acceptable use policy defining authorized use
Alert rules for anomalous logons, privilege changes and large data transfers
Weekly or monthly exception review records
Example investigation with its outcome
